004.name: Afghanistan

word.meaning: "Thank you" in Dari, one of Afghanistan's two main languages along with Pashto, where it's "manana." Afghan hospitality is famous, and you'll say it often: for tea, for bread, for a second helping you didn't ask for.

004.ask: Ask how their family makes Kabuli palaw, rice with lamb, carrots and raisins, and whose version is the best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: the national team's rise from refugee camps to beating England, Pakistan and Australia at world tournaments is a huge source of joy. Asking about Rashid Khan is an easy way in.

Poetry: many Afghans quote Rumi and Hafez from memory, and people who love Rumi in English translation often find they share favorite lines.

Kites: kite flying and kite fighting, famous from The Kite Runner, is a childhood memory for many Afghans, and a fun story to trade.

cards.title: This season: pomegranates
cards.text: In autumn, the orchards of Kandahar are harvested for their famous pomegranates, large, deep red and full of sweet-tart juice. Markets pile up with them, and they're eaten fresh, pressed into juice and sprinkled over dishes.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its poetry, from Rumi, traditionally said to be from Balkh, to the landays of Pashto women. Its hospitality. And its fruits: pomegranates, grapes, melons, apricots and mulberries.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The rubab, a short-necked lute carved from a single piece of mulberry wood, is the national instrument; UNESCO lists the craft of making and playing it as heritage. Homayoun Sakhi, one of its great masters, plays its bright, ringing sound around the world.

links.label: The Art of the Afghan Rubâb, Homayun Sakhi

cards.title: Craft: Istalif pottery
cards.text: In the village of Istalif, north of Kabul, potters make bowls, plates and jugs glazed in a deep turquoise blue, a craft passed down for centuries.

cards.title: Creature: Afghan hound
cards.text: An ancient hunting dog of the mountains, tall and graceful, with a long, silky coat that kept it warm in the cold and a curl at the tip of its tail.

cards.title: Place: Band-e Amir
cards.text: A chain of six lakes of astonishing deep blue, held back by natural walls of travertine, in the mountains of Bamyan. It was the country's first national park.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kabuli palaw. Mantu, steamed dumplings with yogurt and lentil sauce. Bolani, flatbread stuffed with potato or leeks. And sheer yakh, rosewater ice cream.

008.name: Albania

word.meaning: A sacred promise of honor. Giving your besa means you'll keep your word and protect anyone in your care, whatever it costs. It's one of the oldest and most important values in Albanian life.

008.ask: Ask about the family's village and what their grandparents grew or made there, and whether they still go back in summer.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Coffee as an event: Albanians can spend hours over one coffee with friends, and an invitation to sit and talk is a real welcome.

Italian TV and music: many Albanians grew up secretly watching Italian television across the Adriatic and speak some Italian, so Italian food and films are easy shared ground.

Dua Lipa and Rita Ora: pop stars with Albanian roots from Kosovo, and a point of pride for Albanians everywhere.

cards.title: This season: Flag Day
cards.text: On November 28, Albania celebrates its Flag Day and independence: on that day in 1912, Ismail Qemali declared independence in the port city of Vlorë and raised the red flag with the black double-headed eagle. Streets and balconies are hung with flags, and there are parades, concerts and celebrations.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its besa during World War II: Albanians sheltered Jewish refugees in their homes, and the country ended the war with more Jews than at its start. And its hospitality, mountains and a coast along the Adriatic and Ionian seas.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the south, men and women sing iso-polyphony: several voices weave melodies over a steady drone, the iso, sung by the group. UNESCO lists it as heritage. In the north, singers accompany epic songs on the lahuta, a one-stringed fiddle.

cards.title: Craft: the qeleshe
cards.text: The white felt cap of Albanian men, made from sheep's wool, rounded or tall and conical depending on the region. Felt makers in towns like Krujë still shape them by hand.

cards.title: Creature: Dalmatian pelican
cards.text: One of the largest birds that can fly, with a wingspan over three meters, a silvery-white plumage and a curly crest. It nests in the Divjaka-Karavasta lagoon on Albania's coast.

cards.title: Place: Berat
cards.text: "The city of a thousand windows," with white Ottoman houses stacked up the hillside below a castle, their windows looking over the river. Together with Gjirokastër, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tavë kosi, baked lamb with rice and yogurt. Byrek, flaky pastry with spinach, cheese or meat. And fërgesë, peppers, tomatoes and cottage cheese cooked together.

012.name: Algeria

word.meaning: The Algerian way to say "hey, what's up?" ("wesh, labas?"), from the Algerian Arabic word for "what." It's so much a part of everyday speech that it has crossed into French slang too.

012.ask: Ask which couscous their family makes, and for which occasions: with lamb and vegetables, with fish by the sea, or sweet, with raisins and butter.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Algerians are passionate about their national team, the Fennecs, and their 2019 Africa Cup of Nations win. Zinedine Zidane, whose parents were Algerian, is widely loved.

Raï and Khaled: "Aïcha" and "Didi" are songs many people around the world know without knowing they're Algerian.

Couscous on Fridays: many Algerian families gather for a big couscous on Friday, a family meal that's easy to relate to Sunday dinners elsewhere.

cards.title: This season: the date harvest
cards.text: In October and November, the oases of the Algerian Sahara harvest their dates. Around Biskra and Tolga, climbers go up the palms to cut heavy bunches of Deglet Nour, the translucent, honey-colored "date of light," which is picked, sorted and packed for tables across the country and the world.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its size and its beauty: Algeria is the largest country in Africa, stretching from the Mediterranean coast over the mountains to the deep Sahara. And its independence, won in 1962 after a long struggle.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Raï, born in the port city of Oran, started as a voice of young people singing about love, freedom and everyday life, and became a worldwide sound; Khaled, "the King of Raï," had hits across Europe and beyond with songs like "Aïcha." Its roots include chaâbi, the popular music of Algiers's old Casbah, and the Arab-Andalusian tradition.

cards.title: Craft: Kabyle silver jewelry
cards.text: In the mountain villages of Kabylie, especially Beni Yenni, silversmiths make bold jewelry set with red coral and enameled in blue, green and yellow: brooches, bracelets and head pieces handed down through families and worn at weddings.

cards.title: Creature: Algerian nuthatch
cards.text: A small bird found only in a few mountain oak and cedar forests of Kabylie, and first described by scientists only in 1976. It creeps headfirst down tree trunks looking for insects.

cards.title: Place: Tassili n'Ajjer
cards.text: A high sandstone plateau in the Sahara, carved by wind into stone forests and arches, with more than 15,000 rock paintings and engravings of giraffes, cattle, hunters and dancers from a time when the Sahara was green. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Couscous, which UNESCO lists as the shared heritage of the Maghreb. Chakhchoukha, torn flatbread in a spicy tomato stew. Mhajeb, stuffed griddle pancakes sold on the street. And makroud, semolina cakes filled with dates.

024.name: Angola

word.meaning: "Friend" in Angolan Portuguese, borrowed from Kimbundu. "O meu kamba" is my friend, my buddy, and "kambas" are the people you go out dancing with.

024.ask: Ask who in their family dances the best kizomba, and who taught them.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Kizomba: the dance is taught in studios worldwide, so anyone who has taken a kizomba class has something to talk about with Angolans.

Basketball: Angola has long been one of Africa's strongest basketball nations, and fans follow the NBA closely.

Portuguese language and Brazilian soap operas: many Angolans grew up on Brazilian telenovelas and music, a shared world for anyone who knows Brazil.

cards.title: This season: Independence Day
cards.text: On November 11, Angola celebrates its independence, won in 1975. There are concerts, parades and parties, with semba and kizomba playing late into the night along the Marginal, Luanda's seafront.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music and dance: semba, kizomba and kuduro were all born in Angola. And O Pensador, "the Thinker," a Chokwe carving of a seated figure with its head in its hands, a national symbol.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Semba, lively and full of storytelling, is the root of much Angolan music, and it grew into kizomba, the slow, close couples' dance now danced around the world. Bonga's first album, recorded in 1972, became a soundtrack of Angola's hopes for independence. Kuduro, fast and electronic, came out of Luanda in the 1990s.

cards.title: Craft: Chokwe carving
cards.text: Chokwe sculptors in the northeast carve wooden masks, chairs and figures. The best known is the Pensador, copied in wood and stone and found in homes across the country.

cards.title: Creature: giant sable antelope
cards.text: The palanca negra gigante, a glossy black antelope with enormous sweeping horns, found only in Angola. It was feared lost after the civil war, until cameras found survivors in 2005. It's a national symbol, and the national football team is named for it.

cards.title: Place: Kalandula Falls
cards.text: On the Lucala River, water pours over a horseshoe-shaped cliff more than 100 meters high and some 400 meters wide, one of the biggest waterfalls in Africa.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Moamba de galinha, chicken stewed in palm oil and okra, with funje, a smooth cassava porridge. Calulu, dried fish stewed with vegetables. And grilled fish on the beach.

031.name: Azerbaijan

word.meaning: "Enjoy!" Said to someone eating or drinking, it literally wishes that the food be sweet and good for them. Azerbaijanis say it at every table, and the guest might answer "sağ ol," thank you.

031.ask: Ask which jam they like with their tea: cherry, quince, fig, even white cherry or rose petal. Tea comes in pear-shaped armudu glasses, and jam is often eaten by the spoonful alongside it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tea: long tea sessions with jam and sweets are central to hospitality, and a shared love of tea is an easy bond.

Chess: Azerbaijan has produced world-class players, and chess is widely played and followed.

Wrestling and football: Azerbaijanis follow wrestling and football closely, and Baku hosted Euro 2020 games.

cards.title: This season: the pomegranate festival
cards.text: Every autumn, usually in early November, the town of Goychay celebrates its pomegranate harvest with a festival of music, dance, crafts and tables piled with fruit, juice and narsharab, a tangy pomegranate sauce. UNESCO lists Azerbaijan's traditions of growing, cooking and sharing pomegranates as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "The Land of Fire," named for its natural gas flames that have burned from the ground for centuries, like the hillside fire at Yanar Dag. And its poets, above all Nizami Ganjavi, whose 12th-century love stories are known across the Persian-speaking world and beyond.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Mugham is the classical heart of Azerbaijani music: long, improvised songs of love and longing sung over the tar, a long-necked lute, and the kamancha, a spiked fiddle. UNESCO lists it as heritage, and Alim Qasimov is one of its greatest living voices. For the modern bridge, pianist Vagif Mustafazadeh fused mugham with jazz in the 1960s and 70s.

links.label: The Art of Mugham, Alim Qasimov

cards.title: Craft: carpets
cards.text: Azerbaijani weavers knot and weave carpets in regional styles, each with its own patterns, colors and symbols, from Guba to Karabakh and Shirvan. UNESCO lists the carpet weaving tradition as heritage, and Baku has a carpet museum in a building shaped like a rolled-up carpet.

cards.title: Creature: goitered gazelle
cards.text: The jeyran, a slender desert gazelle whose throat swells in the breeding season, once nearly vanished from Azerbaijan. Shirvan National Park helped bring it back, and today herds graze its semi-desert plains.

cards.title: Place: the Old City of Baku
cards.text: Icheri Sheher, the walled old town on the Caspian Sea, with narrow lanes, caravanserais, the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, and the mysterious Maiden Tower, whose origins are still debated. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Plov, the rice dish at every celebration, like shah plov baked in a crust of lavash. Dolma, grape or cabbage leaves stuffed with meat and rice. And qutab, thin griddled flatbreads filled with greens, pumpkin or meat.

032.name: Argentina

word.meaning: The time spent lingering at the table after a meal, talking, laughing, sharing mate or coffee, long after the plates are empty. In Argentina, the sobremesa after a Sunday asado can last longer than the meal.

032.ask: Ask how they take their mate, the bitter herbal tea shared from one gourd and passed around the circle, and who in their family is the cebador, the one who pours for everyone.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football and Messi: the 2022 World Cup win is a shared joy, and talking about Messi or Maradona opens almost any conversation.

The asado: a long weekend barbecue with family and friends is a ritual many people everywhere recognize and love.

Mate and conversation: sharing mate, passed around one cup, is about taking time for friends, like sharing a pot of coffee or tea.

cards.title: This season: jacarandas and gauchos
cards.text: It's spring. In November, Buenos Aires turns violet as its jacaranda trees bloom along the avenues and parks. And on November 10, the Día de la Tradición honors the gaucho, the horseman of the pampas; in San Antonio de Areco, the most gaucho of towns, the celebrations end with a parade of riders in their best ponchos and silver.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Football, and the joy of Lionel Messi lifting the World Cup in 2022, Argentina's third title. And tango, born in the port neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, now danced all over the world and listed by UNESCO as heritage.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Tango grew from the mix of European immigrants, Afro-Argentine rhythms and the milonga, with the bandoneón, a squeezebox brought from Germany, at its heart. Astor Piazzolla transformed it into nuevo tango, and "Adiós Nonino," written for his father, is its most beloved piece. In the northwest, folklore lives in the zamba and chacarera, and Mercedes Sosa became its great voice. For the modern bridge, Bajofondo, led by the Oscar-winning Gustavo Santaolalla, mixes tango with electronic beats; their album Presente won a Latin Grammy.

cards.title: Craft: filete porteño
cards.text: Buenos Aires' own painting style: swirling scrolls, acanthus leaves, flowers, ribbons and elegant lettering in bright colors, with a clever saying or proverb in the middle. It began on horse-drawn delivery wagons around 1900, painted by Italian immigrants, and spread to buses, trucks and shop signs. UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2015.

cards.title: Creature: southern right whale
cards.text: From June to December, southern right whales gather in the calm bays of Península Valdés in Patagonia to give birth and nurse their calves, and September and October are the peak. You can watch them breach and roll from the shore. The peninsula is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Place: Iguazú Falls
cards.text: On the border with Brazil, the Iguazú River drops over a horseshoe of about 275 waterfalls, and a walkway takes you right to the edge of the Devil's Throat, where the roar and spray are overwhelming. The national park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: The asado, beef and sausages grilled slowly over wood embers by the asador, the person trusted with the fire, and served with chimichurri. Empanadas, each province with its own recipe. And dulce de leche, slow-cooked milk caramel, sandwiched between two cookies to make alfajores.

036.name: Australia

word.meaning: In Australian English, to "have a yarn" is to have a good long chat. For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, yarning means more: a respectful, unhurried way of talking together, sharing stories and knowledge, where everyone gets heard.

036.ask: Ask what their family does on Christmas Day, which falls in summer: a barbecue, a swim at the beach, backyard cricket, or all three.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Beaches and the outdoors: surfing, swimming, camping and bushwalking are everyday joys, and many Australians love talking about their favorite spots.

Backyard barbecues: the weekend "barbie" with friends and a sausage sizzle outside the hardware store on Saturdays are rituals Australians love explaining.

Banter: Australians love gentle teasing and nicknames, and being able to laugh at yourself goes a long way.

cards.title: This season: the red crab migration
cards.text: On Christmas Island, an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, the first heavy rains of the wet season, usually in October or November, send somewhere between 40 and 50 million red crabs marching out of the forest to the sea to breed. Roads close, bridges are built for them, and for days the island turns red. Their spawning follows the phases of the moon, and early November is one of the likely times this year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on this continent for at least 65,000 years, making theirs among the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth, with hundreds of languages and a deep knowledge of Country passed on through song, story and art.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: For tens of thousands of years, songs have carried law, knowledge and the map of the land; in Arnhem Land, the Yolŋu play the yidaki, the instrument often called the didgeridoo. Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu, a blind Yolŋu singer from Elcho Island, sang in his own language with a voice that stopped listeners in their tracks, and his 2008 album Gurrumul went triple platinum in Australia.

cards.title: Craft: Western Desert painting
cards.text: In 1971, at Papunya in the Northern Territory, Aboriginal men began painting their Dreaming stories in acrylic on boards, and later canvas, using dots, circles and lines drawn from ancient ground and body designs. The movement they began, and the art centers it inspired across the desert, became one of the great art movements of the 20th century.

cards.title: Creature: platypus
cards.text: A furry, egg-laying mammal with a bill like a duck's, webbed feet and, in males, venomous spurs, which finds its food underwater with its eyes closed by sensing electrical signals. The first specimen sent to Britain was thought to be a hoax.

cards.title: Place: Uluṟu
cards.text: The great red rock rising from the desert in the heart of the continent, sacred to the Aṉangu people, who were handed back title to the land in 1985 and manage the national park jointly. Climbing it has been banned since 2019 out of respect; walking around its base, you see caves, waterholes and rock art. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: The meat pie, eaten at the footy with tomato sauce. Lamingtons, squares of sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut. And Vegemite on buttered toast, spread thin: a taste many Australians grow up with and visitors find very surprising.

040.name: Austria

word.meaning: An Austrian snack break, morning or afternoon: bread with cheese, cured ham and pickles on a wooden board, or coffee and a slice of cake. Hikers stop for a Jause at mountain huts, and families gather for one on Sunday afternoons.

040.ask: Ask which Viennese coffeehouse is their favorite, what they order there, and how long they think it's fine to sit over a single coffee. (The answer is usually "as long as you like.")

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Coffeehouses: sitting for hours over one coffee and a newspaper in a Viennese café is a pleasure anyone who loves a good café understands.

Skiing and hiking: many Austrians grow up on skis and in the mountains, and love to share favorite trails and slopes.

The Sound of Music: Austrians find its fame abroad funny and charming, and a visit to Salzburg is a good story to trade.

cards.title: This season: Krampus and the Christmas markets
cards.text: On the evening of December 5, St. Nicholas visits children with small gifts, and in Alpine towns the Krampus runs: masked, horned, furry figures with bells and switches parading through the streets to scare (and thrill) the crowds. From mid-November, Christmas markets fill squares from Vienna to Salzburg with carved ornaments, roasted chestnuts and mugs of Punsch.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music, from Mozart, Haydn and Schubert to the Strauss waltzes played at Vienna's New Year's Concert. And Vienna's coffeehouses, where people have read newspapers, written and argued for centuries; UNESCO lists Viennese coffeehouse culture as heritage.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Vienna gave the world its great classical music, and also the Wienerlied, the city's own folk song, bittersweet and funny, played in wine taverns on the city's edge with violin, accordion and guitar. For the modern bridge, Ernst Molden sings Wienerlied-style songs in Viennese dialect mixed with blues and folk.

cards.title: Craft: Viennese petit point
cards.text: Tiny, dense needlepoint, with sometimes more than a thousand stitches per square centimeter, made in Vienna since the 1700s for handbags, boxes and pictures of flowers and figures. It takes a magnifying glass and enormous patience.

cards.title: Creature: Alpine marmot
cards.text: A plump, burrowing rodent of the high meadows, which whistles loudly to warn the colony of danger and sleeps through the long winter underground.

cards.title: Place: Hallstatt
cards.text: A village of old wooden houses crowded between a steep mountain and a clear lake, where people have mined salt for about 7,000 years. The Hallstatt-Dachstein landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Wiener Schnitzel, thin, breaded and fried until golden. Sachertorte, dark chocolate cake with apricot jam, and Kaiserschmarrn, torn, fluffy pancake with plum compote. And at Christmas, crescent-shaped vanilla cookies, Vanillekipferl.

044.name: Bahamas

word.meaning: Gossip, the juicy news of the neighborhood. "What's the sip sip?" asks what's going on, and on small islands, the sip sip travels fast.

044.ask: Ask which Junkanoo group they rush with or cheer for, and whether they've ever helped build a costume.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Junkanoo: the Boxing Day and New Year's parades are the high point of the year, much like a favorite parade or carnival elsewhere.

Sports: Bahamians are proud of their Olympic sprinters, like Shaunae Miller-Uibo, and follow the NBA closely.

Fishing and boating: many Bahamians grow up on the water, fishing, sailing and island-hopping.

cards.title: This season: Junkanoo shacks
cards.text: All through autumn, Junkanoo groups work in secret in their "shacks," building huge, glittering costumes and floats out of cardboard, wire and crepe paper. Their big day comes on Boxing Day, December 26, and again on New Year's Day, when they "rush" down Bay Street in Nassau before dawn with goatskin drums, cowbells and horns.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Junkanoo, the heart of Bahamian culture. Its clear turquoise water, around some 700 islands and cays. And conch, in every form.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Junkanoo rhythms come from goatskin drums, cowbells, whistles and brass. Rake-and-scrape, played on accordion, goatskin drum and a carpenter's saw scraped with a knife, is the music of the Out Islands. Joseph Spence, from Andros, played guitar in a style like no one else's.

links.label: Happy All the Time, Joseph Spence

cards.title: Craft: straw work
cards.text: Bahamian women plait palm leaves into long strips and sew them into hats, bags and baskets, decorated with shells, raffia flowers and embroidery, sold in Nassau's straw market.

cards.title: Creature: West Indian flamingo
cards.text: The national bird. On Great Inagua, in the far south, tens of thousands of flamingos nest and feed in the salt ponds of Inagua National Park, turning the shallows pink.

cards.title: Place: the Exuma Cays
cards.text: A chain of hundreds of small islands with white sand and turquoise water, including the Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park, created in 1958, one of the first protected areas of its kind in the world.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Conch salad with lime, peppers and onion. Cracked conch, fried. And guava duff, a rolled, steamed guava pudding with rum sauce.

050.name: Bangladesh

word.meaning: A long, lively, rambling conversation among friends over tea, about everything and nothing: politics, poetry, cricket, gossip. Adda is a Bengali institution, happening at tea stalls, on rooftops and in university canteens.

050.ask: Ask which pitha, winter rice cakes, their family makes, and whether they have a favorite from a street stall on a cold morning.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: Bangladeshis are passionate about their team, and a match is a reason to gather.

Rabindranath Tagore: many Bangladeshis sing and quote his songs and poems, and anyone who has read Tagore has an opening.

Food and hospitality: biryani, fish curry and sweets like roshogolla are loved, and sharing a meal is a real welcome.

cards.title: This season: Nabanna
cards.text: In mid-November, on the first day of the Bengali month of Agrahayan, villages celebrate Nabanna, the festival of new rice, as the aman rice harvest comes in. Families cook the new rice into payesh, a sweet rice pudding, and all kinds of pitha, and there's music, fairs and visits between homes.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its language: on February 21, 1952, students in Dhaka gave their lives defending the right to speak Bengali, and UNESCO made the date International Mother Language Day, observed around the world. And its poets, above all Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam, the national poet.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Bauls are wandering mystic minstrels who sing songs of love and the search for the divine, playing the one-stringed ektara; UNESCO lists their songs as heritage. Lalon Fakir, who lived in the 1800s, wrote hundreds of their best-loved songs, and Farida Parveen, "the Queen of Lalon Song," has sung them for decades.

links.label: A Tribute to Lalon Fakir, Farida Parveen

cards.title: Craft: nakshi kantha
cards.text: Embroidered quilts made by women from layers of old saris and dhotis, stitched together with running stitch and covered in pictures: flowers, fish, elephants, boats and scenes of village life. Once made for family use, they tell stories, and each one is unique.

cards.title: Creature: Ganges river dolphin
cards.text: A nearly blind river dolphin with a long, thin beak, which finds its way through the muddy rivers of Bangladesh by echolocation. It's the national aquatic animal of neighboring India too.

cards.title: Place: the Sundarbans
cards.text: The largest mangrove forest in the world, where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet the sea, a maze of waterways home to Bengal tigers, crocodiles and spotted deer. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Hilsa, ilish, the national fish, cooked in mustard sauce. Bhuna khichuri on a rainy day. And mishti doi, sweet, caramelized yogurt set in clay pots.

051.name: Armenia

word.meaning: "Dear," added after a name to show affection: Anna jan, Papa jan. Armenians use it constantly with family and friends, and it softens almost anything you say.

051.ask: Ask how their family makes dolma, and whether they wrap it in grape leaves or cabbage, or stuff peppers and eggplant instead.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Chess: chess is taught in Armenian schools, and the country has won Olympiad gold. Anyone who plays chess has a friend.

System of a Down: the band's members are Armenian-American, and their music is a point of pride and shared taste.

Big family tables: Armenian gatherings run long with toasts and too much food, like a holiday dinner that goes on for hours.

cards.title: This season: the pomegranate and the grape harvest
cards.text: Autumn brings the grape harvest to the valleys, including Areni, where archaeologists found what may be the world's oldest known winery, about 6,000 years old, in a cave. The pomegranate, which ripens now, is Armenia's great symbol of life and fertility, painted on pottery, woven into carpets and carved in stone.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Armenia was the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion, in the early 300s, and its alphabet, created by Mesrop Mashtots around 405, is still in use. And Mount Ararat, sacred to Armenians, which rises over Yerevan from across the border.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The duduk, a reed pipe made of apricot wood, has a warm, mournful voice, and UNESCO lists its music as heritage; Djivan Gasparyan was its great master, heard on film soundtracks around the world. For the modern bridge, the pianist Tigran Hamasyan weaves Armenian folk melodies and hymns into jazz and heavy, odd-meter grooves on albums like Mockroot.

links.label: The Art of the Armenian Duduk, Djivan Gasparyan

cards.title: Craft: khachkars
cards.text: "Cross-stones": tall stone slabs carved with a cross surrounded by intricate lace-like patterns of vines, rosettes and knots. Tens of thousands stand across Armenia, and no two are alike. UNESCO lists the art of making them as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Armenian mouflon
cards.text: A wild sheep with great curling horns that lives in the mountains of southern Armenia, the ancestor of domestic sheep, and now rare and protected.

cards.title: Place: Geghard Monastery
cards.text: A monastery partly carved into the rock of a mountain gorge, with chambers where singing echoes beautifully. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Lavash, thin flatbread baked against the walls of a clay tandoor oven, which UNESCO lists as heritage. Khorovats, Armenian barbecue. Dolma. And gata, a sweet, buttery bread for celebrations, sometimes with a coin hidden inside for luck.

056.name: Belgium

word.meaning: A Flemish word for appetite, craving, or simply feeling like something: "ik heb goesting in frieten," I really feel like fries. It covers food, plans and people, and there's no neat English equivalent.

056.ask: Ask where to find the best frietkot, the local fry shack, and which sauce they choose: mayonnaise, andalouse, samurai or stoofvleessaus, beef stew gravy.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Comics: Tintin and the Smurfs are Belgian, and many Belgians grew up reading bandes dessinées.

Food: fries, waffles, chocolate and hundreds of beers. Belgians love to talk about where to find the best.

Cycling: Belgians are among the most passionate cycling fans in the world, and the spring classics are a big event.

cards.title: This season: Saint Nicholas
cards.text: On the night before December 6, Saint Nicholas, called Sinterklaas in Flemish and Saint-Nicolas in French, visits Belgian children. They leave out a shoe with a carrot or some hay for his horse or donkey, and wake to find it filled with chocolate, clementines, marzipan and speculoos, the spiced biscuits of the season.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Chocolate, fries, waffles and hundreds of beers; UNESCO lists Belgian beer culture as heritage. And comics: Tintin, the Smurfs and Lucky Luke all come from Belgium, and Brussels has comic-strip murals painted on its walls.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Belgium is home to carillons, sets of bells played from a keyboard high in church and city towers; Mechelen has a world-famous carillon school, and UNESCO lists carillon culture as heritage. Jacques Brel sang great French-language chansons; for the modern bridge, Stromae, from Brussels, mixes dance beats with sharp, tender songs about everyday life.

cards.title: Craft: bobbin lace
cards.text: In Bruges and other Flemish towns, lacemakers work with dozens of bobbins at once, crossing and twisting threads around pins on a pillow to make fine lace. Some still sit at their doorways or in lace shops, working as visitors watch.

cards.title: Creature: the Belgian draft horse
cards.text: One of the world's strongest horse breeds, the Brabant, with a gentle temper, massive build and a chestnut or roan coat. It once worked Belgian farms and still pulls wagons, and in Oostduinkerke riders on these horses catch shrimp in the surf, a tradition UNESCO lists as heritage.

cards.title: Place: the Grand-Place of Brussels
cards.text: The central square of Brussels, surrounded by gilded guild houses and the Gothic town hall. Every two years in August, it's covered in a huge carpet of begonias. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Moules-frites, mussels steamed in a pot with fries on the side. Waffles, crisp Brussels ones or chewy, sugary Liège ones. And stoofvlees, beef stewed in beer.

064.name: Bhutan

word.meaning: "Hello," in Dzongkha, the national language. Add "la" at the end, kuzuzangpo la, to make it polite, which is how most people say it.

064.ask: Ask how spicy they like ema datshi, the national dish of chilies in cheese, and how many times a day they eat it. In Bhutan, chilies are a vegetable, not a spice.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Archery: the national sport, played at festive tournaments with singing, dancing and teasing between teams.

Chilies: Bhutanese cooking is all about chilies and cheese, and fans of spicy food find an instant friend.

Hiking and the mountains: walking in the Himalayan valleys and to monasteries is a way of life, and hikers have a lot to talk about.

cards.title: This season: the Black-necked Crane Festival
cards.text: Each autumn, endangered black-necked cranes fly over the Himalaya from Tibet to spend the winter in the Phobjikha Valley. On November 11, the courtyard of Gangtey Monastery holds a festival to welcome them, with masked dances, folk songs, and children dressed as cranes, bowing and flapping in the crane dance. Local people believe the cranes circle the monastery three times when they arrive.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Gross National Happiness, Bhutan's idea that a country should measure its progress by its people's well-being, not only by wealth. And its forests: its constitution requires that at least 60 percent of the land stay forested.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bhutanese folk music includes zhungdra, slow, ornamented songs of the central valleys, and boedra, gentler court songs, often accompanied by the dramnyen, a long-necked lute. At every tshechu, the great religious festivals, masked dancers whirl to the sound of long horns, cymbals and drums in the courtyards of the dzongs. Jigme Drukpa, a master of the dramnyen and the flute, has recorded these songs for listeners abroad.

links.label: Bhutan Himalaya: Folk Music from Bhutan, Jigme Drukpa

cards.title: Craft: thagzo weaving
cards.text: Bhutanese women weave on backstrap and floor looms, making the brilliant, intricately patterned cloth used for the kira and gho, the national dress, with complex supplementary-weft patterns that can take months to finish.

cards.title: Creature: black-necked crane
cards.text: A tall grey crane with a black head and neck and a red crown, the only crane that lives on high plateaus. It's sacred in Bhutan, where songs and dances celebrate its return each winter.

cards.title: Place: Paro Taktsang
cards.text: The Tiger's Nest monastery, clinging to a sheer cliff 900 meters above the Paro Valley, where Guru Rinpoche is said to have flown on the back of a tigress in the 700s to meditate in a cave. The hike up takes a few hours through pine forest strung with prayer flags.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ema datshi, green or red chilies stewed in melted cheese. Red rice, grown in the high valleys. Momos. And suja, butter tea, salty and rich, sipped all day in the cold.

068.name: Bolivia

word.meaning: An Andean blessing ritual: sprinkling alcohol, confetti and flower petals on a new house, car, shop or field, and pouring a little onto the ground as an offering to Pachamama, Mother Earth, asking for good fortune. Bolivians ch'allar almost anything new.
word.sayIt: CHAH-yah (with a little catch on the ch)

068.ask: Ask where to get the best salteña, the juicy baked pastry eaten mid-morning, and how they manage to eat one without spilling a drop.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football at altitude: Bolivians love football and joke about how visiting teams struggle to breathe in La Paz.

Carnival and dance: many Bolivians dance in the Oruro Carnival or other festivals, and practice for months with their groups.

Salteñas at mid-morning: the juicy pastries are a daily treat, and figuring out how to eat one without spilling is a shared joke.

cards.title: This season: Todos Santos
cards.text: On November 1 and 2, families welcome the souls of their dead home with altars of flowers, candles, sugar-cane arches, the loved one's favorite food, and t'antawawas, "bread babies" in Aymara: sweet bread figures with little painted faces, alongside bread ladders, horses and crowns to help the souls on their journey. Visitors come to pray and are given bread in return.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its Indigenous heritage: Bolivia recognizes 36 Indigenous languages alongside Spanish, and Aymara and Quechua are spoken every day. And La Paz, the highest seat of government in the world, where cable cars now float people over the city.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Andean music, played on the charango, a small, bright ten-stringed guitar, the zampoña panpipes and the quena flute, sounds from Bolivia's highlands across the world. Los Kjarkas, founded in the 1960s, are its most famous band, and their song "Llorando se fue" traveled the globe.

links.label: Lo Mejor de los Kjarkas, Los Kjarkas

cards.title: Craft: Tarabuco and Jalq'a weaving
cards.text: In the villages around Sucre, Indigenous women weave some of the finest textiles in the Andes on backstrap looms: Tarabuco cloths with bright bands of people, animals and scenes of daily life, and Jalq'a weavings full of strange, swirling red-and-black creatures from the underworld.

cards.title: Creature: Andean flamingo
cards.text: Three kinds of flamingo, including the rare Andean and James's flamingos, feed in the salty lakes of the high plateau, turning Laguna Colorada, a red lake, pink with birds.

cards.title: Place: Salar de Uyuni
cards.text: The largest salt flat in the world, a blinding white plain so flat that in the rainy season a thin layer of water turns it into a giant mirror of the sky.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Salteñas, baked empanadas with a sweet, soupy filling of meat and vegetables. Api morado, a hot, thick purple corn drink, with a pastel, a cheese pastry dusted with sugar. And at Todos Santos, t'antawawas.

070.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina

word.meaning: The neighborhood, and the bond between neighbors: sharing coffee, food and help, looking after each other's children and homes, and celebrating each other's holidays. Good komšiluk is one of the most valued things in Bosnian life.

070.ask: Ask how their family makes Bosnian coffee, boiled in a small copper džezva and served with a sugar cube and rahat lokum, and how long a proper coffee should take.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Coffee rituals: Bosnian coffee is meant to be slow, with conversation, like a leisurely coffee date anywhere.

Football and basketball: Bosnians follow both closely, and Edin Džeko is a hero.

Ćevapi: talking about the best ćevapi place is a favorite argument, like debating the best burger or pizza.

cards.title: This season: plum time
cards.text: In early autumn, the plum orchards are heavy with fruit, and families gather to make pekmez, a thick plum butter, stirred for hours in big copper pots over a fire, and to put up preserves for the winter.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Sarajevo, where mosques, churches and a synagogue stand close together in the old town. The Old Bridge of Mostar, rebuilt after the war. And sevdalinka, its love songs.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Sevdalinka, or sevdah, is slow, passionate song about love and longing, sung in the old towns since the Ottoman era, often with the saz, a long-necked lute. UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2024. Damir Imamović, from Sarajevo, sings it for a new generation.

cards.title: Craft: Konjic woodcarving
cards.text: In the town of Konjic, carvers decorate furniture, chests, doors and panels with intricate carved patterns of flowers, vines and geometric shapes, a family craft passed down for generations. UNESCO lists it as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: brown trout
cards.text: Clear, cold rivers like the Una, the Neretva and the Drina run through the mountains, famous for their emerald-green water and their trout.

cards.title: Place: the Old Bridge of Mostar
cards.text: A single stone arch built by the Ottomans in the 16th century over the Neretva River. It was destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt stone by stone, and divers still leap from it into the river below. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ćevapi in somun, fluffy flatbread, with onions and kajmak. Burek, flaky pastry filled with meat. And Bosnian coffee.

072.name: Botswana

word.meaning: "Rain," in Setswana, and in a dry country, the most precious blessing there is. Pula is also the name of the currency, the national motto, and a cheer shouted at the end of speeches: "Pula!"

072.ask: Ask how their family makes seswaa, the slow-cooked, pounded beef served at weddings and celebrations, and who gets to pound it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Wildlife: many Batswana are proud of the Okavango Delta and elephants, and love to share safari stories.

The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency: Alexander McCall Smith's novels set in Gaborone are a fun, warm topic.

Football and choirs: Batswana love football, gospel and choir singing, and church choirs are a big part of community life.

cards.title: This season: the first rains and the zebra migration
cards.text: In November and December, the first rains arrive and the dry land turns green. Following the rain, tens of thousands of zebra leave the rivers of the north and trek hundreds of kilometers south to the fresh grasslands of the Makgadikgadi and Nxai Pans, one of the longest migrations of any land mammal in Africa, staying until about February.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wildlife and its care for it: Botswana has the largest population of elephants in the world, and much of its land is protected. And its peaceful democracy, with regular elections since independence in 1966.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Setswana music ranges from choirs and the traditional folk songs of the villages to the bright, fast guitar picking of the Tswana folk style and, today, kwaito, gospel and hip-hop in the cities. Vee Mampeezy blends kwaito with kwasa kwasa, a Congolese-rooted dance style, into a sound of his own.

cards.title: Craft: Okavango baskets
cards.text: In villages around the Okavango Delta, especially Etsha and Gumare, Hambukushu and Bayei women weave tightly coiled baskets from the leaves of the mokola palm, dyed with bark and roots into patterns with names like "Tears of the Giraffe" and "Forehead of the Zebra."

cards.title: Creature: African elephant
cards.text: Around 130,000 elephants roam Botswana, the largest population on Earth, gathering in great herds along the Chobe River in the dry season.

cards.title: Place: the Okavango Delta
cards.text: A vast inland delta where a river flows into the Kalahari Desert and never reaches the sea, spreading into a maze of channels, lagoons and islands that fills with wildlife. Visitors glide through it in mokoro, dugout canoes. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Seswaa, pounded beef, with pap, a stiff maize porridge. Magwinya, fat, golden fried dough balls. And phane, mopane worms, a crunchy, protein-rich seasonal delicacy dried and fried with tomato and onion.

076.name: Brazil

word.meaning: Gently running your fingers through the hair of someone you love, to soothe them or send them to sleep. The word came to Brazil from Kimbundu, a language of Angola, carried by Africans who were enslaved and brought across the Atlantic.

076.ask: Ask which samba school they cheer for at Carnival, or which football team, and settle in: both come with stories, songs and strong loyalties.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Pelé, Ronaldo, Marta and the national team are loved by almost everyone, and it's the easiest way into a conversation.

Music: bossa nova, samba and MPB are loved worldwide. If you know "The Girl from Ipanema," you've got a start.

Barbecues and beaches: the churrasco with friends and weekends at the beach are rituals many people share.

cards.title: This season: Círio de Nazaré
cards.text: On the second Sunday of October, which is October 11 this year, the city of Belém at the mouth of the Amazon fills for one of the largest religious processions in the world. Devotees walk barefoot for hours behind a carriage bearing a small image of Our Lady of Nazareth, many straining to touch the long rope that pulls it. UNESCO lists the Círio as heritage. Afterward, families sit down to the Círio lunch: pato no tucupi and maniçoba.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Football: Brazil has won the men's World Cup five times, more than any other country, playing a style Brazilians call jogo bonito, "the beautiful game." And the Amazon: most of the world's largest rainforest lies within Brazil's borders.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Samba grew from Afro-Brazilian traditions, including the samba de roda of Bahia, which UNESCO lists as heritage, and took shape in Rio de Janeiro in the early 20th century. Cartola, one of the founders of the Mangueira samba school, wrote some of its most beautiful songs, like "As Rosas Não Falam." In 1959, João Gilberto's Chega de Saudade quietened samba's rhythm into the whisper of bossa nova. For the modern bridge, Liniker's 2024 album Caju, soulful and full of Brazilian rhythm, won two Latin Grammys.

cards.title: Craft: Marajoara pottery
cards.text: On Marajó, a vast island at the mouth of the Amazon, people made ceramics of astonishing elegance from around 400 CE: urns, bowls and small clay coverings painted and incised with swirling, symmetrical designs. Today, potters in Icoaraci, a district of Belém, study the ancient pieces held by the city's Goeldi Museum and make replicas and new work in the same style.

cards.title: Creature: boto
cards.text: The Amazon river dolphin, which turns pinker as it ages. In Amazonian folklore, the boto can take the form of a handsome man in a white hat who charms his way into village parties at night, then slips back into the river before dawn.

cards.title: Place: Lençóis Maranhenses
cards.text: White dunes that stretch like rumpled bedsheets (lençóis) along the coast of Maranhão, the largest dune field in South America. Each rainy season, from January to June, rain collects between the dunes in blue and green lagoons up to five meters deep, and because the dunes keep moving, the lagoons come back in new shapes every year. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pato no tucupi, duck in a tangy yellow broth made from wild cassava, served with jambu, a leaf that makes your lips tingle. In Belém, açaí is not a sweet breakfast bowl but a thick purple pulp eaten with fish and cassava flour. And at every party, brigadeiros: chocolate fudge balls rolled in sprinkles.

084.name: Belize

word.meaning: "What's going on?" in Belizean Kriol, the language most Belizeans share alongside English, Spanish, Garifuna, Maya languages and more. It's the everyday way to say hello.

084.ask: Ask who makes the best rice and beans with stew chicken, the Sunday meal, and whether it's cooked with coconut milk.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
The Caribbean and the reef: snorkeling, diving and fishing on the barrier reef are shared joys.

A mix of cultures: Belizeans move easily between Kriol, Spanish, Garifuna and English, and anyone who loves languages will find it fascinating.

Rice and beans on Sunday: the family Sunday meal of rice and beans with stew chicken is a comforting tradition, like a Sunday roast or dinner elsewhere.

cards.title: This season: Garifuna Settlement Day
cards.text: On November 19, Belize celebrates the arrival of the Garifuna people by boat on its southern coast in 1832. In Dangriga and Hopkins, the landing is reenacted at dawn, with dugout canoes coming ashore to drumming, singing and dancing, followed by church services, food and parties all day.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Belize Barrier Reef, the largest in the Western Hemisphere, and the Great Blue Hole. Its mix of peoples: Kriol, Mestizo, Garifuna, Maya, Mennonite, East Indian and Chinese. And its protected forests: much of the country's land is set aside for nature.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Garifuna drumming and song are the roots, and in the 1970s and 80s musicians turned them into punta rock. Andy Palacio, a Belizean singer and champion of the Garifuna language, recorded "Wátina" with singers from Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, and it was hailed around the world.

links.label: Wátina, Andy Palacio and the Garifuna Collective

cards.title: Craft: slate carving
cards.text: In the Maya village of San Antonio in the Cayo District, carvers make slate plaques with images inspired by ancient Maya art: gods, glyphs, jaguars and calendar symbols.

cards.title: Creature: jaguar
cards.text: The biggest cat in the Americas, with a golden coat of black rosettes. Belize created the world's first jaguar reserve, the Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary, in 1986.

cards.title: Place: the Great Blue Hole
cards.text: A nearly perfect circle of deep blue, about 300 meters across and more than 120 meters deep, in the middle of Lighthouse Reef. It's part of the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Rice and beans with stew chicken and potato salad. Fry jacks, puffy fried dough, for breakfast. And hudut, Garifuna fish in coconut broth with mashed plantain.

090.name: Solomon Islands

word.meaning: "Thank you very much" in Pijin, the language Solomon Islanders share across more than 60 local languages. It's said often, and warmly.

090.ask: Ask which island their family comes from, and what their language there is called.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football and futsal: both are hugely popular, and the national futsal team, the Kurukuru, is loved.

Panpipes and music: bamboo bands are a joy, and music lovers have an opening.

Island life: fishing, paddling dugout canoes and swimming are everyday joys, and people love telling stories of their home island.

cards.title: This season: turtle time on the Arnavons
cards.text: On the Arnavon Islands, a marine park run together by local communities, hawksbill turtles nest all year, and November to January is one of the seasons protected by law, when rangers guard the beaches at night and hatchlings dash to the sea.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its panpipe music. Its reefs and islands, nearly a thousand of them. And its community-run conservation, where villages protect their own reefs and turtles.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Panpipe ensembles from Malaita play bamboo pipes of many sizes, some blown and some struck with sandals, in joyful, rolling rhythms. Narasirato, from the village of Oterama, revived this music and have played festivals like Glastonbury and WOMAD.

cards.title: Craft: shell money
cards.text: In the Langa Langa Lagoon of Malaita, families grind and polish tiny discs of colored shell, red, white and black, and string them into long strands of shell money, still used for bride price and ceremonies.

cards.title: Creature: monkey-tailed skink
cards.text: The largest skink in the world, a green lizard found only in the Solomon Islands, which lives in treetops, eats leaves and uses its tail to grip branches like a monkey.

cards.title: Place: East Rennell
cards.text: The southern part of Rennell Island, the largest raised coral atoll in the world, with Lake Tegano, once a lagoon, now a lake full of islands. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fish and root vegetables cooked in coconut milk. Slippery cabbage, a leafy green. And cassava pudding, baked in leaves.

096.name: Brunei

word.meaning: The national dish, and a word Bruneians are proud of: a sticky, glue-like starch made from the sago palm, twirled onto a two-pronged bamboo fork called a candas and dipped in sour, spicy sauces. Eating ambuyat is a shared, messy, happy meal.

096.ask: Ask how they twirl ambuyat on the candas, and which sauce, the sour cacah, is best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food and night markets: Bruneians love eating out, and the Gadong night market is a favorite.

Badminton and football: popular sports across the region, followed closely.

Nature: many Bruneians are proud of their rainforest, and enjoy trips to Ulu Temburong.

cards.title: This season: the monsoon rains
cards.text: From November to January, the northeast monsoon brings heavy rains to Borneo, and the rivers of Brunei's rainforest run high. The forests of Ulu Temburong are at their greenest, loud with frogs, insects and birds.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its rainforest: most of Brunei is still covered in forest, and much of it is protected. And Kampong Ayer, one of the largest water villages in the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Adai-adai is an old work song sung by fishermen as they rowed and hauled their nets, with a dance of rowing movements. Gulingtangan, a set of small bronze gongs, is played at weddings and celebrations.

cards.title: Craft: brassware
cards.text: Bruneian metalworkers have long been famous for brass and bronze, casting kettles, trays and small ceremonial cannons, and passing the craft down in the water village.

cards.title: Creature: proboscis monkey
cards.text: A reddish monkey of Borneo's mangroves and rivers, whose males have huge, drooping noses. They leap between trees and swim across rivers.

cards.title: Place: Kampong Ayer
cards.text: A water village of houses on stilts over the Brunei River, linked by wooden walkways and water taxis, with schools, mosques and shops, home to thousands of people for centuries.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ambuyat. Nasi katok, a simple packet of rice, fried chicken and sambal. And kelupis, sticky rice steamed in leaves.

100.name: Bulgaria

word.meaning: A passion or deep desire to do something for the pure love of it: cooking, gardening, singing, fixing an old car. Something done "s merak" is done with heart. One more thing: in Bulgaria, a nod of the head usually means no, and a shake means yes.

100.ask: Ask how their family makes banitsa, the flaky pastry with cheese, and whether they hide lucky charms in it for New Year's Eve.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Yogurt: Bulgarians are proud that their bacteria give yogurt its name, and love to talk about the real thing.

Mountains and the sea: skiing in Bansko and summers on the Black Sea are shared joys.

Folk dance: horo line dances happen at every wedding and celebration, and anyone who has danced a line dance can join.

cards.title: This season: Enlighteners' Day
cards.text: On November 1, Bulgaria honors its buditeli, "awakeners": the writers, teachers and scholars who kept Bulgarian language, learning and culture alive. Schoolchildren have the day off and join parades carrying portraits of these heroes, and it's also a day to thank teachers.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Cyrillic alphabet, developed in the First Bulgarian Empire and now used by some 250 million people. Its yogurt, with the bacterium named Lactobacillus bulgaricus. And the rose oil of the Valley of Roses.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bulgarian women's choirs sing in close, ringing harmonies and dissonances, with complex, uneven rhythms. The album "Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares," recorded by the Bulgarian State Radio and Television Female Vocal Choir, amazed listeners around the world in the 1980s.

cards.title: Craft: Troyan pottery
cards.text: Potters around Troyan, in the Balkan Mountains, make earthenware plates, jugs and bowls glazed in brown, green and ochre, with flowing drip patterns and peacock-eye swirls. It's used at family tables across the country.

cards.title: Creature: Karakachan dog
cards.text: An ancient, shaggy shepherd dog bred by nomadic herders to guard sheep from wolves and bears. Once nearly gone, it's been brought back, and now helps protect flocks while wild predators live nearby.

cards.title: Place: Rila Monastery
cards.text: Founded in the 10th century by Saint John of Rila, high in the Rila Mountains, with striped arches and a church covered in colorful frescoes. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Shopska salad: tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and grated white cheese. Banitsa with yogurt or boza for breakfast. And lyutenitsa, a roasted pepper and tomato relish, spread on bread.

104.name: Myanmar

word.meaning: "Hello!" It comes from the word for "blessing" or "auspiciousness," so each greeting wishes the other person good fortune.

104.ask: Ask how their family makes mohinga, the fish noodle soup eaten for breakfast, and which street stall makes the best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: mohinga and tea leaf salad are loved, and Myanmar people love to share them.

Football and chinlone: Myanmar fans follow the Premier League closely, and chinlone, a graceful game of keeping a rattan ball in the air with the feet, is fun to ask about.

Teashops: meeting friends in teashops over sweet milky tea and snacks is a daily ritual.

cards.title: This season: Tazaungdaing
cards.text: On the full moon of the month of Tazaungmon, in November, people light candles and lanterns at homes and pagodas. In Taunggyi, in Shan State, the festival usually brings a hot-air balloon competition, with glowing paper balloons shaped like animals and pagodas rising into the night. At pagodas, weavers compete to weave a robe for the Buddha in a single night.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its golden pagodas, above all the Shwedagon in Yangon, covered in gold. Bagan's thousands of temples. And thanaka, the pale, fragrant paste made from ground bark that people wear on their cheeks to protect and cool their skin.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The saung gauk, an arched harp shaped like a boat, is the national instrument, played for gentle classical songs. The hsaing waing ensemble, with a circle of tuned drums around the player, plays for festivals and theater.

links.label: Mahagitá: Harp and Vocal Music of Burma, Inle Myint Maung and Yi Yi Thant

cards.title: Craft: lacquerware
cards.text: In Bagan, artisans make bowls, boxes and trays from bamboo or wood coated with many layers of lacquer, then engrave fine designs by hand and fill them with color. A single piece can take months.

cards.title: Creature: Myanmar snub-nosed monkey
cards.text: A black monkey with a white beard and an upturned nose, discovered by scientists in 2010 in the mountains of the north. Local people say it sneezes when it rains, because the rain gets into its nose.

cards.title: Place: Bagan
cards.text: On a plain beside the Irrawaddy River, more than 2,000 temples and pagodas built from the 11th to 13th centuries rise from the fields. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mohinga. Lahpet thoke, a salad of fermented tea leaves with crunchy beans and nuts. And Shan noodles, rice noodles with a tomato and meat sauce.

108.name: Burundi

word.meaning: Peace. In Kirundi, "amahoro" is also a greeting, wishing peace to the person you meet, and a farewell.

108.ask: Ask whether they've ever seen the drummers perform, and what it feels like when the big drums start.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Drumming: the royal drummers are a great source of pride, and many people abroad have seen or heard them.

Football: Burundians love football, played everywhere from city streets to villages.

Coffee: Burundi grows excellent coffee, and coffee lovers may already have tried it.

cards.title: This season: fishing lights on Lake Tanganyika
cards.text: On dark nights, fishermen on Lake Tanganyika paddle out in boats lit with lanterns to catch ndagala, small silvery sardine-like fish drawn to the light. From the shore near Bujumbura, the lake glitters with their lamps, and in the morning the catch is dried in the sun.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its drums. The royal drum ritual, with drummers carrying huge drums on their heads and dancing as they play, is listed by UNESCO as heritage. And Lake Tanganyika, one of the oldest and deepest lakes in the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Drummers of Burundi play ingoma, big drums made from tree trunks and cowhide, in thundering rhythms with leaps and dances. Once played only for kings, births and harvests, they've been heard around the world since the 1980s.

cards.title: Craft: basket weaving
cards.text: Burundian women weave fine baskets with pointed lids, in coiled grass with patterns in black and natural colors, once used to hold grain and gifts.

cards.title: Creature: chimpanzee
cards.text: In the Kibira National Park, a mountain rainforest in the north, chimpanzees live among tea plantations and forest, alongside colobus monkeys and many birds.

cards.title: Place: the Gishora Drum Sanctuary
cards.text: Near Gitega, a sacred place where royal drums were kept and played, and where drummers still perform for visitors.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Beans with plantains or cassava. Ndagala, fried or dried. And brochettes, grilled skewers of goat or beef.

112.name: Belarus

word.meaning: "Thank you" in Belarusian. "Vialiki dziakuj" is a big thank you.

112.ask: Ask how their family makes draniki, crispy potato pancakes, and whether they're best with sour cream or machanka, a rich pork gravy.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Potatoes: Belarusians joke about their love of potatoes and have hundreds of dishes. Anyone who loves potatoes is on familiar ground.

Dachas and gardening: many families grow vegetables, berries and flowers at summer cottages, a shared joy for gardeners.

Hockey and the outdoors: ice hockey, cross-country skiing and mushroom picking in the forests are popular pastimes.

cards.title: This season: Dziady
cards.text: In early November, many Belarusian families mark Dziady, "forefathers," a traditional day to remember their ancestors. Families clean the graves, light candles, and gather at home for a special dinner, setting out dishes for the departed and telling family stories.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its forests, lakes and wetlands, among the wildest in Europe, with Belovezhskaya Pushcha, one of the last primeval forests. Its folk songs and crafts. And its potatoes, loved in hundreds of dishes.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Belarusian folk songs are sung at harvests, weddings and holidays. Pesniary, formed in 1969, turned them into folk-rock with electric guitars and harmonies, with songs like "Kupalinka," and became one of the most famous bands of the Soviet era.

cards.title: Craft: straw weaving
cards.text: Belarusian craftspeople weave straw into figures, baskets, dolls and hats, and into bright, glittering ornaments for holidays. Straw is a symbol of the harvest and of home.

cards.title: Creature: Eurasian beaver
cards.text: Belarus's rivers and wetlands are full of beavers, which build dams and lodges that create ponds and wetlands for other animals.

cards.title: Place: Mir Castle
cards.text: A 16th-century castle with red-brick towers and white-trimmed walls, reflected in a pond, in the village of Mir. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Draniki with sour cream. Machanka. And kalduny, potato dumplings filled with meat.

116.name: Cambodia

word.meaning: Happy, well, comfortable, enjoying yourself. "Sok sabay?" means "Are you well?", and "sabay" on its own can describe a good meal, a cool breeze or a lazy afternoon with friends.

116.ask: Ask what their family does for Khmer New Year in April, and which games they played as children; many involve throwing things, splashing water and a lot of laughter.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Angkor Wat: Cambodians are deeply proud of it, and anyone who has visited or dreams of visiting has an easy opening.

Food: fish amok, lok lak and Khmer noodle soup for breakfast are loved, and trading favorite dishes is easy.

Karaoke and dancing: family parties and weddings often end with karaoke and slow circle dances called romvong, and guests are pulled in to join.

cards.title: This season: the Water Festival
cards.text: Bon Om Touk, the Water Festival, marks the moment in late November when the Tonlé Sap River reverses its flow and the floodwaters begin to drain from the great lake. This year's national holiday is November 23 to 25. Traditionally, hundreds of long, painted dragon boats with dozens of paddlers race on the river in Phnom Penh, with illuminated floats and fireworks at night, though one report says the capital's races are cancelled this year, so check before planning around them.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Angkor, the vast temple city of the Khmer Empire, and above all Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century, the largest religious monument in the world, which appears on the national flag.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Pinpeat ensembles of xylophones, gongs, oboes and drums accompany the Royal Ballet of Cambodia, which UNESCO lists as heritage. In the 1960s and early 70s, Phnom Penh had a thrilling rock scene, led by Sinn Sisamouth and Ros Sereysothea, which blended Khmer melody with surf guitar and soul. Many of its stars died under the Khmer Rouge, but their songs survived and are loved again. For the modern bridge, the Cambodian Space Project revived that sound for a new generation.

links.label: Not Easy Rock 'n' Roll, Cambodian Space Project

cards.title: Craft: silk ikat
cards.text: In villages in Takeo province and along the Mekong, weavers tie and dye silk threads before weaving to make hol, a shimmering silk with intricate patterns, woven into sampot, the traditional wrapped skirt worn at weddings and festivals.

cards.title: Creature: Irrawaddy dolphin
cards.text: A shy, round-headed river dolphin with no beak, which lives in a stretch of the Mekong around Kratie. Boats take visitors out quietly to watch them surface.

cards.title: Place: Angkor
cards.text: Near Siem Reap, hundreds of temples spread across the forest: Angkor Wat at sunrise, the smiling stone faces of the Bayon, and Ta Prohm, wrapped in the roots of giant trees. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fish amok, fish steamed in banana-leaf cups with coconut milk and kroeung, a fragrant paste of lemongrass, galangal and turmeric. Num banh chok, fresh rice noodles with a green fish curry, for breakfast. And dishes seasoned with Kampot pepper, grown in the south and prized by cooks around the world.

120.name: Cameroon

word.meaning: A savings group of friends, neighbors or coworkers who each pay into a shared pot at every meeting and take turns receiving the whole pot, to start a business, pay school fees or build a house. Njangi meetings are also where news, food and laughter get shared.

120.ask: Ask which of Cameroon's many regions their family comes from, and what food they miss most from there. The country is often called "Africa in miniature" for its variety.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Roger Milla, Samuel Eto'o and the Indomitable Lions are loved, and the 1990 World Cup is a golden memory.

Music: makossa and bikutsi, plus Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa," which many people know from its samples.

Variety: Cameroonians love talking about their many regions, languages and dishes.

cards.title: This season: the Ngondo
cards.text: In late November and early December, the Sawa peoples of the coast around Douala hold the Ngondo, their great water festival, which ends on the first Sunday of December. A diver goes down into the Wouri River to receive messages from the ancestral water spirits, and the days around it bring canoe races, wrestling, dances and a beauty pageant. UNESCO lists the Ngondo as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "Africa in miniature": beaches, rainforest, savanna, mountains and volcanoes, and some 250 languages, in one country. And its football, including the Indomitable Lions and Roger Milla's famous corner-flag dance at the 1990 World Cup.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Makossa, from Douala, is bright, bass-heavy dance music; Manu Dibango's saxophone hit "Soul Makossa," from 1972, became a global disco anthem and was later sampled around the world. Bikutsi, fast and hypnotic, comes from the Beti people of the center.

cards.title: Craft: ndop cloth
cards.text: In the Grassfields of the west, artisans make ndop, indigo-dyed cotton cloth with bold white geometric designs made by stitching the pattern tight with raffia before dyeing. It's worn by kings and hung at royal ceremonies.

cards.title: Creature: Goliath frog
cards.text: The largest frog in the world, which can grow over 30 centimeters long and weigh more than three kilograms, found in the fast rivers of the rainforests of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea.

cards.title: Place: the Dja Faunal Reserve
cards.text: A huge, almost untouched rainforest nearly encircled by the Dja River, home to gorillas, chimpanzees and forest elephants. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves, peanuts and meat or shrimp, the national dish. Poulet DG, chicken fried with plantains and vegetables. And beignets with beans and pap, for breakfast.

124.name: Canada

word.meaning: In Inuktitut, "something that acts in the capacity of a person": the stone figures Inuit build across the Arctic to guide travelers, mark good hunting or fishing places, or say "you are on the right path." Some look like people with outstretched arms; most are simple stacks of stone.

124.ask: Ask what their favorite winter tradition is, from skating on a frozen lake or canal to a visit to a sugar shack in spring for maple taffy poured on snow.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hockey: many Canadians grew up playing or watching it, and asking about their team is a sure start.

The outdoors: camping, canoeing, skiing and cottage weekends are shared joys.

Tim Hortons and winter: coffee runs and cheerful complaining about the cold are near-universal experiences.

cards.title: This season: polar bears at Churchill
cards.text: From mid-October to mid-November, roughly 900 polar bears gather on the shore of Hudson Bay near the small town of Churchill, Manitoba, waiting for the sea to freeze so they can walk out onto the ice to hunt seals. Visitors watch them from big-wheeled tundra vehicles, until, usually in late November, the ice forms and the bears head out to sea.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wide-open land and water: Canada has the longest coastline of any country and more lakes than the rest of the world combined. And maple syrup, most of the world's supply of which comes from Quebec's sugar bushes.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Inuit throat singing, katajjaq, is traditionally a friendly contest between two women, face to face, trading rhythmic sounds made breathing in and out until one of them laughs or runs out of breath. For the modern bridge, Tanya Tagaq, from Nunavut, turned throat singing into fierce, experimental music; her album Animism won the Polaris Music Prize in 2014.

cards.title: Craft: Kinngait prints
cards.text: In Kinngait (Cape Dorset), on Baffin Island, Inuit artists and printmakers have released a collection of prints every year since 1959: owls, birds, sea spirits and scenes of camp life cut in stone and stencil. Kenojuak Ashevak's The Enchanted Owl, from 1960, became so beloved it was put on a Canadian stamp.

cards.title: Creature: polar bear
cards.text: The largest land carnivore, perfectly built for the Arctic sea ice, where it hunts seals. Its fur looks white but each hair is actually clear and hollow, and its skin underneath is black.

cards.title: Place: the Bay of Fundy
cards.text: Between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world: twice a day, the sea rises and falls as much as 16 meters. At low tide you can walk on the ocean floor around the Hopewell Rocks, tall "flowerpot" rock pillars that stand in water hours later.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Poutine, from Quebec: fries topped with cheese curds that squeak and hot gravy. Butter tarts, small pastries with a gooey syrup filling. And maple syrup on everything, or poured hot on clean snow and rolled onto a stick as tire d'érable.

140.name: Central African Republic

word.meaning: "Hello!" in Sango, the language nearly everyone in the country shares. "Balao!" and a handshake start every conversation.

140.ask: Ask how their family makes ngunza, cassava leaves cooked with peanut paste, and what goes with it: gozo, cassava dough, or rice.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Central Africans follow the national team and the European leagues closely.

Music: Congolese rumba and local bands fill parties, and anyone who loves to dance is welcome.

The forest: many are proud of their forests and the elephants of Dzanga-Sangha.

cards.title: This season: the dry season in Dzanga-Sangha
cards.text: From December, the dry season comes to the southwestern rainforest, and paths through the forest open up. At Dzanga Bai, a large clearing, forest elephants gather by the dozens to drink mineral-rich water and socialize, watched by visitors from a wooden platform.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its forests, full of elephants, gorillas and birds. The singing of the Aka people. And Sango, a language that brings the whole country together.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Aka people of the southwestern forest sing in complex polyphony, many voices weaving together with yodeling and clapping, for hunting, honey gathering and celebrations. UNESCO lists their singing as heritage.

links.label: Aka Pygmies: Musics and Polyphonic Songs from the Great Forest

cards.title: Craft: butterfly-wing art
cards.text: In Bangui, artists make pictures of villages, animals and landscapes from the colorful wings of butterflies, arranged piece by piece like a mosaic.

cards.title: Creature: forest elephant
cards.text: Smaller than savanna elephants, with rounder ears and straighter tusks, forest elephants live in the rainforest and gather at clearings like Dzanga Bai.

cards.title: Place: Boali Falls
cards.text: West of Bangui, the Mbali River pours over a wide rock face in a curtain of water about 50 meters high, especially powerful after the rains.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ngunza with gozo. Grilled fish from the rivers. And kanda, meatballs cooked in a sauce.

144.name: Sri Lanka

word.meaning: The Sinhala greeting, said with palms pressed together and a small bow, meaning "may you live long." It's how you say hello, goodbye and welcome.

144.ask: Ask how they like their hoppers, the bowl-shaped rice-flour pancakes crisp at the edges and soft in the middle, and whether an egg hopper is the best kind.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: Sri Lanka's 1996 World Cup win is a proud memory, and cricket fans have instant common ground.

Tea: Ceylon tea is loved, and tea lovers have a friend.

Food: rice and curry, hoppers and kottu are family favorites.

cards.title: This season: blue whales off Mirissa
cards.text: From about November to April, the calm seas off Mirissa on the south coast become one of the best places in the world to see blue whales, the largest animals that have ever lived, as well as sperm whales, spinner dolphins and more. December to March is usually best.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Ceylon tea, grown on emerald hillsides in the cool central highlands since the 1800s and picked by hand. And its long history, including Anuradhapura's sacred Bodhi tree, grown from a cutting of the tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment, more than 2,000 years ago.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Kandyan drums of the hill country, played for dancers in elaborate silver headdresses at temple festivals like the Esala Perahera, are the heartbeat of Sinhala tradition. On the coast, baila, brought by the Portuguese and made Sri Lankan, is the lively party music of every wedding and celebration. W. D. Amaradeva, singer, violinist and composer, shaped modern Sinhala music from these roots.

cards.title: Craft: Ambalangoda masks
cards.text: In the coastal town of Ambalangoda, carvers make vivid painted wooden masks of demons, kings and animals, used in traditional dance-dramas and healing rituals, with bulging eyes, fangs and cobra headdresses.

cards.title: Creature: Sri Lankan leopard
cards.text: A leopard found only on the island, and Sri Lanka's top predator. Yala National Park has one of the highest densities of leopards in the world.

cards.title: Place: Sigiriya
cards.text: A fortress on top of a huge rock rising 200 meters from the jungle, built by a king in the 400s, with painted maidens on its walls and a staircase entered through the paws of a giant stone lion. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Rice and curry, with many small curries at once: dhal, jackfruit, beetroot, fish and sambol. Kiribath, milk rice cut into diamonds for New Year and special mornings. And a cup of strong Ceylon tea with milk.

148.name: Chad

word.meaning: Health, peace and well-being, used in greetings across the Sahel. Chad has more than 120 languages, with French and Chadian Arabic shared by many, and lafiya is one of the words that travels between them.

148.ask: Ask what they drink when it's hot: karkanji, a sweet, deep red hibiscus drink with ginger, or something else, and how their family makes it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
