Tea: small glasses of strong, sweet tea, brewed three times and shared with friends through the afternoon, are an everyday ritual.

Wrestling: traditional wrestling draws big, cheering crowds, and anyone who loves a sport with deep roots can ask about it.

Music and dance: celebrations bring the music of the country's many peoples, and fans of Saharan and Central African music have a lot to talk about.

cards.title: This season: Zakouma in the dry season
cards.text: From December, as the rains' water dries up, animals gather around the remaining pools of Zakouma National Park: herds of buffalo, giraffes, antelopes, lions and elephants. Zakouma's elephants, once devastated by poaching, have been protected and are growing again, and their calves are a sign of hope.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its landscapes, from the Sahara and the sandstone arches of the Ennedi to the savannas of the south and Lake Chad. And the rebirth of Zakouma, one of Africa's great conservation stories.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Chad's music mixes the rhythms and songs of its many peoples, played on lutes, harps and drums. Mounira Mitchala, "the Sweet Panther," sings in Chadian Arabic and other languages with a modern sound, and won the RFI Discoveries prize.

cards.title: Craft: basketry
cards.text: Women weave colorful baskets, food covers and mats from palm and grass, dyed in bright reds, greens and purples, in tight coiled patterns. They're used every day and sold in the markets of N'Djamena.

cards.title: Creature: Kordofan giraffe
cards.text: Zakouma is one of the last homes of the Kordofan giraffe, a rare kind of giraffe of Central Africa, whose numbers have grown there with protection.

cards.title: Place: the Ennedi Massif
cards.text: In the northeast, wind and water have carved the sandstone into arches, towers and canyons, with ancient rock paintings of cattle and people and a guelta where desert crocodiles once lived. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Boule, a firm millet or maize porridge, with okra or peanut sauce. Grilled meat from the market. And karkanji.

152.name: Chile

word.meaning: Chile's early-evening meal of tea or coffee with bread, avocado, cheese, ham and cake, somewhere between afternoon tea and a light supper. Families gather for onces instead of a big dinner, and it's where a lot of the day's news gets shared.

152.ask: Ask what goes on the table at their family's onces, and whether their bread of choice is the round marraqueta or the soft hallulla.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
The outdoors: hiking in Patagonia, skiing in the Andes, and stargazing in the Atacama are shared passions.

Food and wine: empanadas, asados and Chilean wine are loved at home and abroad.

Poetry: Pablo Neruda and Gabriela Mistral, both Nobel winners, are read and quoted, and anyone who loves Neruda has a friend.

cards.title: This season: the flowering desert
cards.text: This year the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is in flower. Heavy winter rains brought by El Niño woke seeds that had waited under the sand for years, and more than 200 species are blooming across what could be the largest desierto florido ever recorded. The most flowers are expected from late September to mid-October, with the bloom lasting into late November: carpets of magenta pata de guanaco, yellow, white and violet as far as the eye can see.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its poets: two Chileans, Gabriela Mistral in 1945 and Pablo Neruda in 1971, have won the Nobel Prize in Literature. And its skies: the clear, dry air of the Atacama makes northern Chile home to some of the world's greatest astronomical observatories.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Chilean folk runs from the cueca, the national dance, where partners circle each other waving handkerchiefs, to the nueva canción of the 1960s. Violeta Parra, singer, songwriter, collector of folk songs and artist, wrote "Gracias a la vida," a hymn of gratitude sung around the world, and released it on her last album in 1966. For the modern bridge, Mon Laferte, from Viña del Mar, moves between bolero, cumbia, rock and ranchera with a voice full of feeling.

cards.title: Craft: horsehair weaving in Rari
cards.text: In the tiny village of Rari, in the Maule region, women have woven dyed horsehair for over 300 years into miniature flowers, butterflies, birds and jewelry, so fine they look like lace. UNESCO has honored the craft with a Seal of Excellence for Handicraft Products.

cards.title: Creature: huemul
cards.text: A stocky Andean deer that appears on Chile's coat of arms, alongside the condor. It lives in the forests and mountains of Patagonia and is endangered, with only a few thousand left.

cards.title: Place: Rapa Nui
cards.text: Easter Island, far out in the Pacific, where the Rapa Nui people carved nearly a thousand moai, giant stone figures of their ancestors, and raised many of them on platforms facing inland to watch over their communities. The national park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Empanadas de pino, filled with beef, onion, egg and an olive, baked for the national holidays. Pastel de choclo, a baked corn pie. And in summer, mote con huesillo, a sweet drink of peach nectar with dried peaches and husked wheat.

156.name: China

word.meaning: "Hot and noisy," and meant as praise: the happy bustle of a crowded market, a family banquet with everyone talking at once, a street festival full of lanterns and music. A place that's rènao is alive.
word.sayIt: ruh-NOW (both syllables fairly even, the first falling)

156.ask: Ask how their family makes dumplings for the New Year, who folds them best, and whether anyone hides a coin inside one for luck.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: regional cuisines are a huge source of pride, and people love talking about their hometown dishes, like Sichuan hotpot or Cantonese dim sum.

Lunar New Year: the family reunion dinner, red envelopes and fireworks are a shared joy, much like holiday gatherings elsewhere.

Badminton, ping-pong and basketball: all hugely popular, and many follow the NBA.

cards.title: This season: Double Ninth
cards.text: On the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, October 18 this year, the Chongyang Festival honors older people. Families climb hills to enjoy the autumn view, admire chrysanthemums, which bloom now, and eat chongyang gao, layered steamed cakes, since the word for cake sounds like the word for "high." It's also Seniors' Day, a time to visit grandparents.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: One of the world's oldest continuous civilizations, with a written language used for more than 3,000 years, and inventions that changed everything: paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder. And its food, one of the world's great cuisines, with a different style in every province.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The guqin, a seven-stringed zither played for about 3,000 years, was the instrument of scholars and poets, quiet enough to play for oneself; UNESCO lists its music as heritage. For the modern bridge, the singer Gong Linna, from Guizhou, joins traditional Chinese vocal styles with new composition in what she calls New Chinese Art Music.

links.label: Master of Traditional Chinese Music: Guqin, Guan Pinghu

cards.title: Craft: Suzhou embroidery
cards.text: In Suzhou, embroiderers split silk thread into strands finer than a hair to stitch cats, fish and flowers so delicate they look painted, sometimes on both sides of a single sheer panel, with a different image on each side. It's one of China's four great embroidery traditions.

cards.title: Creature: giant panda
cards.text: The black-and-white bear of the bamboo forests of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, which spends most of its day eating bamboo. Decades of protection have helped wild numbers grow, and it's no longer classed as endangered.

cards.title: Place: the Li River at Guilin
cards.text: Near Guilin and Yangshuo, the Li River winds between hundreds of steep, green limestone peaks, a landscape painted and written about for centuries and pictured on the 20-yuan note. The karst hills of South China are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Jiaozi, dumplings, for the New Year. Hot pot, a bubbling pot of broth in the middle of the table for cooking meat and vegetables together. Peking duck, with its crisp skin wrapped in thin pancakes. And autumn's hairy crabs from the lakes around Shanghai, a seasonal treat.

158.name: Taiwan

word.meaning: Just the letter Q, and a favorite Taiwanese food word: bouncy, springy and chewy, like good noodles, mochi, fish balls or the tapioca pearls in bubble tea. Something extra chewy is "QQ."

158.ask: Ask which night market has the best food, and what they always order there first.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Night markets: Taiwanese love sharing favorite stalls and snacks, and anyone who loves street food has a friend.

Bubble tea: invented in Taiwan, and people have strong opinions about sweetness levels and toppings.

Baseball: Taiwan's 2024 Premier12 win was a huge celebration, and baseball is a national passion.

cards.title: This season: persimmon drying
cards.text: From September to December, the dry autumn wind blows through Xinpu, in Hsinchu, and Hakka families lay out thousands of peeled persimmons on bamboo trays in their courtyards. The fields glow orange, and the fruit slowly turns into sweet, chewy dried persimmons.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food, from night markets to beef noodle soup and bubble tea, which was invented in Taiwan. Its mountains, forests and coast, packed into one island. And its friendliness to visitors.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Teresa Teng, one of the most beloved singers in Asian history, sang gentle love songs like "The Moon Represents My Heart" in Mandarin, Japanese and other languages from the 1970s to the 90s. Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, like the Amis, have their own traditions of polyphonic singing.

cards.title: Craft: Meinong oil-paper umbrellas
cards.text: In the Hakka town of Meinong, craftspeople make umbrellas from bamboo frames and hand-painted paper, oiled to keep out the rain, with flowers and birds on them. They're given as gifts for weddings and coming of age.

cards.title: Creature: Taiwan blue magpie
cards.text: A long-tailed bird of brilliant blue with a red beak and legs, found only in Taiwan's mountain forests. Families move through the trees together, and all help raise the chicks.

cards.title: Place: Taroko Gorge
cards.text: A deep marble canyon cut by the Liwu River, with sheer walls, tunnels, shrines and trails, in the mountains of eastern Taiwan.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Beef noodle soup. Xiaolongbao, soup dumplings. Bubble tea. And pineapple cakes, buttery pastries filled with pineapple jam.

170.name: Colombia

word.meaning: In Colombia, a tinto isn't red wine: it's a small cup of black coffee, often sold for a few coins from a thermos on the street. "¿Nos tomamos un tinto?" ("Shall we have a tinto?") is really an invitation to sit down and talk.

170.ask: Ask what their family eats at Christmas, and who makes the buñuelos and natilla. The answer usually comes with memories of cousins, music and staying up late.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music and dancing: salsa, cumbia, vallenato and stars like Shakira and Carlos Vives make music an easy connection.

Coffee: Colombians are proud of their coffee, and coffee lovers have lots to talk about.

Football: the national team and James Rodríguez are loved, and match days are big gatherings.

cards.title: This season: Día de las Velitas
cards.text: On the night of December 7, the Day of the Little Candles, Colombians set candles and paper lanterns on windowsills, balconies, sidewalks and plazas in honor of the Virgin Mary, on the eve of the Immaculate Conception. Whole streets glow, and the night marks the start of the Christmas season.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its birds: Colombia has recorded more than 1,900 bird species, more than any other country in the world, from tiny hummingbirds to the Andean condor. And its coffee, grown on steep Andean slopes and picked by hand.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Cumbia was born on Colombia's Caribbean coast, mixing African drums, Indigenous gaita flutes and Spanish verse, and it has since spread across Latin America. From the same coast come vallenato, played on accordion, and the joyful Afro-Colombian champeta. Totó la Momposina, a great singer of the coast's traditional music, recorded the classic La Candela Viva in 1993. For the modern bridge, Bomba Estéreo blends cumbia and other Colombian rhythms with electronic music; their 2021 album Deja is a good way in.

links.label: La Candela Viva, Totó la Momposina

cards.title: Craft: Wayuu mochilas
cards.text: The Wayuu people of the La Guajira desert, in the far north, crochet mochilas, shoulder bags patterned with bold, colorful geometric designs, each one taking weeks. Traditionally, girls learn the craft as they come of age, and each pattern carries meaning.

cards.title: Creature: Andean condor
cards.text: Colombia's national bird, one of the largest flying birds in the world, which can glide for hours over the Andes on wings spanning about three meters.

cards.title: Place: Caño Cristales
cards.text: The "river of five colors," in the Serranía de la Macarena. From roughly June to November, an aquatic plant found only in Colombia, Macarenia clavigera, blooms red and pink on the riverbed, among yellow sand, green algae and blue water, and in September and October the red is at its brightest.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Arepas, corn cakes eaten across the country, each region with its own style. Ajiaco, Bogotá's comforting chicken and potato soup flavored with the herb guasca, served with cream, capers and avocado. And at Christmas, buñuelos, fried cheese fritters, with natilla, a soft, spiced custard.

178.name: Republic of the Congo

word.meaning: "Hello!" in Lingala, spoken on both banks of the Congo River. "Mbote na yo," hello to you, and the answer is "mbote."

178.ask: Ask what they think of the sapeurs, and whether anyone in their family dresses up for Sunday.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rumba: Congolese rumba is loved, and anyone who loves to dance has a friend.

La Sape: dressing up elegantly is celebrated, and fashion lovers have lots to talk about.

Football: Congolese follow their national team and the European leagues passionately.

cards.title: This season: the sapeurs of Brazzaville
cards.text: Any season is the season for the Sape: on Sundays and holidays, the sapeurs, Brazzaville's elegant dandies, parade through the streets in bright designer suits, silk ties, polished shoes and pipes, showing off their style with poses and wit. It's a proud celebration of elegance and joy.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Congolese rumba, which UNESCO lists as heritage, shared with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its rainforests, full of gorillas and forest elephants. And the Poto-Poto school of painting.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Congolese rumba, born in Brazzaville and Kinshasa in the 1940s and 50s, mixes Cuban rhythms with Congolese guitar and song. Les Bantous de la Capitale, formed in Brazzaville in 1959, were among its greatest bands, and their music still fills dance floors.

cards.title: Craft: Poto-Poto painting
cards.text: The Poto-Poto School of Painting in Brazzaville, founded in 1951, is known for its bright, elongated figures of people, fish, animals and market scenes, a style that spread across Africa.

cards.title: Creature: western lowland gorilla
cards.text: The rainforests of the north, like Odzala-Kokoua National Park, are home to many western lowland gorillas, which gather in forest clearings to feed on plants and minerals.

cards.title: Place: the Sangha Trinational
cards.text: A huge, untouched rainforest shared with Cameroon and the Central African Republic, with forest elephants, gorillas, chimpanzees and clearings where animals gather. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Saka-saka, pounded cassava leaves cooked with peanuts and fish. Poulet moambé, chicken in palm nut sauce. And chikwangue, fermented cassava bread wrapped in leaves.

180.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo

word.meaning: "To dance," in Lingala. In a country whose music has set the whole continent dancing, kobina is an invitation you'll hear at every party, wedding and bar in Kinshasa.

180.ask: Ask who their favorite rumba singer is, Franco, Papa Wemba, Koffi Olomidé, Fally Ipupa, and which song gets their family on the dance floor.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rumba and soukous: Congolese music has set Africa dancing for decades, and fans of African music have a lot to share.

Style: la sape, dressing up elegantly, is celebrated, and anyone who loves fashion has a way in.

Football and basketball: Congolese follow both, and NBA players like Dikembe Mutombo are heroes.

cards.title: This season: Christmas in Kinshasa
cards.text: In December, Kinshasa, one of Africa's biggest cities, gets ready for Christmas and New Year, with church choirs rehearsing, families saving for new clothes, and bands playing late into the night. Congolese churches are famous for their powerful choirs.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Congolese rumba, listed by UNESCO as heritage together with the Republic of the Congo, and the soukous that grew from it. The Congo River, the deepest river in the world. And its rainforest, the second largest on Earth.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Congolese rumba, with its sweet, interlocking guitars and smooth vocals, was shaped in Kinshasa in the 1950s and 60s; Franco and his OK Jazz orchestra were its giants. Papa Wemba, "the king of rumba rock," and today's stars like Fally Ipupa carry it on.

cards.title: Craft: Kuba cloth
cards.text: Kuba men weave raffia palm fiber into squares, and women embroider and cut them into velvety patterns of lines and shapes, with no two alike. The cloths were once used as currency and are still treasured.

cards.title: Creature: okapi
cards.text: A forest animal found only in the Congo, with a giraffe's head and long tongue, a chocolate-brown body and zebra-striped legs. It's the national animal, and a close relative of the giraffe.

cards.title: Place: Salonga National Park
cards.text: Africa's largest tropical rainforest reserve, reached only by river, home to bonobos, great apes found only in the Congo and known for their peaceful, playful ways. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Moambe chicken, cooked in palm nut sauce, the national dish. Pondu, pounded cassava leaves. And liboke, fish steamed in banana leaves with spices.

188.name: Costa Rica

word.meaning: "Pure life": hello, goodbye, thanks, no worries, and a whole outlook of enjoying simple things and not sweating the small stuff. Costa Ricans say it constantly.

188.ask: Ask how they like their gallo pinto, rice and beans fried together for breakfast, and whether Salsa Lizano is essential. (It usually is.)

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Nature: sloths, volcanoes, beaches and cloud forests are a source of pride, and many Ticos love hiking, surfing and birdwatching.

Football: the 2014 World Cup run to the quarterfinals, and goalkeeper Keylor Navas, are happy memories.

Gallo pinto for breakfast: rice and beans every morning, with Salsa Lizano on top, is a comfort worth asking about.

cards.title: This season: the arribadas
cards.text: At Ostional, on the Pacific coast, olive ridley sea turtles come ashore by the thousands, sometimes hundreds of thousands, over a few nights to nest, in mass arrivals called arribadas. They happen year-round on a roughly monthly cycle, but the biggest usually come in the rainy season, from July through November, peaking in September and October.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and put the money into schools and health care. And about a quarter of its land is protected in national parks and reserves, home to around five percent of the world's species.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In Guanacaste, the northwest, the marimba and guitars accompany the punto guanacasteco, the national dance, and people shout bombas, funny rhyming verses, between the music. On the Caribbean coast, Afro-Costa Rican calypso keeps its own tradition alive. Its great calypsonian, Walter Ferguson of Cahuita, sang witty songs about village life until he was over 100.

cards.title: Craft: painted oxcarts
cards.text: Oxcarts once carried coffee from the mountains to the ports, and their owners painted them in bright geometric patterns and flowers, with each region having its own style and each wheel making its own "song" as it turned. UNESCO lists the oxherding and oxcart traditions as heritage, and the town of Sarchí still paints them.

cards.title: Creature: three-toed sloth
cards.text: A slow-moving tree dweller that spends most of its life hanging upside down, sleeping many hours a day and coming down to the ground only about once a week. Algae growing in its fur gives it a greenish tint.

cards.title: Place: Monteverde Cloud Forest
cards.text: A misty forest high in the mountains, where trees are draped in moss, orchids and ferns, and hanging bridges let visitors walk through the canopy looking for quetzals.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Gallo pinto for breakfast. A casado for lunch: rice, beans, salad, plantain and meat or fish on one plate. At Christmas, families gather to make tamales wrapped in banana leaves. And coffee, grown in the Central Valley.

191.name: Croatia

word.meaning: A Dalmatian word for a sweet, drowsy state of doing nothing at all, usually on a hot summer afternoon by the sea. Fjaka isn't laziness; it's the art of letting the world slow down.

191.ask: Ask what their family cooks under the peka, the bell-shaped iron lid buried in embers, and how many hours they wait for the lamb or octopus to be ready.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Luka Modrić and the 2018 World Cup final run are a huge source of pride, and Croatians love to talk about it.

The sea: summers on the islands, swimming off the rocks and sailing are shared joys, and everyone has a favorite island.

Game of Thrones: Dubrovnik and Split were filming locations, a fun topic with fans of the show.

cards.title: This season: Advent in Zagreb
cards.text: From November 28 this year until early January, Zagreb turns into one of Europe's best-loved Christmas cities, with light displays, ice skating, concerts and food stalls in squares and parks across the Upper and Lower Towns, and fritule, little doughnuts dusted with sugar, everywhere.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its coast of more than a thousand islands, and the necktie: the cravat takes its name from the scarves worn by Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France. October 18 is celebrated as Cravat Day.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Klapa is Dalmatian a cappella singing by small groups of men or women, in close, rich harmonies about love, the sea and home, sung in harbors and konobas, taverns. UNESCO lists it as heritage.

cards.title: Craft: lace
cards.text: Croatian women make lace in three very different traditions: needle lace from the island of Pag, like a spider's web, bobbin lace from Lepoglava in the north, and delicate lace from Hvar made from threads of the agave plant, a skill kept by the Benedictine nuns. UNESCO lists all three as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: the Dalmatian
cards.text: The spotted dog is named after Dalmatia, the Croatian coast, where it's thought to have been bred as a carriage and guard dog.

cards.title: Place: Plitvice Lakes
cards.text: Sixteen terraced lakes in shades of turquoise and emerald, joined by waterfalls and crossed by wooden walkways through the forest. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Peka, meat or octopus slow-baked under an iron bell in the embers. Štrukli, pastry filled with cottage cheese, from Zagreb. Black risotto made with cuttlefish ink along the coast. And fritule at Christmas.

192.name: Cuba

word.meaning: A big, joyful party, traditionally a country one, with music, dancing, roast pork and friends and neighbors who drop by and stay till dawn.

192.ask: Ask what song always gets their family dancing, and who in the family dances best. In Cuba that's rarely a hard question to answer.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music and dance: son, salsa, the Buena Vista Social Club and dancing at every party.

Baseball: Cubans are passionate about baseball, and many Cuban players have starred in the Major Leagues.

Dominoes: games of dominoes played loudly with friends on the street or porch are a beloved pastime.

cards.title: This season: the Parrandas of Remedios
cards.text: On the night of December 24, the small town of Remedios splits into two rival neighborhoods, San Salvador and El Carmen, which spend the whole year secretly building enormous illuminated floats and towers of lights and planning fireworks. On the night, they compete with music, drums and dazzling displays until dawn. The tradition began in 1820 and, with the other parrandas of central Cuba, is on UNESCO's heritage list.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music, which has shaped the world's dance floors: son, rumba, mambo, cha-cha-chá and salsa's roots all grew here. Rumba, and the bolero Cuba shares with Mexico, are both on UNESCO's heritage list.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Son cubano, born in the east of the island, joins Spanish guitar, the Cuban tres and African rhythm played on bongos and claves. In 1996 a group of veteran musicians gathered in Havana to record Buena Vista Social Club, and it became one of the best-loved albums of its kind ever made. For the modern bridge, the singer Daymé Arocena blends son, rumba, jazz and soul; her album Alkemi came out in 2024.

cards.title: Craft: the guayabera
cards.text: A light, loose shirt for the heat, worn untucked, with four pockets and fine vertical pleats or embroidery down the front and back. It's worn everywhere from the countryside to state occasions, and making one well is a tailor's art.

cards.title: Creature: bee hummingbird
cards.text: The smallest bird in the world, found only in Cuba, about five centimeters long and lighter than a dime. Its wings beat about 80 times a second.

cards.title: Place: the Viñales Valley
cards.text: In the west, green tobacco fields and red earth lie beneath mogotes, steep, rounded limestone hills covered in forest, farmed in traditional ways with oxen. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ropa vieja, shredded beef stewed with peppers and tomato. Moros y cristianos, black beans and rice cooked together. Roast pork on Christmas Eve, and a tiny cup of strong, sweet café cubano.

196.name: Cyprus

word.meaning: "Come, join us!" Called out to a passerby when people are eating, it's an invitation to sit down and share the meal. In Cyprus, it's meant.

196.ask: Ask how they like their halloumi, grilled, fried or fresh with watermelon in summer, and whose family makes the best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Halloumi: Cypriots love that the world loves their cheese, and have strong opinions about grilling it.

Sunday meze: long family lunches with dozens of small dishes are a ritual anyone who loves a long meal understands.

Summer and the sea: life moves to the beach in summer, and Cypriots love recommending their favorite coves.

cards.title: This season: grape sweets
cards.text: In autumn, when the grapes are harvested in the wine villages of the Troodos foothills, families boil fresh grape juice into palouze, a soft grape pudding. Then they dip strings of almonds or walnuts into it again and again, and hang them to dry into soutzoukos, chewy sweets that look like candles.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its sunshine, beaches and mountains, and a long history layered in one island, from ancient mosaics to Byzantine churches. And its food: halloumi, meze and slow-cooked kleftiko, loved across the island.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Cypriot folk music is played on violin and laouto, a long-necked lute. In tsiattista, singers trade improvised rhyming verses back and forth, trying to top each other with wit; UNESCO lists it as heritage.

cards.title: Craft: Lefkara lace
cards.text: Women in the village of Lefkara have embroidered fine white lace for centuries, with geometric patterns stitched on linen. Legend says Leonardo da Vinci took a Lefkara altar cloth to Milan Cathedral. UNESCO lists it as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Cyprus mouflon
cards.text: A wild sheep found only on Cyprus, with curved horns and a reddish-brown coat, living in the forests of the Troodos and Paphos mountains. It's a symbol of the island.

cards.title: Place: the painted churches of the Troodos
cards.text: Small stone churches with steep wooden roofs, hidden in mountain villages, painted inside from floor to ceiling with Byzantine frescoes. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Halloumi. Meze, a long parade of small dishes. Kleftiko, lamb slow-cooked in a sealed clay oven. And loukoumades, honey-soaked doughnuts.

203.name: Czechia

word.meaning: Calm contentment, ease, the feeling that all is well: a quiet evening, a good beer, a walk in the woods. "V pohodě" means "no problem, it's fine," and Czechs say it all the time.

203.ask: Ask how their family celebrates Christmas Eve, and whether anyone still keeps a live carp in the bathtub before the Christmas dinner, a tradition some families love and others have happily retired.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hockey: the national team's wins, especially at the 1998 Olympics, are proud memories, and many follow the NHL.

Hiking and cottages: weekend trips to the chata or chalupa, a country cottage, and marked hiking trails everywhere are a shared joy.

Beer: Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone, and love to talk about Pilsner and local breweries.

cards.title: This season: St. Nicholas Eve
cards.text: On the evening of December 5, St. Nicholas (Mikuláš), in his bishop's robes, walks the streets with an angel and a devil. Children recite a poem or sing a song and receive sweets and fruit from the angel, while the devil rattles his chains at anyone who's been naughty. Then Advent markets fill Prague's squares.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Prague itself, with its bridges, spires and old town, largely spared in the wars. And its music and stories, from Dvořák and Smetana to the fairy-tale films and animated characters, like the little Mole, that generations have grown up with.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Czech classical music grew from folk songs and dances; Antonín Dvořák wove their spirit into his symphonies, including the "New World" Symphony, written in America with longing for home. Moravian folk music, with fiddles and cimbalom, a hammered dulcimer, is still played and sung at village festivals.

links.label: Dvořák: Complete Symphonies, Neeme Järvi and the Royal Scottish National Orchestra

cards.title: Craft: glass-bead Christmas ornaments
cards.text: In Poniklá, in northern Bohemia, craftspeople blow tiny glass beads by hand, silver them, color them, and thread them on wire into stars, snowflakes, angels and cars. It's the only place in the world where the craft survives, and UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2020.

cards.title: Creature: European otter
cards.text: Czechia's rivers and fishponds are home to the otter, which has made a strong comeback after decades of decline.

cards.title: Place: Český Krumlov
cards.text: A small town wrapped in a tight loop of the Vltava River, with a huge castle, red roofs and winding lanes, barely changed since the Renaissance. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with bread dumplings and cranberries. Christmas cookies, baked by the dozen kinds. Vánočka, a braided Christmas bread. And some of the world's most loved beer.

204.name: Benin

word.meaning: The motorbike taxis of Cotonou, whose drivers wear bright yellow shirts. The name comes from Fon and means "take me quickly." Hop on the back, say where you're going, and weave through the city.

204.ask: Ask how they like their amiwo, red cornmeal cooked with tomato and spices and served with chicken, and who makes the best at family celebrations.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Angélique Kidjo: many people abroad know her songs, and she's a source of great pride.

Market life: bargaining, chatting and shopping at huge markets like Dantokpa in Cotonou is a shared joy for anyone who loves markets.

Football: Beninese follow their national team and the big European leagues closely.

cards.title: This season: getting ready for Vodun Days
cards.text: Benin celebrates its Vodun heritage every January, and from January 2 to 9, 2027, Vodun Days will fill the coastal town of Ouidah with ceremonies, masked Egungun dancers, drumming, open-air concerts and visitors from across Africa and the diaspora.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its history as the Kingdom of Dahomey, with its royal palaces and the Agojie, its famous women soldiers. Its music, carried around the world by Angélique Kidjo. And its place as the birthplace of Vodun, now celebrated as a national holiday.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Rhythms from Vodun ceremonies, played on drums and bells, run through Beninese music, along with brass bands and highlife. Angélique Kidjo, from Ouidah, mixes these roots with funk, jazz and pop, and has won five Grammy awards.

cards.title: Craft: Abomey appliqué
cards.text: In Abomey, families of tailors once made banners and hangings for the kings of Dahomey, sewing bright cutout figures of animals and symbols onto cloth, each one standing for a king and his motto. They still make them today.

cards.title: Creature: West African lion
cards.text: In the Pendjari National Park in the north, one of the last strongholds of lions in West Africa, they share the savanna with elephants, buffaloes and hippos. The park is part of the W-Arly-Pendjari UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Place: Ganvié
cards.text: A village built on stilts in Lake Nokoué, home to thousands of people, where homes, schools and a floating market are reached by pirogue, a dugout canoe. It's often called "the Venice of Africa."

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Amiwo with chicken. Pâte, a smooth maize porridge, with tomato or peanut sauce and fish. And aloko, fried plantains.

208.name: Denmark

word.meaning: The warm, cozy feeling of being together with people you like, in a relaxed, unhurried way: candles, a pot of coffee, a blanket, good talk. Danes use it constantly, and "hyggelig" is a high compliment for an evening, a room or a person.

208.ask: Ask what their favorite smørrebrød is, the open-faced rye sandwiches, and in what order you're supposed to eat them.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hygge: candles, coffee, cake and cozy evenings with friends, which many people love too.

Cycling: biking everywhere is a shared joy for anyone who commutes by bike.

LEGO: many people grew up with LEGO, invented in Denmark, and Danes are proud of it.

cards.title: This season: Mortensaften
cards.text: On November 10, Danish families gather for Mortensaften, Saint Martin's Eve, with roast duck or goose, red cabbage, gravy and caramelized potatoes. The story goes that Saint Martin hid among geese to avoid being made a bishop, but their honking gave him away. Then comes the Christmas season, with candles in every window.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Hans Christian Andersen, whose fairy tales, like "The Little Mermaid" and "The Ugly Duckling," are known all over the world. LEGO, invented in the small town of Billund. And cycling: Copenhagen has more bikes than cars.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Danish village fiddle tunes, played for weddings and dances, live on in folk music today. The Danish String Quartet, famous for classical music, recorded these old Nordic folk tunes in their album "Wood Works."

cards.title: Craft: woven Christmas hearts
cards.text: Julehjerter are heart-shaped baskets woven from two strips of glossy paper, hung on the Christmas tree and filled with sweets. Hans Christian Andersen made one of the oldest known, in 1860, and families still spend December afternoons cutting and weaving new ones.

cards.title: Creature: the starling's black sun
cards.text: In spring and autumn, huge flocks of starlings gather over the marshes of the Wadden Sea in southwest Denmark. At sunset they swirl in vast, shifting shapes that can darken the sky, which the Danes call "sort sol," the black sun.

cards.title: Place: Kronborg Castle
cards.text: A Renaissance castle at Helsingør guarding the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden, and the Elsinore of Shakespeare's "Hamlet," which is still performed there. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Smørrebrød on dark rye bread. Frikadeller, pan-fried meatballs. Flæskesteg, roast pork with crackling, at Christmas. And wienerbrød, flaky pastries that the rest of the world calls Danishes.

214.name: Dominican Republic

word.meaning: "Thing," "stuff," "whatever-it-is": the most useful word in Dominican Spanish. "Pásame esa vaina" (pass me that thing), "¡qué vaina!" (what a mess!), "esa vaina está buena" (that's great). If you forget a word, vaina will do.

214.ask: The winter baseball league plays from October into January. Ask which team they cheer for, Licey, Escogido, Águilas or another, and who the best player from their town is.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Baseball: many Dominicans follow their players in the Major Leagues, like David Ortiz and Juan Soto, and a talk about baseball goes a long way.

Merengue and bachata: dancing at every party, and bachata classes are popular worldwide.

Family and food: big family gatherings with sancocho and la bandera, the national plate, are a comfort many people understand.

cards.title: This season: Christmas starts early
cards.text: Dominicans start Christmas early: by November, homes and streets are hung with lights, and through December friends, classmates and coworkers play angelito, a secret gift exchange. Christmas Eve brings a big family dinner with roast pork, and merengue and bachata keep the parties going late.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Merengue and bachata, danced around the world. Baseball: the Dominican Republic has sent more players to the Major Leagues than any country outside the United States. And Santo Domingo, the first European city in the Americas.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Merengue, fast and joyful, with accordion, güira and the two-headed tambora drum, is the national dance; bachata, born in poor neighborhoods as guitar songs of love and heartbreak, grew into a global sound. UNESCO lists both as heritage. Juan Luis Guerra's 1990 album "Bachata Rosa" helped carry bachata to the world.

cards.title: Craft: larimar
cards.text: Larimar, a sky-blue stone streaked with white like sunlight through seawater, is found only in the mountains of Barahona in the southwest. Jewelers polish it and set it in silver, often alongside Dominican amber.

cards.title: Creature: palmchat
cards.text: The national bird, a chatty olive-brown bird found only on Hispaniola. Palmchats build big shared nests in royal palms, with separate rooms for each pair.

cards.title: Place: the Colonial City of Santo Domingo
cards.text: The old town, founded in 1498, with the first cathedral, university and hospital in the Americas along its stone streets. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: La bandera, "the flag": rice, red beans and stewed meat, with salad and fried plantains. Mangú, mashed green plantains with pickled red onions, for breakfast. And sancocho, a rich stew of many meats and root vegetables.

218.name: Ecuador

word.meaning: "Brrr!" An exclamation for "it's so cold!", borrowed from Kichwa, the Indigenous language of the Andes. Its opposite is "arrarray!", for "ouch, that's hot!" Both are part of everyday Ecuadorian Spanish.

218.ask: Ask where to find the best encebollado, the tangy fish-and-onion soup Ecuadorians swear by, especially the morning after a party.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Nature: the Galápagos, the volcano road through the Andes and the Amazon are sources of pride, and nature lovers have plenty to talk about.

Football: Ecuadorians follow the national team, La Tri, and stars like Moisés Caicedo of Chelsea.

Food: ceviche, locro de papa and bananas in every form, and Ecuadorians love comparing dishes from the coast and the highlands.

cards.title: This season: the Fiestas de Quito
cards.text: In early December, Quito celebrates its founding with a week of parades, concerts, street dancing, and chivas, open-sided party buses with bands playing on board, winding through the city. It's also the season of canelazo, a hot cinnamon and fruit drink sold on cold highland nights.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its astonishing variety: the Amazon rainforest, the Andes and the Pacific coast, plus the Galápagos Islands, all in a country about the size of Colorado. And it was the first country in the world to give nature its own rights in its constitution, in 2008.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The pasillo, a slow, heartfelt song form, is the soul of Ecuadorian popular music, and UNESCO lists it as heritage, as it does the marimba music of the Afro-Ecuadorians of Esmeraldas. For the modern bridge, the producer Nicola Cruz mixes Andean flutes, rhythms and chants with slow electronic beats in a style he calls "Andes Step," starting with his album Prender el Alma.

cards.title: Craft: the toquilla straw hat
cards.text: The so-called Panama hat is actually from Ecuador: woven by hand from the fine fibers of the toquilla palm, in towns like Montecristi and Cuenca. The finest can take months to weave and be rolled up without creasing. UNESCO lists the craft as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Galápagos giant tortoise
cards.text: Huge tortoises that can live well over a hundred years, found only on the Galápagos, each island's tortoises with a slightly different shell. They helped inspire Charles Darwin's thinking on evolution.

cards.title: Place: the Galápagos Islands
cards.text: Volcanic islands 1,000 kilometers off the coast, where fearless sea lions, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies and giant tortoises live alongside visitors. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Encebollado, fish and onion soup with yuca. Llapingachos, potato patties stuffed with cheese, from the highlands. And canelazo, hot cinnamon and naranjilla drink.

222.name: El Salvador

word.meaning: "Cool! Great!" In Salvadoran Spanish, anything wonderful is chivo: a chivo party, a chivo view, "¡qué chivo!" Literally, it means "goat."

222.ask: Ask which pupusa filling they love most: cheese, beans, chicharrón, loroco flowers or all mixed together as a revuelta, and how much curtido they pile on.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Pupusas: Salvadorans love to share their favorite fillings, and many people in the US have eaten them at a local pupusería.

Surfing: beaches like El Tunco and Punta Roca are world-famous surf spots, and surfers have instant common ground.

Football: Salvadorans follow the national team, La Selecta, and local clubs with great passion.

cards.title: This season: La Calabiuza
cards.text: On November 1, the town of Tonacatepeque, north of San Salvador, celebrates La Calabiuza. People dress up as the creatures of Salvadoran legend, like La Siguanaba, her mischievous son El Cipitío in his big hat, and the black dog El Cadejo, and parade creaking carts decorated with skulls and torches. Children once went door to door asking for pumpkin cooked in honey.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Pupusas, the national dish, with their own National Pupusa Day in November. Its volcanoes, lakes and Pacific surf beaches. And the determination and warmth of its people, in El Salvador and abroad.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The marimba and cumbia fill Salvadoran celebrations; cumbia salvadoreña, played by big dance bands, is heard at every party and fiesta. Folk songs celebrate villages, volcanoes and pupusas. Los Hermanos Flores, ten brothers from San Vicente, became the country's most famous dance orchestra.

cards.title: Craft: La Palma painting
cards.text: In the mountain town of La Palma, artists paint wooden boxes, crosses and panels in bright, simple, joyful designs of houses, birds, flowers and people, a style started in the 1970s by artist Fernando Llort.

cards.title: Creature: turquoise-browed motmot
cards.text: The torogoz, the national bird, with a turquoise brow and two long tail feathers that end in racket-shaped tips, which it swings like a pendulum. Both parents raise the chicks, a symbol of family.

cards.title: Place: Joya de Cerén
cards.text: A farming village buried by volcanic ash around 600 CE, preserving houses, kitchens, gardens and even food, like a snapshot of everyday Maya life. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, sometimes called "the Pompeii of the Americas."

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pupusas with curtido, a tangy cabbage slaw, and tomato salsa. Yuca frita with chicharrón. And horchata made from morro seeds.

226.name: Equatorial Guinea

word.meaning: "Hello!" in Fang, the most widely spoken language on the mainland. Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa where Spanish is an official language, so you might hear "mbolo" and "¿qué tal?" in the same breath.

226.ask: Ask what their favorite dish is from home, and whether it's from the island of Bioko or the mainland.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Spanish: it's the only African country with Spanish as an official language, a connection for Spanish speakers.

Football: the national team's run to the Africa Cup of Nations semifinals in 2015 is a happy memory.

Music and dance: Equatoguineans love dancing, with music from across Central Africa and Latin America.

cards.title: This season: turtles on Bioko
cards.text: From November to February, with a peak in December and January, leatherback and green turtles come ashore to nest on the black-sand beaches of southern Bioko Island, near the village of Ureca. Researchers and local guides watch over the nests.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its islands and forests, especially Bioko, with volcanoes, cloud forest and beaches. Its mix of Spanish and African cultures. And its turtles and primates.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Bubi people of Bioko dance the balélé, especially at Christmas, with drums and colorful costumes. The duo Hijas del Sol sing in Bubi and Spanish, mixing Hispanic and African sounds.

cards.title: Craft: Fang carving
cards.text: Fang sculptors carve wooden masks and figures, with long, calm faces, once used to guard family reliquaries and in ceremonies. They're admired in museums around the world.

cards.title: Creature: drill
cards.text: A large, rare monkey with a black face framed in white fur, found on Bioko and in a small area of the mainland nearby, living in noisy troops in the forest.

cards.title: Place: the Moka Valley
cards.text: High in the mountains of southern Bioko, a cool, green valley of crater lakes, waterfalls and cloud forest, home to rare monkeys and birds.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pepper soup with fish or meat. Plantains and cassava. And grilled fish with spicy sauce, by the sea in Malabo.

231.name: Ethiopia

word.meaning: Feeding someone a bite of injera and stew with your own hand. The bigger the bite, the bigger the affection.

231.ask: Ask how the coffee ceremony works in their family: who roasts, which pot, and whether anyone really stays for all three rounds.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Coffee: Ethiopia is coffee's birthplace, and the coffee ceremony is a joy to share.

Running: Ethiopians are proud of champions like Haile Gebrselassie and Tirunesh Dibaba.

Food with friends: eating from a shared plate of injera, and feeding each other a bite called gursha, is a lovely custom to learn about.

cards.title: This season: Meskel
cards.text: In late September, a towering bonfire called the demera is lit in Addis Ababa's Meskel Square to mark the finding of the True Cross, and UNESCO lists the celebration as heritage. The yellow Meskel daisies bloom across the highlands at the same time, as the rains end.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Apart from a five-year Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941, Ethiopia was never colonized, and its 1896 victory over Italy at Adwa is celebrated every March 2. It also keeps its own script and its own calendar, in which the new year began on September 11 and it's now 2019. And its distance runners are legends, starting with Abebe Bikila, who won the 1960 Olympic marathon barefoot.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Ethiopia has its own family of musical modes, called qenet: tizita, bati, ambassel and anchihoye. Its church chant tradition is credited to Saint Yared in the 6th century. In 1960s and 70s Addis Ababa, Mulatu Astatke fused those modes with jazz and Latin rhythm into Ethio-jazz, and the Éthiopiques record series later carried that sound worldwide.

links.label: Éthiopiques Vol. 4: Mulatu Astatke, with “Yègèllé Tezeta”

cards.title: Craft: habesha kemis
cards.text: A white handwoven cotton dress edged with tibeb, bands of bright woven pattern. Holidays fill streets with them.

cards.title: Creature: gelada
cards.text: Sometimes called the bleeding-heart monkey for the red patch on its chest. It lives only in the Ethiopian highlands, eats mostly grass, and gathers in herds of hundreds that chatter constantly.

cards.title: Place: Lalibela
cards.text: Eleven churches carved downward into solid volcanic rock around 800 years ago. Bete Giyorgis, cut in the shape of a cross, sits in its own pit like a jewel in a setting.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: The coffee ceremony: green beans roasted over coals, ground by hand, brewed in a clay jebena, and served in three rounds (abol, tona and baraka) with frankincense in the air. Injera, a spongy flatbread made from teff, is plate, spoon and bread at once.

232.name: Eritrea

word.meaning: "Peace," and the everyday greeting in Tigrinya. People greet each other warmly, often with several kisses on the cheek or a shoulder bump between friends.

232.ask: Ask about their family's coffee ceremony: roasting the beans, the smell of frankincense, and the three rounds of coffee poured from the clay jebena.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cycling: Eritreans are passionate about cycling, and Biniam Girmay's Tour de France stage wins made them proud.

The coffee ceremony: roasting, brewing and sharing coffee over three rounds is a long, happy ritual to be invited into.

Café culture: Asmara's cafés serve excellent espresso and cappuccino, and coffee lovers have a friend.

cards.title: This season: the green belt
cards.text: From October to March, rains fall on the eastern escarpment between Asmara and the Red Sea coast, when the rest of the highlands are dry. The forests and terraces of the "green belt" around Filfil turn lush and misty, a favorite escape for people from Asmara.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Asmara, with its beautifully preserved modernist buildings from the 1930s, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its cycling: Biniam Girmay became the first Black African to win a stage of the Tour de France, in 2024. And its perseverance.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The krar, a five- or six-stringed lyre, carries the melodies of Tigrinya song, with the kebero drum and shoulder-shaking dances. Yemane Barya was one of Eritrea's most loved singer-songwriters.

cards.title: Craft: the jebena
cards.text: The round-bellied clay coffee pot with a long neck, set on a straw ring and used in the coffee ceremony at home. Potters shape and fire them by hand.

cards.title: Creature: African wild ass
cards.text: The wild ancestor of the donkey, gray with striped legs, survives in the hot, dry Danakil desert of Eritrea and Ethiopia. It's one of the rarest mammals in Africa.

cards.title: Place: Asmara
cards.text: A capital of palm-lined avenues, cafés and Art Deco and modernist buildings, including the Fiat Tagliero, a gas station shaped like an airplane. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Zigni, a spicy stew, with injera. Ful, mashed fava beans, for breakfast. And a macchiato in one of Asmara's cafés.

233.name: Estonia

word.meaning: The wave of soft, hot steam that rises when water is thrown on the stones of a sauna. A good sauna is judged by its leil, and in the south, families still keep smoke saunas, a tradition UNESCO lists as heritage.

233.ask: Ask whether they've sung at the Song Festival, the huge gathering where tens of thousands of singers perform together, and which song always brings tears.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Singing: the Song Festival brings tens of thousands of singers together, and anyone who sings in a choir has a friend.

Tech: Estonians are proud of Skype's roots and their digital government, a fun topic for people who work in tech.

Saunas and forests: forest walks, bog boardwalks, berry picking and saunas are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: Mardipäev and Kadripäev
cards.text: In late autumn, children dress up and go door to door on two old folk holidays: Mardipäev, St. Martin's Day, on November 10, when mardisandid in men's clothes and masks sing, dance and wish good luck, and Kadripäev, St. Catherine's Day, on November 25, when kadrisandid in white bring blessings for the herds and home, in return for treats.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its songs: in the late 1980s, hundreds of thousands of Estonians gathered to sing national songs in what became known as the Singing Revolution, on the road to regaining independence in 1991. And its digital life: Estonia is famous for doing almost everything online, from voting to starting a company.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Song and Dance Celebration, held about every five years in Tallinn, brings a choir of tens of thousands onto one giant stage, and UNESCO lists the Baltic song and dance celebrations as heritage. For the modern bridge, Arvo Pärt, from Paide, writes spare, bell-like music inspired by chant; he's one of the most performed living composers in the world.

links.label: Arvo Pärt, Viktoria Mullova, Estonian National Symphony Orchestra and Paavo Järvi

cards.title: Craft: Kihnu textiles
cards.text: On the small island of Kihnu, women still wear handwoven striped red skirts and knit mittens and stockings in patterns passed down through families. UNESCO lists the island's cultural space, with its songs, dances and crafts, as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Eurasian lynx
cards.text: Estonia's forests are home to one of the healthier lynx populations in Europe, a big-pawed, tufted-eared cat that hunts roe deer and hares in the snow.

cards.title: Place: Tallinn's Old Town
cards.text: A walled medieval town of red-roofed merchant houses, church spires and cobbled streets, one of the best-preserved in northern Europe. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Black rye bread, leib, dark and dense, at every meal. Kiluvõileib, rye bread with spiced sprats, egg and herbs. And at Christmas, blood sausage with lingonberry jam and sauerkraut.

238.name: Falkland Islands

word.meaning: Everywhere outside the capital, Stanley. "Going out to camp" means heading into the open countryside of sheep farms, peat and sea, from the Spanish "campo," countryside.

238.ask: Ask about smoko, the tea break with cakes and biscuits, and what's always on the table on the farms in camp.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Penguins and wildlife: islanders love sharing where to see king penguins, albatrosses and sea lions.

Farm life: many families work sheep farms out in camp, and anyone who grew up rural has stories to trade.

Community events: the Stanley Sports horse races after Christmas and local dances bring everyone together.

cards.title: This season: penguin summer
cards.text: November is the heart of the penguin season. Gentoo penguins sit on their eggs, which hatch in early December; rockhopper penguins lay theirs in early November; and king penguins, Magellanic penguins and albatrosses crowd the colonies, noisy and busy under long summer days.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wildlife: five kinds of penguins breed here, along with black-browed albatrosses, sea lions and elephant seals. And its small, close-knit community, where everyone knows everyone.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Music in the islands is homemade: country and folk songs at dances and community gatherings, fiddles and guitars at the Stanley town hall, and songs about the islands and the sea.

cards.title: Craft: knitting
cards.text: Islanders spin and knit wool from their own sheep into warm sweaters, hats and gloves for the windy weather, and sell them in Stanley's craft shops.

cards.title: Creature: black-browed albatross
cards.text: A great seabird with a wingspan over two meters and a dark "eyebrow" line. The Falklands are home to most of the world's population, nesting in huge colonies on cliffs like those of Steeple Jason.

cards.title: Place: Volunteer Point
cards.text: A long white-sand beach and green grassland where the islands' largest colony of king penguins stands in orange-and-gold groups, alongside gentoos and Magellanic penguins.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mutton, often called "365" because it's eaten every day. Fresh fish and squid. And cakes and scones at smoko.

242.name: Fiji

word.meaning: "Life," and the Fijian greeting, called out with a big smile: "Bula!" It means hello, welcome and good health all at once, and you'll hear it everywhere, many times a day.

242.ask: Ask what goes into a lovo, the feast cooked in an earth oven for big occasions, and who in their family is in charge of wrapping the food in leaves.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rugby sevens: Fiji's Olympic gold medals in 2016 and 2021 are a huge joy, and rugby is a sure conversation starter.

Kava: sharing a bowl of kava with friends and talking late into the night is a social ritual worth learning about.

Singing: church choirs and harmonies are everywhere, and Fijians love to sing together.

cards.title: This season: Diwali, and summer
cards.text: In Fiji, where many families descend from Indians who came in the 1800s and early 1900s, Diwali is a national holiday, on November 8 this year, and homes and streets glow with lamps and fairy lights. November also brings the start of summer, mango season and warm, calm seas.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its warmth and welcome, and its rugby: Fiji won the first-ever Olympic gold medal in rugby sevens in 2016, and again in 2020, and the whole country celebrated.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The meke is Fiji's traditional dance and song, telling stories of history and legend, performed to the beat of the lali, a hollowed log drum, and clapping. Singing is everywhere in Fiji, from church choirs to the guitar and ukulele songs sung around the kava bowl in the evening.

links.label: Meke Songs: Fijian Dance Music, Kavaholics Dance Group

cards.title: Craft: masi
cards.text: Bark cloth made by soaking and beating the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree into thin sheets, then printing it with bold black and brown geometric patterns using stencils. It's given at weddings and important ceremonies.

cards.title: Creature: Fiji crested iguana
cards.text: A striking bright green iguana with white bands and a crest along its back, found only in Fiji and critically endangered, with its largest population protected on the tiny island of Yadua Taba.

cards.title: Place: Levuka
cards.text: Fiji's first colonial capital, on the island of Ovalau, a small port town of wooden buildings between the mountains and the sea, largely unchanged since the 1800s. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kokoda, raw fish marinated in lime and coconut milk with chili and vegetables. Food from the lovo, slow-cooked over hot stones. And kava, or yaqona, a peppery drink made from a root, shared from a big wooden bowl in a ceremony of welcome.

246.name: Finland

word.meaning: Quiet, stubborn inner strength: the grit to keep going when things are hard, without making a fuss about it. Finns see sisu as part of who they are.

246.ask: Ask about their family's summer cottage, the mökki, and how many times a day they go from the sauna into the lake. In winter, some go through a hole in the ice.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Saunas: there are about three million saunas in Finland, and anyone who loves a sauna has an instant friend.

Summer cottages: the mökki by a lake, with swimming, berry picking and long light nights, is a cherished ritual.

Hockey and heavy metal: Finns love both, and Finland has more metal bands per person than almost anywhere.

cards.title: This season: two candles for Independence Day
cards.text: On December 6, Finland's Independence Day, families light two candles in their windows at six in the evening, often one blue and one white for the flag, a tradition with roots in quiet acts of resistance in the 1800s. As the dark season deepens, homes and streets fill with candles and stars, and on Christmas Eve, the "Declaration of Christmas Peace" is read out in Turku, as it has been for centuries.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its saunas, of which Finland has about three million for five and a half million people; UNESCO lists Finnish sauna culture as heritage. And the Kalevala, the national epic, collected from folk singers in the 1800s, which helped Finns find their voice as a nation.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Kalevala's old poems were sung in runo song, to a simple repeating melody, often accompanied by the kantele, a plucked zither and the national instrument. For the modern bridge, Värttinä, formed in Karelia in the 1980s and later developed at the Sibelius Academy, turned that ancient poetry into fierce, many-voiced modern folk music.

cards.title: Craft: ryijy rugs
cards.text: Thick, long-pile knotted rugs, once used on beds and in sleighs for warmth, later hung on walls as art, with bold patterns of trees of life, flowers and geometric shapes. Finnish designers of the 20th century made ryijy an art form. Each tuft is tied with a Ghiordes (Turkish) knot, row by row.

cards.title: Creature: Saimaa ringed seal
cards.text: One of the rarest seals in the world, found only in Lake Saimaa, a freshwater lake left behind by the Ice Age. Down to as few as 100 to 150 in the 1980s, it has been protected back to an estimated 530 in 2025, and pups are born in snow lairs on the ice.

cards.title: Place: Lapland
cards.text: Finland's far north of fells, forests and frozen lakes, home to the Sámi people and to reindeer. In winter, the sun barely rises for weeks, the snow glows blue, and the northern lights fill the sky.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Karelian pies, thin rye crusts filled with rice porridge and topped with egg butter. Cinnamon buns (korvapuusti) with coffee; Finns drink more coffee per person than almost anyone in the world. And at Christmas, joulutorttu, star-shaped pastries with plum jam.

250.name: France

word.meaning: To stroll without any purpose, wandering a city's streets just to look, to notice, to enjoy. Someone who does it is a flâneur or flâneuse, and 19th-century Paris made it into an art.

250.ask: Ask which bakery near them makes the best baguette, and whether they eat the crusty end, the quignon, on the walk home.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food and markets: Saturday markets, the local bakery and long meals with friends are shared pleasures.

Cycling and football: the Tour de France and Kylian Mbappé are easy topics.

Books and films: many French people love talking about novels, bandes dessinées and cinema.

cards.title: This season: Beaujolais Nouveau
cards.text: On the third Thursday of November, which is November 19 this year, the first wine of the new harvest from the Beaujolais region is released all at once, with a cry of "Le Beaujolais nouveau est arrivé!" Cafés and wine bars across France, and around the world, celebrate with the light, fruity young wine, bread, cheese and charcuterie. Soon after, the Christmas markets open, from Strasbourg to Colmar.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food and the way it's shared: UNESCO lists the French gastronomic meal, a festive meal of several courses with good company, as heritage, and in 2022 added the craft of the baguette too.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Chanson, the French song tradition, puts the words first: Édith Piaf, "the little sparrow," sang "La vie en rose" and "Non, je ne regrette rien" with a voice that seemed too big for her small frame. For the modern bridge, Christine and the Queens (Héloïse Letissier) brought the spirit of chanson into electronic pop with the album Chaleur Humaine, first released in 2014.

links.label: La vie en rose, Édith Piaf
Chaleur Humaine (Deluxe Edition), Christine and the Queens

cards.title: Craft: Aubusson tapestry
cards.text: In the town of Aubusson, in central France, weavers have made tapestries on low-warp looms for centuries, working from the back with hand-dyed wool to create landscapes, gardens and, today, contemporary art. UNESCO added Aubusson tapestry to its heritage list in 2009.

cards.title: Creature: Camargue horse
cards.text: In the wetlands of the Rhône delta, white Camargue horses, among the oldest breeds in the world, run half-wild through the marshes beside black bulls and pink flamingos, ridden by the gardians, the region's cowboys.

cards.title: Place: Mont-Saint-Michel
cards.text: A rocky tidal island off the Normandy coast, crowned by a medieval abbey, with a village climbing its slopes. At high tide the sea surrounds it; at low tide, sand stretches for miles. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: A fresh baguette, a wedge of cheese from among hundreds of French varieties, and a buttery croissant with café crème. In winter, a steaming bowl of French onion soup, and on January 6, the galette des rois, an almond pastry hiding a small charm; whoever finds it becomes king or queen for the day.

254.name: French Guiana

word.meaning: The queen of Guianese Carnival: a woman dressed from head to toe in lace, gloves, a mask and a wig, so that no one can recognize her. At the Saturday-night touloulou balls, only the touloulous choose their dance partners, and the men can't refuse.

254.ask: Ask whether they've ever danced at a touloulou ball, and how anyone ever guesses who is behind the mask.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Carnival: Guianese Carnival runs for weeks every year, and people love telling Carnival stories.

Space: many locals have watched rockets launch from Kourou, a fun thing to ask about.

Nature: hiking, river trips and turtle-watching on the beaches are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: Carnival is coming
cards.text: Guianese Carnival, one of the longest in the world, starts at Epiphany, January 6, and runs until Ash Wednesday, with Sunday parades in Cayenne, Kourou and Saint-Laurent, and dances every weekend.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its rainforest, which covers almost the whole territory and is protected by the Guiana Amazonian Park. Its many peoples, from Creole, Indigenous and Maroon communities to Hmong and Brazilian ones. And its rockets, launched from the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Kasékò, from the Creole "casser le corps," to break the body, is a fast drum and dance music with three drums and a stick beaten on wood, heard at Carnival and celebrations. The carnival balls have their own dances too, like the piké djouk and the biguine.

cards.title: Craft: Hmong embroidery
cards.text: In the village of Cacao, Hmong families who arrived from Laos in the 1970s make embroidered and appliqué textiles with fine geometric patterns, sold at the lively Sunday market alongside their fruits and vegetables.

cards.title: Creature: black caiman
cards.text: In the Kaw marshes, the largest caimans in the Americas glide through the flooded grasslands at night, their eyes glowing red in the beam of a flashlight.

cards.title: Place: the Kaw marshes
cards.text: A huge wetland of flooded savanna and forest, reached by boat, full of caimans, hoatzins, scarlet ibis and other birds, where visitors can spend the night on a floating lodge.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Blaff, fish poached in a spicy lime broth. Colombo, a curry of chicken or pork. And bouillon d'awara, a rich stew made with palm fruit, eaten at Easter.

262.name: Djibouti

word.meaning: "Peace," in Somali, one of the main languages of Djibouti alongside Afar, French and Arabic. Greetings ask whether all is peaceful, and the answer is "nabad," peace.

262.ask: Ask how their family makes skoudehkaris, spiced rice with lamb, and whether they eat it with a banana on the side, as many do.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
The sea: diving, snorkeling and swimming with whale sharks in the Gulf of Tadjoura are shared joys.

Afternoon gatherings: long afternoons of tea and conversation with friends are part of daily life.

Food: Djiboutians love sharing skoudehkaris and fah-fah, and anyone curious about food from the Horn of Africa is welcome.

cards.title: This season: whale sharks
cards.text: From November to February, plankton blooms draw whale sharks into the Gulf of Tadjoura, peaking in December and January. Djibouti's whale sharks are young, often just three or four meters long, and snorkelers can swim beside them in calm water.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its astonishing landscapes: Lake Assal, one of the lowest and saltiest places on Earth, the limestone chimneys of Lake Abbé, and the Red Sea's coral reefs. And its welcome, at the crossroads of Africa and Arabia.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Djiboutian music mixes Somali and Afar songs with sounds from across the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. Groupe RTD, the house band of the national radio and television, released Djibouti's first internationally distributed album in 2020, with horns, synths and soaring vocals.

links.label: The Dancing Devils of Djibouti, Groupe RTD

cards.title: Craft: woven mats
cards.text: Afar and Somali women weave mats and baskets from palm fronds, dyed in bright colors, which are used to cover the domed nomadic houses and to serve food.

cards.title: Creature: Djibouti francolin
cards.text: A partridge-like bird found only in the juniper forests of the Day Forest and the Mabla Mountains of Djibouti, and one of the rarest birds in Africa.

cards.title: Place: Lake Abbé
cards.text: On the border with Ethiopia, a salt lake surrounded by tall limestone chimneys that steam and smoke, with flamingos in the shallows. At sunrise, it looks like another planet.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Skoudehkaris. Fah-fah, a spicy goat soup. And lahoh, spongy sourdough flatbread, with honey and tea.

266.name: Gabon

word.meaning: "What's up?" Literally "what are they saying?", it's the everyday Gabonese greeting between friends, asking for the latest news.

266.ask: Ask how their family makes poulet nyembwe, chicken in a rich palm-nut sauce, and whether it comes with rice or bâtons de manioc, cassava sticks wrapped in leaves.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang is a national star, and the Panthers are followed closely.

Nature: many Gabonese are proud of their parks, forest elephants and surfing hippos.

Music and dancing: parties bring Congolese rumba, Afrobeats and Gabonese pop.

cards.title: This season: leatherback turtles
cards.text: From November to April, with a peak in December and January, Gabon's beaches host the largest population of nesting leatherback turtles in the world. On some nights, hundreds of these giant sea turtles, the largest on Earth, crawl ashore near Mayumba to lay their eggs in the sand.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its forests: most of the country is covered in rainforest, and in 2002 Gabon created 13 national parks to protect it. It's one of the last great strongholds of forest elephants.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The ngombi, an arched harp, is played in Bwiti ceremonies, with singing and dancing through the night. Pierre Akendengué, a singer, guitarist and poet, brought Gabonese languages, stories and rhythms into songs heard across Africa and France.

cards.title: Craft: Punu masks
cards.text: Punu carvers make wooden masks with serene white faces, high arched eyebrows, almond eyes and elaborate hairstyles, worn by stilt dancers at celebrations and funerals. They're among the most admired masks of Central Africa.

cards.title: Creature: mandrill
cards.text: The world's largest monkey, with a bright red and blue face. In Lopé National Park, mandrills gather in hordes of hundreds, among the largest groups of any primate other than people.

cards.title: Place: Loango National Park
cards.text: Where rainforest meets the Atlantic, forest elephants, buffaloes and hippos walk out onto the beaches, and hippos have been seen swimming in the surf. Whales and dolphins pass offshore.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Poulet nyembwe. Bâtons de manioc. And atanga, a purple "butter fruit," softened in hot water or roasted and eaten with bread.

268.name: Georgia

word.meaning: “I accidentally ate the whole thing.” What you say when the food was too good to stop.
word.sayIt: sheh-moh-meh-CHAH-mah (Georgian stress is light; the ch is a crisp, popped sound)

268.ask: Ask about the best tamada (toastmaster) they've ever seen, and which toast they still remember. Supra stories come with laughter and usually a song.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Feasts: the supra, with a toastmaster and long, heartfelt toasts, is a joyful tradition to learn about.

Wine: Georgia has made wine for 8,000 years in clay qvevri, and wine lovers have lots to talk about.

Polyphonic singing: many Georgians sing in harmony at the table, and anyone who sings will be welcomed.

cards.title: This season: Rtveli
cards.text: The grape harvest runs through September and October. Families and neighbors pick together, press grapes in wooden troughs, and sing while they work. The fresh juice becomes wine and churchkhela.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Georgians created their own alphabet, the rounded, curling Mkhedruli script, and two older Georgian scripts are still used in church; UNESCO lists the living culture of all three. Hospitality is a close second, summed up in the saying that a guest is a gift from God.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Georgian polyphonic singing weaves three independent voices into close, ringing harmonies, and UNESCO counts it as world heritage. One song, Chakrulo, rides the Voyager Golden Record, now beyond the solar system. For a modern bridge, the band Iriao carried polyphony onto the Eurovision stage in 2018.

cards.title: Craft: qvevri wine
cards.text: Wine ferments in large beeswax-lined clay vessels buried in the earth, a method Georgians have used for roughly 8,000 years. Both the vessel and the method are on UNESCO's heritage list.

cards.title: Creature: East Caucasian tur
cards.text: A stocky wild goat with thick, backswept horns that lives only in the Greater Caucasus, balancing on cliffs most animals avoid.

cards.title: Place: Ushguli
cards.text: A cluster of villages in Upper Svaneti at about 2,100 meters, crowded with medieval stone watchtowers, under the snowy wall of Shkhara, Georgia's highest peak.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Adjarian khachapuri is a boat of bread filled with molten cheese; a raw egg and a knob of butter get stirred in at the table. Churchkhela are walnuts threaded on string and dipped in thickened grape juice, hung to dry like candles. Both belong at a supra, a long feast guided by a tamada, the toastmaster.

270.name: Gambia

word.meaning: "How are you?" in Wolof, one of the Gambia's main languages. The answer is "maa ngi fi," I'm here. Greetings are long and warm, with questions about family, health and home.

270.ask: Ask how their family makes domoda, a rich peanut stew with meat or fish, and whether benachin, one-pot rice, is better.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football and wrestling: both are popular, and traditional wrestling matches draw big crowds.

Attaya: long rounds of green tea with mint, brewed and shared over hours of conversation.

Kora music: many people have heard Sona Jobarteh or other kora players and love talking about it.

cards.title: This season: the birds arrive
cards.text: From late October and November, migrating birds arrive from Europe and elsewhere in Africa, and the Gambia, with more than 560 bird species along its river, mangroves and forests, becomes one of the best places for birdwatching in Africa. Kingfishers, bee-eaters, rollers and herons are everywhere.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "The Smiling Coast of Africa," its nickname for the warmth of its people. The Gambia River, which gives the country its long, narrow shape. And its griots and kora music.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Griot families have played the kora, a 21-string harp-lute made from a calabash, for centuries, passing down songs and history. Sona Jobarteh, from one of the Gambia's great griot families, is the first woman to become a professional kora virtuoso from such a family.

cards.title: Craft: tie-dye and batik
cards.text: Gambian women dye cotton cloth in bold colors and patterns, tying, folding or waxing it before dipping it in dye, and sell it at markets like Serekunda for dresses and wrappers.

cards.title: Creature: Egyptian plover
cards.text: The "crocodile bird," with a black cap, a blue-gray back and a peach belly, runs along sandbanks of the Gambia River. It's one of the most sought-after birds in West Africa.

cards.title: Place: the Wassu stone circles
cards.text: Circles of carved stone pillars set up more than a thousand years ago as burial monuments, in fields along the river. They're part of the Senegambian stone circles, a UNESCO World Heritage Site shared with Senegal.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Domoda. Benachin. Yassa, chicken or fish with onions and lemon. And wonjo, a red hibiscus drink.

275.name: Palestine

word.meaning: "Bless your hands," said to whoever cooked the meal, made the coffee or did you a kindness. The answer is "wa idek," and yours.

275.ask: Ask how their family makes musakhan, and who in the family bakes the best taboon bread.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: musakhan, maqluba and knafeh are family favorites, and cooks love sharing their recipes.

Dabke: the line dance at every wedding, and anyone can be pulled in to join.

Olive oil: many families have olive trees, and the autumn harvest is a family time.

cards.title: This season: the olive harvest
