cards.text: In October and November, Palestinian families head out together to their olive groves, some with trees hundreds of years old. They spread tarps under the branches, pick and shake down the olives, share meals under the trees, and bring the harvest to the press for fresh green oil.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its olive trees and oil. Tatreez, its embroidery. Its food, from musakhan to knafeh. And its poetry, above all Mahmoud Darwish.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Dabke, a line dance of stamping feet and linked arms, is danced at every wedding. Le Trio Joubran, three brothers from Nazareth, play the oud together in intricate, flowing music heard around the world.

cards.title: Craft: tatreez
cards.text: Women embroider dresses with cross-stitch in deep reds and other colors, in patterns that once told which village a woman came from, like cypress trees, stars and flowers. UNESCO lists the art of embroidery in Palestine as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Palestine sunbird
cards.text: A tiny bird that sips nectar from flowers; the male glitters in metallic blue, green and purple. It's the national bird.

cards.title: Place: Jericho
cards.text: One of the oldest towns in the world, in an oasis of palms and springs near the Dead Sea. Its ancient mound, Tell es-Sultan, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Musakhan, taboon bread with roasted chicken, onions, sumac and olive oil. Maqluba, an upside-down pot of rice, vegetables and meat. And knafeh from Nablus, warm cheese pastry soaked in syrup.

276.name: Germany

word.meaning: The moment work ends and your own time begins, and that evening time itself. "Schönen Feierabend!" ("Have a lovely evening off!") is how colleagues say goodbye, and Germans take it seriously.

276.ask: Ask what they bake for Christmas, from Plätzchen, the little cookies baked by the tray, to Stollen, and whether their family has a secret recipe.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: the Bundesliga and the national team are followed passionately, and everyone has a club.

Hiking, biking and beer gardens: weekend walks and bike trips that end at a beer garden are shared pleasures.

Christmas markets: mulled wine, gingerbread and wooden stalls are beloved, and many people abroad love them too.

cards.title: This season: lanterns and Christmas markets
cards.text: On November 11, St. Martin's Day, children walk through the streets after dark carrying paper lanterns they've made, singing lantern songs. Then, near the start of Advent, the Christmas markets open: Nuremberg's famous Christkindlesmarkt opens on November 27 this year, with wooden stalls, gingerbread, roasted almonds and mugs of hot mulled wine, Glühwein.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music and ideas, from Bach, Beethoven and Brahms to printing with movable type. And its forests, which run deep in German stories, from the Brothers Grimm's fairy tales to weekend hikes.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Johann Sebastian Bach, who worked as a church musician in Leipzig, wrote some of the most loved music ever made; the Goldberg Variations, played on piano by Glenn Gould, is a good way in. For the modern bridge, Kraftwerk, from Düsseldorf, invented electronic pop in the 1970s with machine-like precision; Trans-Europe Express, from 1977, influenced hip-hop and dance music around the world.

links.label: Bach: Goldberg Variations (1981 Recording), Glenn Gould

cards.title: Craft: Erzgebirge wood carving
cards.text: In the Ore Mountains of Saxony, former mining villages turned to wood carving, and now make Germany's best-loved Christmas decorations: nutcrackers, incense-smoking figures, and candle-powered Christmas pyramids whose turning blades spin scenes of the Nativity or of miners at work.

cards.title: Creature: white stork
cards.text: Every spring, white storks return from Africa to build huge nests on rooftops, church towers and chimneys in German villages, and are said to bring good luck, and babies.

cards.title: Place: the Upper Middle Rhine Valley
cards.text: Between Bingen and Koblenz, the Rhine flows through a deep gorge of vineyards and castles perched on the cliffs, past the Lorelei rock of legend. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pretzels and sausages, of course, and at Christmas, Stollen, a buttery fruit bread dusted with powdered sugar, and Lebkuchen, spiced gingerbread from Nuremberg. Germany has more than a thousand kinds of sausage and around 3,000 kinds of bread, and German bread culture is on UNESCO's national heritage list.

288.name: Ghana

word.meaning: "Welcome," in Twi, the most widely spoken of Ghana's Akan languages. You'll hear it, and see it painted on signs, from the moment you arrive.

288.ask: Ask whose jollof rice is best, Ghana's or Nigeria's. The friendly rivalry is legendary, and everyone has a strong opinion and a family recipe to defend.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Jollof rice: Ghanaians love the friendly argument over whose jollof is better, Ghana's or Nigeria's.

Football: the Black Stars and the 2010 World Cup run to the quarterfinals are happy memories.

Music: highlife and Afrobeats, and stars like Sarkodie, Stonebwoy and Black Sherif, fill parties.

cards.title: This season: Hogbetsotso
cards.text: On the first Saturday in November, which is November 7 this year, the Anlo Ewe people gather at Anloga on the Volta coast for Hogbetsotso, the festival of the exodus. It remembers their ancestors' escape from the walled town of Notsie, in present-day Togo, and begins with a period of peacemaking in which old disputes are settled. Then come drumming, dancing and chiefs in splendid kente, carried in procession.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: On March 6, 1957, Ghana became the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from colonial rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah, and the black star at the center of its flag stands for African freedom. The national football team is called the Black Stars after it.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Highlife grew up in Ghana's port towns in the early 20th century, blending local rhythms with guitars and brass. E. T. Mensah, the "King of Highlife," led dance bands that spread it across West Africa. In the 1990s, hiplife mixed highlife with hip-hop, and today's stars keep the thread going: Black Sherif, from Konongo, sings in Twi and English over beats that mix drill and highlife on his 2022 debut album, The Villain I Never Was.

links.label: Ghana Special: Modern Highlife, Afro-Sounds & Ghanaian Blues 1968–81
The Villain I Never Was, Black Sherif

cards.title: Craft: kente
cards.text: Kente is woven on narrow horizontal strip looms, mostly by men, in bands about four inches wide that are then sewn edge to edge into a cloth. Bonwire, near Kumasi, has woven it for the Asante kings for centuries, and Ewe weavers in the Volta region have their own style, with patterns drawn more from daily life. Each pattern has a name, often a proverb.

cards.title: Creature: mona monkey
cards.text: In the Volta region, the people of Tafi Atome have protected the mona monkeys in their sacred forest for generations, believing them to be messengers of the gods. Since 1993 the grove has also been a community-run sanctuary, where the monkeys come down from the trees to take bananas from visitors' hands.

cards.title: Place: Kakum National Park
cards.text: A rainforest near Cape Coast where you can walk through the treetops on a canopy walkway 350 meters long, strung between seven trees about 40 meters above the forest floor.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Jollof rice, cooked in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce. Kelewele, ripe plantain cut into cubes, tossed with ginger and chili and fried until caramelized, sold from roadside stalls at night. And waakye, rice and beans cooked together with dried sorghum leaves that turn them a deep reddish brown.

300.name: Greece

word.meaning: Doing something with your whole soul: care, creativity and love poured into the work, whether it's a meal, a garden or a fishing net being mended. The word came into Greek from the Turkish merak, "passion, eager interest."

300.ask: Ask about their family's village and what grows there. Many Greek families still return to a home village for holidays, the olive harvest, or a name day celebration.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food and long meals: Greeks love meals that last for hours, with meze, grilled fish and good company.

Summer islands: many Greeks spend summers on the islands and love to share favorites.

Basketball: Giannis Antetokounmpo is a national hero, and Greece is passionate about basketball.

cards.title: This season: the olive harvest
cards.text: From late October through December, families head back to their villages to bring in the olives. Nets are spread under the silvery trees, branches are combed with rakes so the fruit drops softly, and the local presses run day and night. The first oil of the season, green, peppery and cloudy, is a celebration of its own, best poured over bread.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The ideas that grew here, in theater, philosophy, mathematics and democracy, which took its name from the Greek dēmos, "the people," and kratos, "rule." And the Olympic Games, first held at Olympia in ancient times, revived in Athens in 1896.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Rebetiko is often called the Greek blues: songs of love, hardship and life on the margins, played on the bouzouki and baglamas. It took root in the port cities after refugees from Asia Minor arrived in the 1920s, blending Greek, Turkish, Roma and Jewish sounds, and UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2017. Markos Vamvakaris, from Piraeus, was its patriarch. For the modern bridge, the Athens band Imam Baildi remixes old rebetiko and folk records with brass and beats.

cards.title: Craft: Chios mastic
cards.text: Only in the south of the island of Chios do mastic trees weep their fragrant resin. From summer, growers score the bark, and the drops harden into clear "tears" that women gather, clean and sort by hand. The mastic flavors sweets, bread and liqueur, and has been chewed as a gum since ancient times. UNESCO lists the know-how of growing it as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: loggerhead sea turtle
cards.text: Loggerheads, called caretta caretta in Greece, come ashore on beaches like Laganas Bay on Zakynthos to lay their eggs in the sand each summer, and the hatchlings scramble to the sea at night. A national marine park protects the nesting beaches.

cards.title: Place: Meteora
cards.text: Monasteries perched on top of towering pillars of rock above the plain of Thessaly. Monks began living here in the 14th century, and for centuries the only way up was by ladder or a net hauled on a rope. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Horta, wild greens boiled and dressed with olive oil and lemon. Spanakopita, spinach and feta in crisp layers of phyllo. And loukoumades, little fried dough balls soaked in honey and dusted with cinnamon.

304.name: Greenland

word.meaning: "It's all right, it doesn't matter, it'll be fine." In a land of wild weather, where plans often change with the sea ice and the wind, ajunngilaq is a way of taking things calmly.

304.ask: Ask about the best kaffemik they've been to. For birthdays and big days, families open their homes and the whole town drops in for coffee, cake and food, all day long.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Kaffemik: open-house gatherings with coffee and cakes for birthdays and big days, where the whole town drops in.

The outdoors: fishing, boating, dog sledding and hiking are part of life, and outdoors lovers have lots to share.

Football and handball: both are hugely popular, played on gravel pitches and in town halls through the long winters.

cards.title: This season: the northern lights
cards.text: As autumn nights lengthen, the aurora borealis dances across Greenland's skies in green and violet, visible even from towns like Nuuk and Kangerlussuaq. In the far north, the polar night begins, when the sun doesn't rise for weeks.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its Inuit heritage and self-government, with Greenlandic, Kalaallisut, as the official language. The qajaq, the kayak, invented by Inuit for hunting at sea. And the scale of its nature: the biggest island in the world, mostly covered by ice.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Inuit drum dancing, with a large, flat frame drum and songs of stories and teasing, is Greenland's oldest music. For the modern bridge, Nanook, a band of two brothers, sings indie rock in Greenlandic and is one of the country's most popular bands.

cards.title: Craft: beaded collars
cards.text: Women's national dress includes a wide collar of tiny glass beads in bright geometric patterns, worn with sealskin trousers and tall, embroidered boots called kamiks, on National Day and at big celebrations.

cards.title: Creature: narwhal
cards.text: The "unicorn of the sea," a small Arctic whale whose males grow a single long, spiraled tusk. Narwhals live in the icy waters off Greenland.

cards.title: Place: Ilulissat Icefjord
cards.text: One of the fastest-moving glaciers in the world pushes giant icebergs into the fjord at Ilulissat, where they drift, crack and roar. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Suaasat, a hearty soup of seal, whale or reindeer with rice or barley. Dried fish. And musk ox and reindeer, from the land.

320.name: Guatemala

word.meaning: Guatemalan slang for "cool," "great," "awesome": "¡Qué chilero!" A concert, a view of the volcanoes or a new pair of shoes can all be chilero.

320.ask: Ask what their family puts in the fiambre, the huge, colorful cold salad of meats, cheeses and pickled vegetables made only for November 1, and how many ingredients it has. Some families use more than fifty.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Weaving: Maya women's weaving is a living art, and anyone who weaves or loves textiles has lots to talk about.

Football: Guatemalans follow local clubs like Municipal and Comunicaciones and the big European leagues.

Food: tamales, pepián and chocolate are shared joys, especially at Christmas.

cards.title: This season: the giant kites
cards.text: On November 1, All Saints' Day, the towns of Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez raise barriletes gigantes: giant round kites of colored tissue paper and bamboo, up to 20 meters across, made over months by local groups. The smaller ones fly over the cemeteries to carry messages to the dead; the biggest stand on display. UNESCO added the tradition to its heritage list in 2024.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its living Maya culture: more than 20 Maya languages are spoken today, and many women still wear traditional dress woven in their own town's style. And its landscape of volcanoes and lakes, above all Lake Atitlán.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The marimba, a large wooden xylophone played by several musicians at once, is Guatemala's national instrument, heard at every town festival. For the modern bridge, the singer-songwriter Gaby Moreno, from Guatemala City, moves between bolero, blues, folk and jazz and has won a Latin Grammy.

cards.title: Craft: backstrap weaving
cards.text: Maya women weave on backstrap looms tied to a post and around their waists, making huipiles, blouses covered in patterns of birds, flowers and diamonds. Each town has its own designs and colors, so a huipil tells where its wearer is from.

cards.title: Creature: resplendent quetzal
cards.text: Guatemala's national bird, with a glowing green body, crimson breast and tail streamers up to a meter long, sacred to the ancient Maya. The currency is named after it.

cards.title: Place: Tikal
cards.text: A great Maya city rising out of the jungle of Petén, with temple-pyramids towering above the treetops, where howler monkeys roar at dawn. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pepián, a rich, smoky stew of chicken, roasted seeds and chilies, often called the national dish. Tamales and chuchitos. And fiambre on November 1.

324.name: Guinea

word.meaning: "Thank you" in Pular, the language of the Fula people of the Fouta Djallon highlands. It also greets and blesses, and you'll hear it again and again in a single conversation.

324.ask: Ask how their family makes sauce arachide, the peanut stew served over rice, and whether it's better with fish or meat.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: Guinea's griots, bands like Bembeya Jazz and the djembe are known worldwide, and anyone who has taken a drum class has a way in.

Football: Guineans follow the national team, the Syli, and stars like Naby Keïta and Serhou Guirassy.

Tea and conversation: long afternoons of strong green tea with friends, brewed in small pots, are an everyday ritual.

cards.title: This season: the Fouta Djallon after the rains
cards.text: As the rainy season ends in October and November, the cool, green highlands of the Fouta Djallon are at their most beautiful, with rivers and waterfalls still running full and hikers following paths between villages and cliffs. The Niger, the Senegal and the Gambia rivers all begin in these hills.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music: in the 1960s and 70s, Guinea's national orchestras and ballets made it one of the great musical capitals of Africa. And its water: the "water tower of West Africa," where great rivers are born.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Griots have sung history and praise for centuries with the kora and the balafon. Bembeya Jazz National, formed in 1961, turned Manding classics into electric dance music with guitars and horns, and became a national treasure. Mory Kanté's "Yé ké yé ké" became a worldwide hit in the 1980s.

cards.title: Craft: the djembe
cards.text: Guinea is one of the homes of the djembe, the goblet-shaped hand drum carved from a single log and topped with goatskin. Master drummers like Mamady Keïta took its rhythms to drum circles around the world.

cards.title: Creature: Nimba toad
cards.text: A tiny toad that lives only on the grassy slopes of Mount Nimba, and gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs, which is almost unheard of among frogs and toads.

cards.title: Place: Mount Nimba
cards.text: A mountain rising above the forest on the borders with Côte d'Ivoire and Liberia, home to rare animals found nowhere else. The Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Rice with sauce arachide. Sauce feuille, cassava leaves cooked in palm oil. And fonio, a tiny, ancient grain, cooked like couscous.

328.name: Guyana

word.meaning: To chat, chit-chat, and swap stories with friends: "we was just gaffing." In Guyana, a good gaff on the porch or at the rum shop can go on for hours.

328.ask: Ask how their family makes pepperpot, the dark, slow-cooked meat stew flavored with cassareep from cassava, eaten at Christmas with bread.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: Guyanese are passionate about West Indies cricket and heroes like Shivnarine Chanderpaul.

Food: roti, curry, pepperpot and cook-up rice are loved, and Guyanese love to share them, especially at Christmas.

Music: chutney, soca and reggae fill parties, and anyone who loves Caribbean music has an opening.

cards.title: This season: Diwali
cards.text: Diwali falls on November 8 in 2026. On the night before, in Georgetown, the Diwali motorcade winds through the city, a parade of floats glowing with lights and images of Hindu deities, as it has since the 1970s. On Diwali itself, homes, yards and villages glitter with thousands of clay diyas.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its rainforest, which covers most of the country. Kaieteur Falls. And its mix of peoples, of Indian, African, Indigenous, Chinese, Portuguese and European ancestry. Guyana is also the only English-speaking country in South America.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Chutney, a lively music sung in English and Hindustani with dholak drums and harmonium, grew among Indo-Guyanese families. At Christmas, masquerade bands of flute and drums dance through the streets, and calypso and soca fill the parties.

cards.title: Craft: nibbi furniture
cards.text: Artisans weave chairs, baskets and tables from the aerial roots of the nibbi vine, which hang down from rainforest trees. Indigenous weavers are also known for tightly woven baskets and hammocks.

cards.title: Creature: hoatzin
cards.text: The national bird, a strange, spiky-crested bird of riverbanks that smells like manure because it digests leaves by fermentation. Its chicks have claws on their wings and climb back up through branches if they fall.

cards.title: Place: Kaieteur Falls
cards.text: The Potaro River plunges 226 meters in a single drop over the edge of a sandstone plateau into a deep gorge, in a rainforest national park. It's one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pepperpot at Christmas. Cook-up rice, rice and peas cooked in coconut milk with meat. Roti and curry. And black cake, dark fruitcake soaked in rum.

332.name: Haiti

word.meaning: "Honor! Respect!" In the Haitian countryside, a visitor arriving at a home calls out "Onè!" and the host answers "Respè!" before welcoming them in. It's a greeting that puts dignity first.

332.ask: Ask how their family makes soup joumou, the pumpkin soup every Haitian family eats on New Year's Day, which celebrates independence.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: konpa and rara, and artists like Wyclef Jean, are easy conversation openers.

Art: Haitian painting and metal art are famous, and art lovers have a lot to share.

Soup joumou: the New Year's Day pumpkin soup is a warm tradition to ask about.

cards.title: This season: Fèt Gede
cards.text: On November 1 and 2, Haitians honor the dead and the Gede, the spirits of death and fertility in Vodou, led by Baron Samedi in his top hat. In cemeteries and towns, there's drumming, dancing and bawdy humor, and families visit the graves of their relatives with flowers and candles.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its independence in 1804, won by the only successful revolt of enslaved people to found a nation. Soup joumou, which celebrates it and which UNESCO lists as heritage. And its art, full of color and imagination.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Konpa, smooth and danceable, is Haiti's great popular music, played at every party. Mizik rasin, "roots music," mixes Vodou drumming and chants with rock and reggae; Boukman Eksperyans made it famous.

cards.title: Craft: Croix-des-Bouquets metal art
cards.text: In the town of Croix-des-Bouquets, artists cut and hammer flattened oil drums into lacy metal sculptures of trees of life, mermaids, birds and spirits, a craft started by blacksmith Georges Liautaud in the 1950s.

cards.title: Creature: Hispaniolan trogon
cards.text: The national bird, with a green back, gray chest and red belly, echoing the colors of the flag. It lives only on Hispaniola, in the mountain forests.

cards.title: Place: the Citadelle Laferrière
cards.text: A massive mountaintop fortress built after independence to defend the new nation, looking out over the north. Together with the Sans-Souci Palace below, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Soup joumou. Griot, fried marinated pork, with pikliz, a spicy pickled slaw. And diri djon djon, rice turned black with wild mushrooms.

340.name: Honduras

word.meaning: A Honduran, said with affection and pride: "soy catracho," or "catracha" for a woman. The nickname is said to come from a 19th-century general, Florencio Xatruch, whose soldiers were called "los xatruches."

340.ask: Ask how they like their baleada, a thick flour tortilla folded over refried beans, cheese and cream, and what else they add: eggs, avocado or meat.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Hondurans follow the national team and local clubs like Olimpia and Motagua with great passion.

Baleadas: the favorite street food, a warm tortilla folded over beans and cream, is fun to compare and to try.

The Bay Islands: many love diving, snorkeling and the beaches of Roatán and Utila, and divers have instant common ground.

cards.title: This season: whale sharks off Utila
cards.text: Whale sharks visit the waters around Utila, in the Bay Islands, all year, and October to December is one of the best times to see them. Boats watch for feeding frenzies of small tuna and birds, and snorkelers slip into the water beside the largest fish in the sea.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Copán, one of the great cities of the ancient Maya. The Bay Islands, on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest reef in the world. And the warmth of its people.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: On the Caribbean coast, the Garifuna people, descended from West Africans and Indigenous Caribbeans, sing and dance punta to fast drums; UNESCO lists Garifuna language, dance and music as heritage. Aurelio Martínez, a Garifuna singer from Plaplaya, blends it with guitar and paranda.

cards.title: Craft: Lenca pottery
cards.text: In the western highlands, Lenca women in villages like La Campa shape clay by hand, without a potter's wheel, into pots, jugs and figures, and polish and paint them in red, black and white earth tones.

cards.title: Creature: scarlet macaw
cards.text: The national bird: a big, loud parrot in brilliant red, yellow and blue. At the ruins of Copán, macaws fly free again among the ancient temples, where the Maya once carved them in stone.

cards.title: Place: Copán
cards.text: A Maya city in a green valley near the border with Guatemala, famous for its finely carved stone stelae of kings and its Hieroglyphic Stairway, the longest known Maya text. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Baleadas. Sopa de caracol, conch soup with coconut milk, from the coast. And plato típico: grilled beef, beans, plantains, cheese, cream and tortillas.

348.name: Hungary

word.meaning: The mood or atmosphere of a place or a moment: a café full of chatter, a thermal bath at dusk, a dinner that turns into singing. A good evening "has hangulat."

348.ask: Ask which thermal bath is their favorite, and whether they play chess in the warm water like the regulars at Budapest's Széchenyi Baths.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Thermal baths: soaking in Budapest's baths, even playing chess in the water, is a shared pleasure.

Food: goulash, lángos and chimney cake are loved, and Hungarians love to explain paprika.

Inventions and puzzles: the Rubik's Cube was invented in Hungary, a fun topic for anyone who ever tried to solve one.

cards.title: This season: St. Martin's Day
cards.text: On November 11, Márton-nap, Hungarians feast on goose, roast goose legs with red cabbage, goose soup and more, and taste the year's new wine. An old saying warns that whoever doesn't eat goose on St. Martin's Day will be hungry all year, and in some villages people read the next winter's weather in the goose's breastbone.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its inventors and thinkers, from the Rubik's Cube, invented by Ernő Rubik in 1974, to vitamin C, isolated by Albert Szent-Györgyi, who won a Nobel Prize for it. And its thermal waters: Budapest sits on more than a hundred hot springs.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Hungary's village music, with fiddles, bagpipes, zithers and the hurdy-gurdy, fascinated the composer Béla Bartók, who collected thousands of folk songs. In the 1970s, the táncház ("dance house") movement brought those dances and tunes back to city young people, and UNESCO lists it as heritage. Muzsikás and the singer Márta Sebestyén are its best-known voices.

links.label: The Bartók Album, Muzsikás and Márta Sebestyén

cards.title: Craft: Matyó embroidery
cards.text: In Mezőkövesd, in the northeast, the Matyó people cover clothing, pillows and tablecloths with dense, brilliant embroidery of roses, peonies and tulips in red, pink, blue and yellow. UNESCO lists Matyó folk art as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Hungarian grey cattle
cards.text: A handsome grey breed with enormous lyre-shaped horns, once driven in great herds across Europe, and still grazing on the great plain of the Hortobágy.

cards.title: Place: the Hortobágy
cards.text: Central Europe's largest natural grassland, the puszta, with wide skies, wells with long sweep-poles, horsemen performing feats of riding and thousands of migrating cranes in autumn. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Gulyás, beef soup rich with paprika, first cooked by herdsmen in kettles over open fires. Lángos, fried flatbread with sour cream and cheese. And kürtőskalács, chimney cake: dough wrapped around a spit, roasted over coals and rolled in sugar and cinnamon.

352.name: Iceland

word.meaning: "Window weather": the kind that looks lovely through the glass, bright sun and blue sky, but is freezing or blowing a gale the moment you step outside.

352.ask: Ask which book they're hoping to unwrap this Christmas, and which one they'd give. In Iceland, that's a serious and happy question.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Swimming pools: Icelanders visit their outdoor geothermal pools in all weather, and it's where friends catch up in the hot tubs.

Books: giving and reading books on Christmas Eve, the "Christmas book flood," is a beloved tradition that book lovers adore.

Music: Björk, Sigur Rós and Of Monsters and Men are well known abroad, and music fans have plenty to share.

cards.title: This season: the Christmas Book Flood
cards.text: From late September into mid-November, new Icelandic books pour into the shops in what's called Jólabókaflóð, the Christmas Book Flood. A free catalog of the year's new books, Bókatíðindi, arrives at every home, families choose gifts, and on Christmas Eve people unwrap their books and spend the night reading, often with hot chocolate. It took off during the Second World War, when paper was one of the few things not rationed.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Althing, founded in 930 at Þingvellir, is one of the oldest parliaments in the world. And its love of stories, from the medieval sagas to today, when a remarkable number of Icelanders write and publish books of their own.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Rímur are long epic poems chanted to simple, haunting melodies, a tradition going back to the 14th century; Steindór Andersen is one of its few remaining masters. For the modern bridge, Sigur Rós, whose 1999 album Ágætis byrjun made them international stars, later recorded Rímur with Steindór himself. And Björk, of course, who has never sounded like anyone else.

links.label: Rímur, Sigur Rós and Steindór Andersen

cards.title: Craft: the lopapeysa
cards.text: The Icelandic wool sweater, hand-knit from lopi, soft unspun wool from Icelandic sheep, with a wide patterned yoke circling the shoulders. It took shape in the 1940s and 50s, when Icelandic women knitted at home for sale, and since 2020 only a sweater hand-knit in Iceland from Icelandic wool can carry the name.

cards.title: Creature: the Icelandic horse
cards.text: Small, sturdy and friendly, with a thick mane. It has a smooth extra gait called the tölt, so steady a rider can carry a full glass without spilling. Since 982, no horse may be brought into Iceland, and a horse that leaves can never return, so the breed has stayed pure and free of many diseases.

cards.title: Place: Þingvellir
cards.text: The rift valley where the Althing first met in 930, and where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart, leaving cracks you can walk through; in one, Silfra, divers swim in glacier-melt water so clear they can see a hundred meters. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kjötsúpa, a warming lamb and root-vegetable soup. Skyr, thick and tangy, eaten for centuries. Kleinur, twisted fried pastries, with coffee. And, for a surprise, the hot dog, made with lamb and topped with crispy and raw onions and sweet brown mustard.

356.name: India

word.meaning: A deep, settled peace: the calm that comes when the rush is over and everything is, for now, all right. Shared by Hindi and Urdu, it comes from an Arabic word for stillness.

356.ask: Ask what their family makes for Diwali, and who's in charge of the rangoli, the patterns drawn at the doorway in colored powder, rice or flower petals.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: India's biggest passion, and asking about a favorite player is an easy start.

Food: regional cuisines vary hugely, and people love to talk about their home dishes.

Films and music: Bollywood and regional cinema, and songs everyone knows, are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: Diwali
cards.text: Diwali, the festival of lights, falls on November 8 this year. Homes glow with rows of small clay oil lamps called diyas, doorways get fresh rangoli, families share boxes of sweets, and fireworks fill the night. It carries many stories, including Rama's return to Ayodhya and the worship of Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, and is celebrated across faiths and regions. In December 2025, UNESCO added Deepavali to its heritage list at a meeting held at the Red Fort in Delhi.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its sheer variety: India's constitution recognizes 22 languages, each with its own literature, food and festivals. And on August 23, 2023, Chandrayaan-3 made India the first country to land a spacecraft near the Moon's south pole; the date is now celebrated every year as National Space Day.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: India has two great classical traditions: Hindustani in the north and Carnatic in the south. Both are built on raga, a melodic framework with its own mood and often its own time of day, and tala, rhythmic cycles that can stretch for many beats. Ravi Shankar's sitar carried ragas to the world, and his 1956 album Three Ragas is a fine way in. For a modern bridge, A. R. Rahman, who won two Oscars for Slumdog Millionaire, blended Carnatic melody with electronic and orchestral sound from his very first film score, Roja, in 1992.

cards.title: Craft: block printing
cards.text: In Rajasthan, printers carve patterns into wooden blocks and stamp cloth by hand, one impression at a time. Around Jaipur, Sanganer is known for fine prints on white, while the village of Bagru is known for dabu: a paste of clay, lime and gum is stamped on first to keep areas from taking the dye, then the cloth goes into baths of indigo and other natural dyes such as madder and pomegranate.

cards.title: Creature: Bengal tiger
cards.text: India's 2022 tiger count found about 3,682 wild tigers, around three-quarters of all the wild tigers in the world, up from about 1,411 in 2006.

cards.title: Place: the living root bridges
cards.text: In Meghalaya, one of the wettest places on Earth, Khasi and Jaintia communities guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams until they grow into bridges strong enough to walk on. Shaping one takes ten to fifteen years, and the bridges keep strengthening as they grow. India has proposed them for UNESCO World Heritage status.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Diwali means mithai, sweets: diamond-shaped kaju katli made from cashews and often covered in edible silver leaf, and round laddoos. The rest of the year, a thali, a round tray of small bowls, gives a region's whole meal at once: dal, vegetables, rice, bread, pickle, and something sweet. And everywhere, there is chai.

360.name: Indonesia

word.meaning: A word with two hearts. Sayang means "love" or "darling," what you'd call someone dear to you, and it also means "what a pity," as in "sayang sekali," "such a shame." Both come from caring about something.

360.ask: Ask which island or region their family comes from, and what food they miss most from there. With so many islands, every answer is a different world.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Badminton: Indonesians are passionate about it, and Olympic champions are national heroes.

Food: nasi goreng, satay and rendang are loved, and many people abroad have tried them.

Islands and diving: Bali, Komodo and Raja Ampat are sources of pride, and divers and travelers have lots to talk about.

cards.title: This season: National Batik Day
cards.text: On October 2, Indonesians wear batik to work, school and everywhere else for Hari Batik Nasional, National Batik Day. It marks the day in 2009 when UNESCO added Indonesian batik to its heritage list: cloth patterned by drawing designs in hot wax with a small copper pen called a canting, dyeing, and repeating, layer by layer.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its diversity. Indonesia stretches across more than 17,000 islands and is home to hundreds of ethnic groups and languages, held together by one national language and the motto Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, "Unity in Diversity."

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Gamelan, orchestras of bronze gongs, metallophones and drums played as one interlocking whole, rings out across Java and Bali, and UNESCO lists it as heritage. Balinese gamelan is fast and shimmering, Javanese gamelan slower and more meditative. In the 1970s, Rhoma Irama, the "King of Dangdut," turned dangdut, a blend of Malay, Indian and Arab-influenced melody with a rolling drum beat, into Indonesia's great popular music, still played at every wedding.

links.label: Gamelan Music of Bali, Gamelan Angklung and Gamelan Gong Kebyar

cards.title: Craft: ikat from Sumba
cards.text: On the island of Sumba, weavers tie off bundles of thread and dye them before weaving, so the patterns of horses, ancestors, crocodiles and birds appear as the cloth is woven. The large hinggi cloths, colored with indigo and the red of morinda root, can take months to make and are exchanged at weddings and funerals.

cards.title: Creature: Komodo dragon
cards.text: The largest lizard in the world, up to about three meters long, found only on Komodo and a few neighboring islands in eastern Indonesia, where Komodo National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, protects it.

cards.title: Place: Borobudur
cards.text: In central Java, a vast Buddhist monument built in the 8th and 9th centuries: nine stacked platforms carved with more than 2,600 relief panels and crowned by bell-shaped stupas. Walking up it, pilgrims follow the story of the Buddha's path to enlightenment. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest Buddhist temple in the world.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Rendang, beef slow-cooked for hours in coconut milk and spices until almost dry, from the Minangkabau people of West Sumatra. Nasi goreng, fried rice, with a fried egg on top. Tempeh, fermented soybean cakes, first made in Java. And sambal, the chili paste on every table, in countless versions.

364.name: Iran

word.meaning: The elaborate courtesy of Persian manners: insisting that a guest take the best seat, refusing an offer politely at least once before accepting, a shopkeeper saying "it's not worthy of you" when you ask the price. It takes practice, and it's done with great warmth.

364.ask: Ask what their family puts on the table for Yalda night, and who reads from the poet Hafez, opening his book at random for a fortune.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Poetry: many Iranians quote Hafez and Rumi, and consulting a Hafez book for a fortune is a fun tradition.

Persian New Year: Nowruz, with spring cleaning, family visits and the haft-sin table, is a joyful holiday to ask about.

Food and hospitality: kebabs, saffron rice and long family meals are shared pleasures.

cards.title: This season: Yalda night
cards.text: On the longest night of the year, December 21, families gather at the home of the eldest, stay up late and eat red fruits, pomegranates and watermelon, for warmth and light, along with nuts and sweets, and read poetry, especially Hafez. Yalda, shared with Afghanistan as Chella, was added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2022.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its poetry, which people across Iran know by heart: Hafez, Rumi, Saadi and Ferdowsi, whose Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, preserved the Persian language and its old stories. Many Iranians keep a book of Hafez at home.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Persian classical music is built on the radif, a vast collection of melodies passed from master to student, played on the tar, setar, santur and kamancheh, a bowed fiddle, and UNESCO lists it as heritage. Kayhan Kalhor, a virtuoso of the kamancheh, has carried it to concert halls around the world, including with Yo-Yo Ma's Silk Road Ensemble.

cards.title: Craft: Persian carpets
cards.text: Hand-knotted carpets of wool and silk, woven by families and workshops across Iran, from the city carpets of Isfahan, Kashan and Tabriz to the bold tribal rugs of the Qashqai nomads, can take months or years to finish. UNESCO lists the carpet weaving of Fars and Kashan as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Persian leopard
cards.text: The largest leopard subspecies, with pale, thick fur, living in the mountains of the north and east.

cards.title: Place: Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Isfahan
cards.text: One of the largest city squares in the world, surrounded by arcades, a palace and two mosques covered in blue and turquoise tiles, built around 1600 when Isfahan was the capital. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tahdig, the golden, crispy crust of rice from the bottom of the pot, the part everyone wants. Saffron rice, and fesenjan, a stew of pomegranate and walnut. And a glass of tea, sweetened by holding a sugar cube between your teeth as you sip.

368.name: Iraq

word.meaning: An Iraqi greeting, literally "God in goodness," used like "good day" when meeting someone. The answer is "Allah bil-khair" or "hala," and a long exchange of blessings follows.

368.ask: Ask how their family makes kleicha, the date-filled cookies baked for Eid, and who in the family presses the patterns on top.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Iraqis celebrate their 2007 Asian Cup win as a moment of national joy that brought everyone together.

Food: masgouf, dolma and kleicha are loved, and Iraqi hospitality is famously generous.

Tea: small glasses of strong, sweet tea shared with friends are an everyday ritual, at home and in teahouses.

cards.title: This season: the date harvest
cards.text: From late summer into October, Iraq's date palms are harvested, above all around Basra, famous for varieties like Barhi, Halawi, Khadrawi and Zahidi. Some are eaten fresh and crunchy, others left to ripen soft and sweet, and they end up in kleicha and date syrup.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Mesopotamia, "the land between the rivers," where writing, cities and some of the first laws were born. Its poetry and its music. And the date palm, an Iraqi symbol.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Iraqi maqam is a classical vocal art, sung with the santur, a hammered dulcimer, and the joza, a spiked fiddle; UNESCO lists it as heritage. Munir Bashir, "the prince of the oud," made the oud a solo concert instrument and played around the world.

cards.title: Craft: Baghdad copper
cards.text: In the old Souq al-Safafeer, Baghdad's coppersmiths' market, craftsmen hammer and engrave copper pots, trays and coffee pots, and the ringing of their hammers fills the lanes.

cards.title: Creature: water buffalo of the marshes
cards.text: In the southern marshes, water buffalo wade and swim through the reeds, tended by the Marsh Arabs, whose milk and gaymar, clotted cream, are famous.

cards.title: Place: the Ahwar
cards.text: The Mesopotamian marshes, where the Tigris and Euphrates meet, with reed houses called mudhif, canoes gliding through channels, and flocks of birds. Together with ancient Sumerian cities like Ur, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Masgouf, carp split open and slow-grilled over a fire, the national dish. Dolma. Kahi with gaymar and date syrup for breakfast. And kleicha.

372.name: Ireland

word.meaning: Neighbors coming together to help each other with a big job, like bringing in the harvest or cutting turf, with food and talk at the end of the day. The word is Irish, and it's still used for any group that gathers to pitch in.

372.ask: Ask where to find the best session, where musicians gather to play traditional tunes together, and which tune always gets the room going.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: trad sessions in pubs, and bands from U2 to the Cranberries, are shared joys.

Sport: Gaelic football, hurling and rugby are followed passionately, and asking about a county team is a sure start.

Storytelling and humor: the Irish love banter, a good story and laughing at themselves.

cards.title: This season: Samhain
cards.text: Halloween began in Ireland as Samhain, on October 31, when the harvest was in and winter began, and the boundary between this world and the next was thought to be thin. Before pumpkins, people carved lanterns from turnips. Families still bake barmbrack, a fruit loaf with a ring hidden inside: whoever finds it in their slice is said to be married within the year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its writers. Four Irish writers have won the Nobel Prize in Literature: W. B. Yeats in 1923, George Bernard Shaw in 1925, Samuel Beckett in 1969, and Seamus Heaney in 1995. And the Irish language, still spoken every day in the Gaeltacht communities, mostly along the west coast, and taught in schools across the country.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Traditional music lives in sessions, where fiddles, flutes, tin whistles, button accordions and the bodhrán drum play jigs and reels together. The uilleann pipes, pumped with a bellows under the arm rather than blown, became Ireland's first entry on UNESCO's heritage list in 2017; Liam O'Flynn was one of their great players. For the modern bridge, the Dublin band Lankum makes old ballads sound huge and haunting, and their 2023 album False Lankum was shortlisted for the Mercury Prize.

cards.title: Craft: Aran sweaters
cards.text: Thick cream sweaters from the Aran Islands off Galway, knitted in cables, honeycombs and diamonds. A story says each family had its own pattern so that drowned fishermen could be identified, but there's no evidence for it: it seems to have grown from a J. M. Synge play and was later taken up in marketing. The real story is enough: skilled knitters on the islands, from the early 20th century, creating something new.

cards.title: Creature: Atlantic puffin
cards.text: From April to August, thousands of puffins nest in burrows on Skellig Michael, a rocky island off the Kerry coast where monks built stone beehive huts in the 6th or 7th century. The monastery is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Place: the Burren
cards.text: A landscape of bare gray limestone pavement in County Clare. In the cracks between the stones, arctic-alpine flowers like the blue spring gentian grow beside Mediterranean ones, and 25 of Ireland's 27 native orchid species are found here.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Soda bread, made with baking soda and buttermilk instead of yeast, with a cross cut in the top. At Halloween, colcannon, mashed potato with kale or cabbage and a pool of melting butter, sometimes with a charm hidden inside, like the barmbrack.

376.name: Israel

word.meaning: "Cool, great, no problem!" Everyday Israeli slang, borrowed from Arabic. Plans for the beach? Sababa. Running late? Sababa.

376.ask: Ask where to find the best hummus, and whether it's better with ful, a whole egg or just olive oil. Everyone has a favorite place and will defend it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: hummus, falafel and shakshuka are loved worldwide, and Israelis love recommending places.

The beach: Tel Aviv's beaches and matkot, a paddle-ball game, are summer rituals.

Friday dinners: many families gather on Friday evening for a big meal together.

cards.title: This season: the cranes of the Hula Valley
cards.text: From late October into November, tens of thousands of common cranes fly in from Europe to the Hula Valley in the north, on their way to Africa, and many stay the whole winter. At dawn, their trumpeting calls fill the air as huge flocks rise over the wetlands.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food scene, from street stalls to market kitchens. Its deserts, beaches and hills in a small space. And its music, science and startups.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Israeli music mixes melodies brought from all over the world: Yemenite, Moroccan, Ethiopian, Eastern European and more. The Idan Raichel Project brought singers of many backgrounds and languages together into one band, and became one of Israel's best-loved groups.

cards.title: Craft: Eilat stone
cards.text: A blue-green stone of copper minerals from the ancient mines of Timna in the south, polished and set in silver jewelry.

cards.title: Creature: Nubian ibex
cards.text: A wild mountain goat with long, curving horns, seen climbing the cliffs of the Negev desert and wandering calmly through the town of Mitzpe Ramon.

cards.title: Place: Makhtesh Ramon
cards.text: A huge erosion crater in the Negev, 40 kilometers long, with colorful sandstone, fossils and dark volcanic hills, best seen at sunrise from its rim.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Falafel and sabich, pita stuffed with fried eggplant and egg. Shakshuka, eggs poached in spicy tomato sauce. And an Israeli breakfast of salads, cheeses and breads.

380.name: Italy

word.meaning: The warm, heavy drowsiness that comes over you after a big, delicious meal, especially a long Sunday lunch. There's nothing to do about an abbiocco except give in to it.

380.ask: Ask what their nonna, their grandmother, cooks best, and whether anyone has ever managed to get the recipe written down exactly.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: pasta, pizza and regional dishes, and friendly debates about the right way to make them (no cream in carbonara).

Football: Serie A and the national team are followed passionately, and everyone has a club.

The passeggiata: the evening stroll through town, often with a gelato, is a simple joy anyone can share.

cards.title: This season: white truffles in Alba
cards.text: Autumn is truffle season in Piedmont. From October 10 to December 6 this year, on weekends, the town of Alba holds its International White Truffle Fair, where the rare, pungent white truffles dug by trained dogs in the hills around the town are sold, sniffed and shaved over plates of fresh egg pasta. Mid-November is said to be the best time for their scent.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food: in December 2025, UNESCO added Italian cuisine to its heritage list. And its art, from Roman ruins to Renaissance painting, in the country with the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and UNESCO now lists the art of Italian opera singing as heritage. But every region also has its own folk music. In the Salento, at the heel of Italy's boot, the pizzica, a whirling tarantella danced to tambourines and fiddles, was once used to cure the "bite" of the tarantula; for the modern bridge, Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino has brought it to stages around the world.

cards.title: Craft: Cremona violins
cards.text: In Cremona, where Antonio Stradivari and the Amati and Guarneri families made the world's most prized violins in the 1600s and 1700s, around 150 workshops still carve violins, violas and cellos by hand from spruce and maple. UNESCO lists Cremona's traditional violin craftsmanship as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Marsican brown bear
cards.text: A rare brown bear found only in the Apennine mountains of central Italy, mostly in and around Abruzzo National Park, with only around 60 left, famously gentle and a symbol of the park.

cards.title: Place: the Dolomites
cards.text: Pale limestone peaks in the northeast that glow pink and orange at sunrise and sunset, a light Ladin speakers call enrosadira. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fresh egg pasta with shaved white truffle in autumn. Risotto, pizza from Naples, and gelato. At Christmas, panettone from Milan, a tall, fluffy sweet bread with candied fruit and raisins.

384.name: Côte d'Ivoire

word.meaning: "It's going to be okay." Ivorians say it to comfort, to encourage, and to shrug off a small problem, and it's become something like a national motto of optimism.

384.ask: Ask where to find the best garba, attiéké with fried tuna and chili from a street stall, and whether they add onions and tomato.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Didier Drogba is a national hero, and the Elephants won the Africa Cup of Nations at home in 2024.

Music and dance: coupé-décalé and zouglou fill parties, and anyone who loves to dance has a friend.

Chocolate: Côte d'Ivoire grows more cocoa than any other country, a fun fact for any chocolate lover.

cards.title: This season: Abissa
cards.text: In late October or early November, the N'zima people of Grand-Bassam, the old colonial capital by the sea, celebrate Abissa, their new year, over a week of drumming, dancing and songs. It's also a time when people may speak freely, even to criticize their leaders, and then forgive one another before the year begins.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music, which has set dance floors moving across Africa and beyond, and its cocoa: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Zouglou, born among Abidjan students in the early 1990s, sings about everyday life with humor and heart; Magic System's "Premier Gaou" became a hit across Africa and France. Coupé-décalé, fast and flashy, followed in the 2000s, and reggae has a proud home here too, with Alpha Blondy.

cards.title: Craft: Korhogo cloth
cards.text: Senufo artists in the north paint handwoven cotton cloth with a dark mud-based dye, drawing birds, fish, masked dancers and animals in bold outline. The cloths were once worn by hunters and ritual dancers and are now made for walls and homes.

cards.title: Creature: pygmy hippopotamus
cards.text: A small, shy, forest-dwelling hippo that lives alone in the swamps and streams of West African rainforests, including Taï National Park. It's rare and hard to see.

cards.title: Place: Taï National Park
cards.text: One of the last large blocks of primary rainforest in West Africa, home to pygmy hippos and chimpanzees famous for cracking nuts with stone tools. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Attiéké, fermented cassava couscous, with grilled fish. Alloco, fried ripe plantain with chili sauce. And kedjenou, chicken slow-cooked in a sealed pot.

388.name: Jamaica

word.meaning: In Jamaican Patois, irie means good, peaceful, everything's all right, a feeling of being at ease with the world. It came into wide use through Rastafari and reggae, and "Irie!" works as a greeting, an answer and a blessing.

388.ask: Ask how their family makes sorrel at Christmas, the deep red drink of hibiscus, ginger and spice, and whose Christmas cake, soaked for months in rum and wine, is the richest.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: reggae, Bob Marley and dancehall are loved worldwide, and music is an easy connection.

Sprinting: Usain Bolt and Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce are national heroes, and Jamaicans love to talk about their athletes.

Food: jerk chicken, ackee and saltfish, and beef patties are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: Christmas and Grand Market
cards.text: Christmas in Jamaica means sorrel, fruit cake, and on Christmas Eve, Grand Market, when town squares fill with stalls, music and families shopping and strolling late into the night. In some places, Jonkonnu masqueraders in costumes and masks still dance through the streets, a tradition dating back to the days of slavery.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Reggae, which UNESCO added to its heritage list in 2018, and which carried Jamaica's voice to every corner of the world. And its athletes: Jamaica, a nation of under three million people, has produced some of the fastest sprinters in history, above all Usain Bolt.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Before reggae there was mento, Jamaica's country music of banjo, hand drums and rhumba box, then ska and rocksteady in the 1960s, then reggae, with Bob Marley its most famous voice. Dancehall followed in the 1980s. For the modern bridge, Koffee, from Spanish Town, became the youngest person and first woman to win the Grammy for Best Reggae Album, at 19, for her 2019 EP Rapture; her 2022 album Gifted carries the old roots sound forward.

cards.title: Craft: Jonkonnu masks
cards.text: For Jonkonnu, the Christmas masquerade, makers build costumes and masks for characters such as the Horse Head, the Cow Head, the Devil and Pitchy-Patchy, whose costume is made of hundreds of strips of colorful cloth. It's music, dance and costume-making all at once.

cards.title: Creature: doctor bird
cards.text: The red-billed streamertail, Jamaica's national bird, a hummingbird found only on the island. The male trails two long, fluttering tail feathers as he darts between flowers.

cards.title: Place: the Blue Mountains
cards.text: Misty, forested peaks in the east of the island, where the famous Blue Mountain coffee is grown, and where Maroon communities, descendants of Africans who escaped slavery, found refuge. The Blue and John Crow Mountains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ackee and saltfish, the national dish, where the soft yellow ackee fruit is cooked with salted cod, onions and peppers. Jerk chicken or pork, rubbed with scotch bonnet pepper and allspice and cooked slowly over pimento wood. And a patty, flaky pastry filled with spiced beef.

392.name: Japan

word.meaning: Sunlight filtering through the leaves of trees, in shifting patches on the ground. The characters say it plainly: tree, leaking through, sun.
word.sayIt: koh-moh-reh-bee (keep every syllable even; Japanese doesn't stress one over the others)

392.ask: Ask which season they think Japan is most beautiful in, and where they'd go to see it. Almost everyone has a favorite, and a place to go with it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: sushi, ramen and even convenience-store snacks are fun to talk about, and many people abroad love Japanese food.

Baseball: Shohei Ohtani is a hero, and baseball is hugely popular, from high school tournaments to the major leagues.

Anime and Studio Ghibli: many people grew up with Ghibli films and manga, in Japan and beyond.

cards.title: This season: autumn leaves and Shichi-Go-San
cards.text: Momijigari, "hunting red leaves," is the autumn outing to see the maples turn. The color moves down from the mountains and the north through October, reaching Kyoto and Tokyo in late November. On November 15, at Shichi-Go-San ("seven-five-three"), children aged three, five and seven visit shrines in their best kimono to give thanks for growing up healthy, and go home with chitose-ame, long red-and-white "thousand-year candy" for a long life.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The seasons, and the care taken over them: food, poetry, festivals and even sweets change with each one. Mount Fuji, painted again and again by Hokusai, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as a sacred place and a source of artistic inspiration. And the Shinkansen, the bullet train, has run since 1964, when the first line opened just before the Tokyo Olympics.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Min'yō are Japan's folk songs: work songs, fishing songs and festival dances, each rooted in its own region, often sung over the shamisen, a three-stringed lute, and taiko drums. From the snowy north comes Tsugaru shamisen, played fast and fierce with a big plectrum; Hiromitsu Agatsuma is one of its modern stars. For the bridge, the Tokyo band Minyo Crusaders set old min'yō to cumbia, Afrobeat and reggae on their 2017 album Echoes of Japan, and it works beautifully.

cards.title: Craft: washi
cards.text: Handmade paper, strong and translucent, made from the long fibers of the paper mulberry without bleach, for at least 1,300 years. UNESCO lists the craft as it's practiced in three communities: Hon-minoshi in Mino, Gifu; Sekishū-banshi in Shimane; and Hosokawa-shi in Saitama. It's used for calligraphy, lanterns, and the sliding shōji screens that soften the light in a room.

cards.title: Creature: Japanese macaque
cards.text: The snow monkey, the most northerly living primate apart from people. At Jigokudani, "Hell Valley," in Nagano's snowy mountains, a troop took to bathing in a hot spring in the 1960s, and they still soak there in winter with snow on their heads.

cards.title: Place: Yakushima
cards.text: A mountainous, mossy island south of Kyushu, one of the rainiest places in Japan, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993. Its ancient cedars include Jōmon Sugi, hollow at the center and so hard to date: estimates range from about 2,000 to 7,200 years old.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Autumn tastes of yaki-imo, sweet potatoes roasted on hot stones and sold from trucks that sing a slow call through the streets, and of sanma, Pacific saury grilled with salt, though catches have fallen steeply in recent years. Hoshigaki, persimmons hung to dry under the eaves, turn dark, soft and sugary by winter.

398.name: Kazakhstan

word.meaning: The tablecloth, and the whole generous spread laid on it for guests: bread, sweets, dried fruit, tea, and then the main meal. A full dastarkhan is the heart of Kazakh hospitality, and a guest is never sent away hungry.

398.ask: Ask whether anyone in their family plays the dombra, the two-stringed lute, and which melody they'd most like you to hear.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hospitality: a generous table for guests, the dastarkhan, is a point of pride, and being fed well is part of the welcome.

Dimash: the singer has fans all over the world, and fans love meeting other fans.

The mountains: hiking and skiing near Almaty, and trips to Charyn Canyon and the Kolsai lakes, are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: apple time
cards.text: In September and October, apples ripen around Almaty, a city whose name comes from the Kazakh word for apple. The wild apple forests of the nearby Tian Shan mountains are home to the main wild ancestor of every apple we eat, and markets fill with the big, fragrant local Aport apples.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The steppe: Kazakhstan is the ninth-largest country in the world and the largest landlocked one, with grasslands, mountains, deserts and lakes. And its poet Abai Qunanbaiuly, whose words about learning and kindness are loved by every Kazakh.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Küi are instrumental pieces played on the dombra, each telling a story through melody alone: a horse race, a lament, a legend. UNESCO lists the art of the Kazakh dombra küi as heritage. For the modern bridge, the singer Dimash Qudaibergen, with a vocal range of over six octaves, has fans all over the world and often brings the dombra onstage.

cards.title: Craft: the yurt
cards.text: The kiiz üi, the felt home of the nomads, is built on a wooden lattice frame and covered in felt, then decorated inside with embroidered hangings and felt carpets. It can be put up or taken down in an hour or two, and UNESCO lists the craft as heritage, shared with Kyrgyzstan.

cards.title: Creature: saiga
cards.text: A steppe antelope with a big, bulbous, trunk-like nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Poaching and disease brought Kazakhstan's saigas down to about 21,000 in 2003; thanks to protection, they numbered more than 2.8 million in 2024, one of the great recoveries in conservation.

cards.title: Place: Charyn Canyon
cards.text: East of Almaty, the Charyn River has cut a canyon of red and orange rock towers, with a path called the Valley of Castles winding between them. It's often compared to a small Grand Canyon.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Beshbarmak, "five fingers," boiled meat on wide flat noodles, eaten with the hands at celebrations. Baursak, puffy fried dough, on every dastarkhan. And kumys, tangy fermented mare's milk.

400.name: Jordan

word.meaning: "Welcome," in Arabic, and more than that: it means roughly "you are among family, and your path here is easy." In Jordan you'll hear it constantly, and it usually comes with a cup of coffee or tea.

400.ask: Ask who makes the best mansaf in their family, and whether they eat it the traditional way, standing around a big shared platter and forming the rice into balls with the right hand.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food and hospitality: mansaf, shared from a big platter, is a celebration dish.

Petra and Wadi Rum: Jordanians love hearing that you've visited or dream of visiting.

Football: the national team reached the Asian Cup final in 2024, a happy memory.

cards.title: This season: the olive harvest
cards.text: Autumn is olive season in the hills of the north, around Ajloun, Irbid and Jerash. Families spread cloths under the trees, beat the branches, and take the olives to the press, and the first green, peppery oil of the year is poured over bread with za'atar.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Petra, of course, and its hospitality, rooted in Bedouin tradition, where guests are welcomed and fed without question. And the Dead Sea, the lowest place on land, so salty you float without trying.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The oud and the rababa, a one-stringed Bedouin fiddle, carry the old songs of the desert and villages, and the dabke, a line dance of stamping feet, fills every wedding. For the modern bridge, the Amman band Autostrad sings about everyday Jordanian life in the local dialect, over a mix of rock, reggae and funk.

cards.title: Craft: Bedouin weaving
cards.text: Bedouin women spin goat hair and sheep's wool and weave it on ground looms into tent panels, rugs and cushions with bold stripes and geometric patterns in black, red and white. Weaving projects in villages like Bani Hamida help keep the craft alive.

cards.title: Creature: Arabian oryx
cards.text: A white antelope with long, straight horns, once hunted to extinction in the wild. Oryx bred in captivity have been returned to Jordan's deserts, including Wadi Rum and the Shaumari reserve.

cards.title: Place: Petra
cards.text: The rose-red city of the Nabataeans, carved into sandstone cliffs more than 2,000 years ago, reached through the Siq, a narrow canyon that suddenly opens onto the Treasury. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and one of the new Seven Wonders of the World.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mansaf, lamb cooked in a sauce of fermented dried yogurt called jameed, served on rice with toasted nuts, which UNESCO added to its heritage list in 2022. Knafeh, warm cheese pastry soaked in syrup. And cardamom coffee, poured in small cups.

404.name: Kenya

word.meaning: "Let's all pull together," in Swahili. It's Kenya's national motto, on the coat of arms, and it's also the name for a community fundraiser, where neighbors pool what they can to build a school, pay a hospital bill or send someone to university. It's thought to come from the call of porters lifting heavy loads together.

404.ask: Ask how their family makes chai, and who makes the best chapati at home. Everyone has a favorite, and a story about learning to roll them.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Running: Eliud Kipchoge and Faith Kipyegon are national heroes, and runners have instant common ground.

Wildlife: many Kenyans are proud of their parks and the Great Migration, and safari stories are easy to trade.

Football and music: Kenyans follow the Premier League closely (many support Arsenal or Manchester United) and love Afrobeats and gengetone.

cards.title: This season: the Lamu Cultural Festival
cards.text: On the island of Lamu, off Kenya's northern coast, the Lamu Cultural Festival comes in late November or early December, with dhow races across the channel, donkey races through the lanes, henna painting, bao board games, poetry and Swahili food. Lamu has no cars, so the donkeys are part of daily life.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its runners. Kenyan athletes, many from the highlands of the Rift Valley, have dominated distance running for decades; in 2019 Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in a specially arranged race in Vienna. And Wangari Maathai, who founded the Green Belt Movement, which has planted tens of millions of trees, became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, in 2004.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Benga grew up in western Kenya in the 1960s and 70s, with bright, interlocking electric guitar lines inspired by the Luo nyatiti lyre; D. O. Misiani is known as its father. On the coast, taarab blends Swahili poetry with Arab and Indian melody. For the modern bridge, Sauti Sol, the Nairobi band whose name means "voice of the sun," brought Kenyan sounds into Afro-pop; their 2020 album Midnight Train is a warm place to start.

cards.title: Craft: kiondo baskets
cards.text: Sturdy woven bags made from sisal fiber, traditionally by Kikuyu and Kamba women, patterned in bright dyed stripes and finished with leather straps. Each can take days to weave by hand.

cards.title: Creature: lesser flamingo
cards.text: At the soda lakes of the Rift Valley, Nakuru and Bogoria, more than a million lesser flamingos have been counted at once, turning the shallows pink as they feed on the algae that color them. The lakes are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the most important feeding grounds for the species anywhere.

cards.title: Place: Lamu Old Town
cards.text: The oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement in East Africa, a maze of narrow lanes, carved wooden doors and coral-stone houses, where dhows still sail in and out of the harbor. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Nyama choma, goat or beef grilled slowly over charcoal and shared with friends, served with kachumbari, a fresh tomato and onion salad, and ugali, a firm maize porridge you eat with your hands. And chai, milky and sweet, brewed with the tea leaves, milk and water all in one pot.

408.name: North Korea

word.meaning: The heated floor of a traditional Korean home, warmed from below by a fire or hot water. In winter, families eat, talk and sleep on the warm floor, and the warmest spot is saved for elders and guests.

408.ask: Ask about kimchi-making in their family: who did the most work, and what their grandmother's kimchi tasted like.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Korean food: kimchi, naengmyeon and bindaetteok are loved across Korea and abroad.

"Arirang": the folk song is sung and loved across the whole peninsula, and many people abroad know it too.

Kimchi-making: making kimchi together in November is a family tradition many Koreans share.

cards.title: This season: kimchi-making
cards.text: In November, before the cold sets in, families and neighbors across Korea gather to make kimchi for the winter, salting, spicing and packing hundreds of cabbages together into jars. UNESCO lists the tradition of kimchi-making in North Korea as heritage, and the South's kimjang too.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Korean language, food and song, shared across the peninsula. Its mountains, like Kumgang, the Diamond Mountains, painted and praised by Korean artists and poets for centuries. And Pyongyang naengmyeon, its famous cold noodles.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: "Arirang," a folk song about love and parting, is sung all over Korea in many regional versions and is often called the unofficial anthem of the whole peninsula. UNESCO lists it as heritage, for both North and South Korea.

links.label: Korean Folk Music: Four Thousand Years

cards.title: Craft: Korean embroidery
cards.text: Embroiderers work with fine silk threads to make pictures of flowers, birds, tigers and mountain landscapes, some so detailed they look like paintings.

cards.title: Creature: Siberian tiger
cards.text: The Amur tiger, the largest cat in the world, once roamed the mountains of the Korean peninsula and appears everywhere in Korean folk tales and paintings.

cards.title: Place: Mount Kumgang
cards.text: The "Diamond Mountains," a range of granite peaks, waterfalls, pools and old temples on the east coast, celebrated in Korean painting and poetry for centuries.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pyongyang naengmyeon, buckwheat noodles in icy, tangy broth. Kimchi. And bindaetteok, crispy mung bean pancakes.

410.name: South Korea

word.meaning: The warm, stubborn bond that grows between people, or between a person and a place, simply through time spent together: meals shared, small favors, showing up again and again. There's no single English word for it.
word.sayIt: jung (a short, open "uh" sound, like "jung" in "jungle")

410.ask: Ask how their family does kimjang, the big autumn kimchi-making: who's in charge of the seasoning, and how many cabbages they make. Some families still count them in the hundreds.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
K-pop and K-dramas: BTS, BLACKPINK and dramas are loved worldwide.

Food: Korean barbecue, kimchi and fried chicken are shared joys.

Baseball: the KBO league is followed passionately, with famous cheering songs.

cards.title: This season: kimjang
cards.text: In late autumn, families and neighbors gather to make the winter's kimchi together: salting whole napa cabbages, then rubbing each leaf with a paste of chili, garlic, ginger, radish and fermented seafood. Everyone takes some home, and the work is as much about sharing as about food. UNESCO lists kimjang as heritage. On October 9, Hangeul Day celebrates the Korean alphabet.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Hangeul, the Korean alphabet, which King Sejong the Great and his scholars created so that ordinary people could learn to read and write. It was announced in 1446, and its letters are designed to reflect how the mouth shapes each sound. People take real pride in how quickly it can be learned.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Pansori is epic storytelling in song: a single singer, holding a fan, performs a long tale in voice, speech and gesture, accompanied only by a drummer who calls out encouragement. A complete performance can last for hours, and UNESCO lists it as heritage. For the modern bridge, the band Leenalchi set scenes from the pansori tale Sugungga to bass-driven pop in 2020, and "Tiger Is Coming" became a national hit, helped by the joyful tourism videos danced to it.

cards.title: Craft: jogakbo
cards.text: Patchwork wrapping cloths, sewn by women in the Joseon era from scraps left over from making hanbok and bedding. Pieces of silk, cotton or translucent ramie are joined with a triple-stitched flat seam that makes the cloth reversible and gives it the look of a stained-glass window. Bojagi, wrapping cloths, are still used to wrap gifts.

cards.title: Creature: red-crowned crane
cards.text: Elegant white cranes with black necks and a red cap. From November to February they winter on the Cheorwon plain, just south of the demilitarized zone between the two Koreas, where decades with few people around have left the wetlands and rice fields undisturbed.

cards.title: Place: Jeju Island
cards.text: A volcanic island off the south coast, crowned by Hallasan, South Korea's highest mountain, and laced with lava tubes; UNESCO lists its volcanic landscape as a World Heritage Site. Jeju is also home to the haenyeo, women who free-dive for shellfish and seaweed without breathing gear, some well into their seventies and eighties, a tradition UNESCO also lists.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fresh kimjang kimchi is traditionally eaten on the day with bossam, slices of tender boiled pork wrapped in cabbage leaves. As the weather turns cold, street stalls sell hotteok, griddled pancakes filled with brown sugar, cinnamon and nuts.

414.name: Kuwait

word.meaning: A reception room, and the regular evening gathering held in it, where friends, neighbors and relatives drop by to talk about everything from football to politics over tea and coffee. The diwaniya is the heart of Kuwaiti social life.

414.ask: Ask which diwaniya they go to, and what the best conversation there was about.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Diwaniyas: evening gatherings with friends to talk about everything from football to family, a tradition worth asking about.

Winter camping: families set up tents in the desert in winter for barbecues and stargazing.

Food: machboos and sweets are shared at big family meals, and hospitality is generous.

cards.title: This season: camping season
cards.text: When the heat breaks, Kuwaitis head to the desert. The official camping season usually runs from mid-November to mid-March, and families set up tents with carpets, cushions and generators for weekends of barbecues, stargazing and gatherings.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its seafaring and pearling past, and its music. Its diwaniyas. And Al Sadu weaving, listed by UNESCO.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Kuwait has long been a center of Gulf music, from sailors' songs to sawt, songs with the oud and hand-clapping. Abdullah Al Rowaished, one of the biggest voices in Khaleeji music, has sung love songs since the 1980s.

cards.title: Craft: Al Sadu weaving
cards.text: Bedouin women weave Al Sadu on ground looms from sheep, camel and goat hair, in bold geometric patterns of red, black and white, for tents, rugs and camel bags. UNESCO lists it as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding, and Sadu House in Kuwait City keeps it alive.

cards.title: Creature: mudskipper
cards.text: On the mudflats of Kuwait Bay, mudskippers, fish that can breathe air, hop and skip across the mud at low tide, flipping their fins to show off.

cards.title: Place: Failaka Island
cards.text: An island at the mouth of Kuwait Bay with ruins from the Bronze Age Dilmun civilization and a Greek temple and fortress from the time after Alexander the Great.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Machboos zubaidi, spiced rice with pomfret fish. Gers ogaily, a saffron and cardamom cake. And balaleet.

417.name: Kyrgyzstan

word.meaning: A high summer pasture in the mountains, where families take their herds and live in yurts from June to September, drinking kymyz, fermented mare's milk, and riding horses under huge skies.

417.ask: Ask whether their family goes to a jailoo in summer, and what they love most about it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Horses and summer pastures: many Kyrgyz grew up riding, and summers at the jailoo are cherished memories.

Hospitality: tea, bread and food for every guest, and a guest never leaves hungry.

The World Nomad Games: horseback games like kok-boru and eagle hunting made them famous, a fun topic to ask about.

cards.title: This season: the walnut harvest
cards.text: In late September and October, families in Arslanbob, in the south, head into the largest natural walnut forest on Earth to gather the harvest. They camp among the trees, share meals around campfires and sing, and the town holds a walnut festival in early October.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Epic of Manas, one of the longest epic poems in the world, about the hero Manas and his descendants, recited from memory by storytellers called manaschi. UNESCO lists it as heritage. And its mountains: more than 90 percent of the country is mountainous.
