cards.title: Music
cards.text: The komuz, a three-stringed lute without frets, is the national instrument. Players perform küü, instrumental pieces that tell stories of horses, love and the mountains, sometimes adding flips and tricks as they play.

links.label: The Music of Kyrgyzstan, The Kambarkan Folk Ensemble

cards.title: Craft: shyrdak
cards.text: Felt carpets made by women from sheep's wool, with bold patterns in contrasting colors cut out and sewn together, often shaped like ram's horns. A shyrdak can last a lifetime. UNESCO lists the craft as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

cards.title: Creature: snow leopard
cards.text: The pale, spotted cat of the high mountains, with a long, thick tail it wraps around itself for warmth. The Tian Shan and Pamir mountains are some of its most important homes.

cards.title: Place: Issyk-Kul
cards.text: A huge blue mountain lake, about 1,600 meters above sea level, ringed by snowy peaks. Its slightly salty water never freezes, and its name means "warm lake."

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Beshbarmak and kuurdak, fried meat with onions. Lagman, hand-pulled noodles. Boorsok, puffy fried dough. And kymyz from the jailoo.

418.name: Laos

word.meaning: "No problem," "never mind," "it's nothing": the phrase that sums up the easygoing Lao way of taking life's small troubles in stride.
word.nativeScript: ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງ

418.ask: Ask how their family makes jeow, the chili dips eaten with sticky rice, and how they roll the rice into a ball with their fingers to scoop it up.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Sticky rice: eaten by hand at every meal, and a fun thing to learn to do properly.

Food: larb and papaya salad are loved, and anyone who likes spicy food has a friend.

Festivals: Boun Pi Mai, the New Year water festival in April, is a joyful time full of good memories.

cards.title: This season: That Luang
cards.text: On the full moon of the twelfth lunar month, November 24 this year, Vientiane holds the biggest festival in Laos at Pha That Luang, the great golden stupa that is the national symbol. For about a week there are candlelit processions, monks receiving alms from thousands of people at dawn, and a fair with music and food around the stupa.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its old name, Lan Xang, "Land of a Million Elephants." And its gentleness: the calm of its Buddhist temples and the pace of life along the Mekong.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The khaen, a mouth organ of bamboo pipes, is the sound of Laos, and UNESCO lists khaen music of the Lao people as heritage. It accompanies lam, sung poetry in which pairs of singers improvise stories and playful courting duels. The album Music from Southern Laos, by the Molam Lao ensemble, captures it beautifully.

links.label: Music from Southern Laos, Molam Lao

cards.title: Craft: silk weaving
cards.text: Lao women weave silk on looms under their stilted houses, making the sinh, the wrapped skirt worn every day and on special occasions, with borders of intricate patterns: nagas, the mythical river serpents, diamonds and flowers. Each ethnic group and region has its own designs.

cards.title: Creature: Asian elephant
cards.text: Laos's old name honors the elephant, still found in its forests and once used for logging. Sanctuaries now care for retired working elephants.

cards.title: Place: Luang Prabang
cards.text: The old royal capital on a peninsula where the Nam Khan meets the Mekong, with gilded temples, French colonial houses and, every dawn, a silent procession of saffron-robed monks collecting sticky rice from kneeling residents. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Sticky rice, eaten with every meal from small woven baskets. Larb, a salad of minced meat or fish with lime, mint and toasted rice powder. And khao piak sen, a comforting thick rice-noodle soup.

422.name: Lebanon

word.meaning: "Please, go ahead, come in, have some." Lebanese say it when they open the door, offer a seat, pass a plate or hand over a coffee. To a woman, it's "tfaddale."

422.ask: Ask what their teta, their grandmother, cooks best, and whether anyone has ever matched it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: mezze, tabbouleh and manakish are loved worldwide, and Lebanese love sharing their food.

Music: Fairuz is loved across generations, and her songs are a warm point of connection.

Hospitality: guests are always offered coffee and something to eat, and saying no is almost impossible.

cards.title: This season: Eid il-Burbara
cards.text: On December 4, Lebanese children dress up in costumes and masks and go from house to house singing, and neighbors give them sweets and burbara: boiled wheat with pomegranate seeds, raisins, anise, nuts and sugar. It remembers Saint Barbara, who in the story disguised herself to escape her persecutors and hid in a wheat field that grew up around her.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food and hospitality, known around the world. The cedar tree on its flag, a symbol for thousands of years. And Byblos, one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities on Earth, where Phoenicians wrote with an early alphabet that many later alphabets grew from.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Fairuz, one of the most loved voices in the Arab world, has sung for over half a century, many of her songs written by the Rahbani brothers; across Lebanon, mornings begin with her songs on the radio. Her son Ziad Rahbani blended Arabic music with jazz, and Beirut keeps a lively scene of bands and singers.

cards.title: Craft: Tripoli soap
cards.text: In the old souks of Tripoli, soapmakers still make olive oil soap by hand, as they have for centuries, scenting it with herbs, flowers and honey and cutting it into bars to cure, around the old Khan al-Saboun, the soap caravanserai.

cards.title: Creature: striped hyena
cards.text: A shy, nocturnal scavenger with a shaggy mane and striped legs that lives in Lebanon's hills and valleys. It helps keep the countryside clean, even though it's often misunderstood.

cards.title: Place: the Qadisha Valley and the Cedars of God
cards.text: A deep, green valley in the northern mountains where monks carved monasteries and hermitages into the cliffs over many centuries. Above it grows the Cedars of God, one of the last groves of the ancient cedars of Lebanon. Together they're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tabbouleh, heavy on the parsley. Kibbeh, bulgur and meat shaped into ovals or baked in a tray. And man'oushe, flatbread with za'atar and olive oil, for breakfast.

426.name: Lesotho

word.meaning: Peace. It's the first word of the national motto, "Khotso, Pula, Nala": peace, rain, prosperity. Basotho greet each other with "khotso," and it's also a common name.

426.ask: Ask about their Basotho blanket: its pattern, what it means, and for which occasion they got it. Every family has favorites.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Basotho blankets: many families have favorites, worn with pride for weddings and celebrations, a great topic for anyone who loves textiles.

Horses: riding ponies through the mountains is part of life, and horse lovers have a friend.

Choirs: choral singing is beloved, from church to school competitions.

cards.title: This season: the Morija Arts and Cultural Festival
cards.text: Most years around early October, the historic village of Morija holds its arts festival, with choirs, famo accordion music, traditional dance, horse racing, poetry and food. Exact dates change from year to year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "The Kingdom in the Sky": all of Lesotho lies above 1,000 meters, and its lowest point is higher than any other country's. And the Basotho blanket and the mokorotlo hat, symbols of the nation.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Herd boys in the mountains play the lesiba, a mouth-bow with a feather that vibrates as they breathe across it, making sounds like birdsong. Famo, with accordion, drum and bass, sung and chanted, grew among Basotho mineworkers in the 20th century and is still the sound of the country. Puseletso Seema, "the Queen of Famo," was one of its first great women singers.

cards.title: Craft: the mokorotlo
cards.text: The conical woven-grass hat, with a knob on top, that's said to take its shape from the mountain Qiloane near Thaba Bosiu. It appears on Lesotho's flag and is worn with pride.

cards.title: Creature: bearded vulture
cards.text: A huge vulture with a rust-orange chest and a black "beard," which drops bones onto rocks to crack them and eat the marrow. The Maloti mountains are one of its last homes in southern Africa.

cards.title: Place: Maletsunyane Falls
cards.text: Near Semonkong, "place of smoke," the Maletsunyane River drops about 190 meters in a single fall into a deep gorge. Hikers, horses and abseilers come to see it.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Papa, stiff maize porridge, with moroho, cooked greens. Lamb and mutton from the highlands. And motoho, a fermented sorghum porridge.

428.name: Latvia

word.meaning: To go mushroom hunting. It gets its own verb because autumn weekends in Latvia mean heading to the forest with a basket and a knife, and coming home with chanterelles, boletes and stories.

428.ask: Ask about their best mushroom spot. They probably won't tell you exactly where it is, but the story of the best haul will be worth it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Singing: the Song and Dance Festival brings tens of thousands of singers together, and choir singers have a lot to share.

Mushroom picking: a favorite autumn pastime, with closely guarded secret spots.

Hockey and basketball: both are followed passionately, and Kristaps Porziņģis is a star.

cards.title: This season: November lights
cards.text: November is Latvia's month of candles and celebration. On November 11, Lāčplēsis Day, named for the bear-slaying hero of the national epic, people remember those who fought for the country's freedom by lighting thousands of candles along the old walls of Riga Castle by the river. On November 18, Independence Day, families gather and fireworks light up the sky over the Daugava.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Singing. Latvia's Song and Dance Festival brings together tens of thousands of singers and dancers in one great choir, and UNESCO lists it as heritage, shared with Estonia and Lithuania. And the dainas: more than a million short folk song verses, collected by Krišjānis Barons in a cabinet of tiny drawers.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The dainas are sung in many ways, some with drone singing, and played on the kokle, a small plucked zither. For the modern bridge, the band Tautumeitas, six women, sing old Latvian songs in fresh harmonies with fiddle and drums.

cards.title: Craft: mittens
cards.text: Latvian mittens are knitted in bright, intricate patterns, with ancient symbols for the sun, fire and the gods. A bride once filled a chest with hundreds of pairs to give as gifts at her wedding.

cards.title: Creature: white wagtail
cards.text: The national bird, a slim black, white and gray bird that wags its long tail as it runs along the ground. Its return from the south is one of the first signs of spring.

cards.title: Place: Riga's Art Nouveau
cards.text: Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in the world, many of them in the quarter around Alberta Street, with facades full of faces, peacocks and flowers. The historic center of Riga is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Rye bread, dark and slightly sweet. Grey peas with bacon and onions. Sklandrausis, a rye tart filled with potato and carrot. And smoked fish from the coast.

430.name: Liberia

word.meaning: "Little by little, slowly." In Liberian English, you learn small-small, you walk small-small, and a problem gets fixed small-small. It's patience and hope in two words.

430.ask: Ask them to teach you the Liberian handshake, which ends with both people snapping their fingers together, and how loud the snap should be.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: George Weah, a Ballon d'Or winner, is a national hero, and football is an easy conversation.

Music: hipco and gospel fill Monrovia, and music lovers have plenty to share.

Food: palm butter, cassava leaf and jollof rice are loved, and Liberians love to feed their guests.

cards.title: This season: Thanksgiving Day
cards.text: Liberia celebrates its own national Thanksgiving on the first Thursday of November, November 5 in 2026, a tradition written into law in 1883. Families go to church to give thanks for the harvest and the year, then gather for a big meal.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its resilience and warmth. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Africa's first elected woman head of state, and Leymah Gbowee, who led women's peace protests; both won the Nobel Peace Prize. And its rainforests, among the largest remaining in West Africa.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Traditional music is played on drums, the sasa rattle and the kpanto, a thumb piano. Miatta Fahnbulleh, "the voice of Liberia," sang soulful songs across Africa and beyond from the 1970s. Today, hipco, rap in Liberian English, is the sound of Monrovia's streets.

cards.title: Craft: country cloth
cards.text: Handwoven cotton cloth, spun and dyed by hand and woven on narrow looms into strips, then sewn into gowns, bags and blankets, in patterns of stripes and blocks.

cards.title: Creature: white-necked rockfowl
cards.text: A strange, beautiful bird with a bare yellow head and a white neck, which builds mud nests on the sides of rocks in the rainforest and hops more than it flies.

cards.title: Place: Sapo National Park
cards.text: The country's first national park, a vast rainforest home to pygmy hippos, forest elephants, chimpanzees and hundreds of bird species.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Palm butter, a rich stew made from palm nuts, with rice. Cassava leaf and potato greens. And jollof rice and pepper soup.

434.name: Libya

word.meaning: "Good, fine, okay!" The everyday Libyan word for agreement and well-being. "Kulshi bahi?" Is everything good? "Bahi," all good.

434.ask: Ask how their family makes bazeen, the barley dough dome served in a spicy stew, and how you're supposed to eat it with your hand.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tea: strong green tea, poured high to make foam and often served with peanuts, is shared with friends.

Football: Libyans follow local clubs like Al-Ahli and Al-Ittihad, and the big European leagues, passionately.

Food: couscous, bazeen and sharba are family favorites, especially during Ramadan.

cards.title: This season: the Ghadames Festival
cards.text: In late October, the old desert town of Ghadames holds its festival, when families return to their houses in the old town and open their doors for singing and dancing, with Tuareg music, markets, and horse and camel races outside the walls, all in traditional dress.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its Mediterranean coast, among the longest in Africa. Its Roman cities, like Leptis Magna. And the Sahara, with the rock art of the Acacus Mountains.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Malouf, an Andalusian music brought across North Africa, is played at weddings and festivals. Ahmed Fakroun, from Benghazi, blended Arabic melodies with synthesizers into a pop sound that's been rediscovered around the world.

cards.title: Craft: Ghadames interiors
cards.text: Ghadamsi women paint the white inside walls of their homes with bright red, green and yellow designs, and hang mirrors, copper and baskets to make the rooms glow with light from above.

cards.title: Creature: Barbary sheep
cards.text: The aoudad, a sandy wild sheep with long fringes of hair on its chest and legs, lives in the rocky mountains of the Sahara, like the Acacus.

cards.title: Place: Leptis Magna
cards.text: One of the most magnificent Roman cities in the Mediterranean, by the sea east of Tripoli, with a theater, arches, markets and baths still standing. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Bazeen. Couscous with lamb. Sharba, a spicy soup with orzo and mint. And dates with tea.

440.name: Lithuania

word.meaning: "Hi!" It comes from the word for "good," and it's how Lithuanians greet friends. "Labas rytas" is good morning. Lithuanian is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages, and it keeps many ancient forms.

440.ask: Ask how their family makes cepelinai, big potato dumplings named for zeppelins, and how much sour cream and bacon belongs on top.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Basketball: Lithuanians are passionate about it, and Arvydas Sabonis and Domantas Sabonis are heroes.

Nature: forests, lakes and the Curonian Spit are shared joys, and so is mushroom and berry picking.

Food: cepelinai and pink cold beet soup are fun to talk about, and to try.

cards.title: This season: Vėlinės
cards.text: On November 1 and 2, families across Lithuania visit the graves of their relatives, bringing flowers and candles. After dark, whole cemeteries glow with thousands of small flames, and at home some families keep an empty place at dinner for those who are gone.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Basketball, often called Lithuania's second religion. The national team has won Olympic medals, and hoops hang on barns and houses across the country. And its language, kept alive by the knygnešiai, book smugglers who carried Lithuanian books across the border when printing in the Latin alphabet was banned, from 1864 to 1904.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Sutartinės are ancient songs sung by two to four women in overlapping lines, with sharp, clashing harmonies that sound surprisingly modern. UNESCO lists them as heritage. Lithuania is also part of the great Song Festival tradition with Latvia and Estonia. The Vilnius ensemble Kūlgrinda keeps sutartinės alive in its recordings.

cards.title: Craft: straw gardens
cards.text: Sodai, "gardens," are hanging ornaments made from straws threaded into geometric shapes, pyramids and diamonds, which turn and sway in the air. They're hung at Christmas, weddings and celebrations.

cards.title: Creature: grey heron
cards.text: Near Juodkrantė, on the Curonian Spit, grey herons and great cormorants nest together in one of the largest colonies in Europe, in the pine forest by the lagoon.

cards.title: Place: the Curonian Spit
cards.text: A narrow strip of sand dunes and pine forest nearly 100 kilometers long between the Baltic Sea and the Curonian Lagoon, with huge drifting dunes and old fishing villages. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shared with Russia.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Cepelinai with sour cream. Šaltibarščiai, a cold beet soup so bright pink it looks unreal. And šakotis, a tall "tree cake" baked on a spit, with spiky branches.

442.name: Luxembourg

word.meaning: "Hello!" in Luxembourgish, used at any time of day, in shops, on the street and between strangers. Luxembourgers often switch between Luxembourgish, French, German and English in one conversation, but "moien" is how it starts.

442.ask: Ask how many languages they speak at home, at school and at work, and which one they dream in.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Languages: most Luxembourgers speak several languages, and language lovers have instant common ground.

Cycling and hiking: popular pastimes in the Ardennes and along the Moselle, and cyclists will find a friend.

Food and wine: Moselle wines and local dishes like Gromperekichelcher are shared pleasures.

cards.title: This season: Winterlights
cards.text: From November 20, 2026, to January 3, 2027, Luxembourg City's squares fill with the wooden chalets, lights and music of Winterlights. The lights are switched on on November 21, and people meet after work for mulled wine, potato fritters and a ride on the Ferris wheel.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its language, Luxembourgish, which became a national language in 1984. Its fortress capital, once called "the Gibraltar of the North." And its size: small, but among the most international countries in Europe.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Luxembourg has a strong choir and brass band tradition, with a music society in nearly every town. Every Easter Monday, the Emaischen fair fills Luxembourg City's old town with music, stalls and the sound of clay bird whistles. For the modern bridge, the singer Serge Tonnar writes folk songs in Luxembourgish.

cards.title: Craft: Péckvillchen
cards.text: Little clay bird-shaped whistles, glazed in bright colors, made by potters in Nospelt and sold at the Emaischen fair. Blowing into the tail makes a warbling birdsong, and children and adults collect them year after year.

cards.title: Creature: red kite
cards.text: A graceful bird of prey with a forked, rust-red tail, often seen gliding low over Luxembourg's fields and forests looking for food.

cards.title: Place: the old city and fortifications
cards.text: Luxembourg City sits on a rocky cliff above the valleys of the Alzette and Pétrusse rivers, with medieval walls and the Bock Casemates, miles of tunnels carved into the rock. The old quarters and fortifications are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Judd mat Gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, the national dish. Gromperekichelcher, crispy potato fritters. And Quetschentaart, plum tart, in late summer.

450.name: Madagascar

word.meaning: From havana, "kin," fihavanana is the Malagasy ideal of kinship, solidarity and goodwill: treating neighbors and friends with the closeness of family, keeping the peace, and being ready to help. It reaches back to the ancestors too.

450.ask: Ask how their family eats rice, which in Madagascar comes with almost every meal, and whether they drink ranovola, the toasty water made from the crust of rice at the bottom of the pot.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Wildlife: lemurs and baobabs are world-famous, and Malagasy are proud of them.

Music: salegy and hiragasy are joyful and danceable, and music lovers have an opening.

Rice: eaten at nearly every meal, often three times a day, a fun fact to talk about.

cards.title: This season: lychee time
cards.text: In November and December, the lychee harvest begins on the east coast around Toamasina. Roadsides fill with sellers and red bunches, and ships carry thousands of tons to Europe, just in time for Christmas and New Year tables.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wildlife: Madagascar split from the rest of the world's land millions of years ago, and most of its plants and animals, from lemurs to chameleons to baobabs, are found nowhere else on Earth.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The valiha, the national instrument, is a tube zither made from a length of bamboo with strings running around it, with a delicate, rippling sound; Justin Vali is one of its great players. Along the north coast, salegy is fast and electric, made for dancing. For a bridge between the two, Rossy, one of the island's best-loved musicians, mixes traditional rhythms of the highlands and coast into modern pop.

cards.title: Craft: Antemoro paper
cards.text: In the southeast, the Antemoro people make paper by hand from the bark of the avoha tree, and press fresh flowers and leaves into the wet sheets, so each page carries its own pattern of petals.

cards.title: Creature: indri
cards.text: The largest living lemur, black and white with a teddy-bear face and almost no tail. Families of indri sing to each other across the rainforest each morning in eerie, wailing songs that carry for kilometers.

cards.title: Place: the Avenue of the Baobabs
cards.text: Near Morondava in the west, a dirt road runs between rows of giant baobabs, some hundreds of years old, their trunks rising like pillars to small crowns of branches. At sunset they glow red against the sky.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Romazava, a beef and greens stew with brèdes mafana, a leaf that makes your tongue tingle, served over rice. Mofo gasy, little rice-flour cakes sold warm from street stalls in the morning. And vanilla: Madagascar grows most of the world's supply.

454.name: Malawi

word.meaning: "Thank you" in Chichewa, also used for "excuse me," "sorry for your trouble" and "well done." "Zikomo kwambiri" means thank you very much.

454.ask: Ask how they like their chambo, the fish from Lake Malawi, and whether it's best fried, grilled or cooked in tomato sauce with nsima.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Lake Malawi: fishing, swimming and beaches are shared joys, and Malawians love to talk about the lake.

Netball and football: the national netball team, the Queens, is loved, and so is football.

Music: gospel, reggae and local pop fill parties, and music lovers have plenty to share.

cards.title: This season: mangoes
cards.text: From October to March, mangoes ripen across Malawi, most of all from mid-November to mid-December. Trees along roads and in villages hang heavy with fruit, and children and families eat them fresh from the tree.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "The Warm Heart of Africa," a nickname Malawians love for their friendliness and welcome. And Lake Malawi, about 580 kilometers long, filling much of the country's eastern side.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Malawian music runs from village drumming and choirs to church songs and reggae. The Malawi Mouse Boys, gospel singers who once sold roasted field mice on sticks by the roadside, sing in Chichewa with homemade guitars; their 2012 debut was the first Chichewa-language album released outside the country.

cards.title: Craft: Gule Wamkulu masks
cards.text: For the Gule Wamkulu, "the great dance," Chewa dancers wear masks of wood, feathers, cloth and straw, representing spirits, animals and characters, some funny, some frightening. UNESCO lists the dance as heritage, shared with Zambia and Mozambique.

cards.title: Creature: cichlids
cards.text: Lake Malawi is home to many hundreds of species of cichlid fish, more than any other lake on Earth, most found nowhere else. Many are as brightly colored as coral reef fish, in blues, yellows and oranges.

cards.title: Place: Lake Malawi National Park
cards.text: At the southern end of the lake, clear water, rocky islands and sandy beaches, where snorkelers swim among the cichlids and fish eagles call from the trees. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Nsima with chambo and greens. Kondowole, cassava nsima. And mandasi, sweet fried doughnuts, with tea.

458.name: Malaysia

word.meaning: To hang out and do nothing in particular, usually with friends at a mamak stall late at night, over teh tarik and roti canai. "Jom lepak!" ("Let's hang out!") is an invitation almost no one refuses.

458.ask: Ask where to find the best nasi lemak near them, and whether the sambal should be sweet or fiery. Everyone has a favorite stall and strong opinions.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: nasi lemak, roti canai and hawker stalls are loved, and Malaysians love recommending places to eat.

Badminton: Malaysians are passionate about it, and Lee Chong Wei is a hero.

Open houses: during holidays like Hari Raya and Chinese New Year, families welcome friends of all backgrounds to eat.

cards.title: This season: Deepavali, and open houses
cards.text: Malaysia celebrates the festivals of all its communities, and on November 8 this year it's Deepavali, the Hindu festival of lights, a national holiday. Families decorate their homes with oil lamps and kolam, colorful rice-flour patterns, and hold open houses where friends and neighbors of every background drop by to eat. The same open-house spirit comes back for Hari Raya, Chinese New Year and Christmas.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its mix of Malay, Chinese, Indian and Indigenous cultures, living side by side, which shows in its food, its festivals and a way of speaking that slides between languages in a single sentence. And its rainforests, among the oldest in the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Traditional Malay music includes the gamelan of the old courts, the rebana drums and dikir barat, lively group singing with call-and-response from Kelantan. For the modern bridge, the singer-songwriter Yuna, from Kedah, began posting songs online and went on to an international career in R&B, working with artists like Usher.

cards.title: Craft: songket
cards.text: A luxurious handwoven cloth of silk or cotton with gold or silver threads woven in, forming shimmering flowers and geometric patterns. Made above all in Terengganu and Kelantan, it's worn for weddings and royal occasions.

cards.title: Creature: orangutan
cards.text: The great red ape of the rainforests of Borneo, which in Malaysia means the states of Sabah and Sarawak. Its name comes from Malay, orang hutan, "person of the forest."

cards.title: Place: Kinabalu Park
cards.text: In Sabah, Mount Kinabalu rises above one of the richest botanical areas in the world, with hundreds of kinds of orchids and pitcher plants. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Nasi lemak, rice cooked in coconut milk with sambal, anchovies, peanuts, egg and cucumber, the unofficial national dish. Roti canai, flaky flatbread with curry. And teh tarik, "pulled tea," sweet milky tea poured back and forth between cups until frothy.

466.name: Mali

word.meaning: A Bambara greeting and a thank-you at once, the first line of the long, warm exchange of greetings Malians share: asking after your health, your family, your work, your household, before anything else is said. Skipping the greetings is considered rude.

466.ask: Ask what their family name means and which griot family tells its story. In Mali, a surname can link you to history going back to the Mali Empire.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: Ali Farka Touré, Toumani Diabaté, Salif Keita and Tinariwen are loved around the world, and music lovers have instant common ground.

Tea: three rounds of sweet green tea, brewed slowly and shared with friends, is a daily ritual.

Football: Malians follow the national team, the Eagles, and players in Europe closely.

cards.title: This season: the cool season on the Niger
cards.text: From November, the heat eases and the dry, cool season begins. The Niger River, swollen by the rains, spreads into its great inland delta, and pirogues, long wooden boats, carry people and goods between river towns and weekly markets, where the flood leaves rich pastures and fishing behind.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Mali Empire, which in the 1300s was one of the richest states in the world; its emperor Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca, with so much gold that it changed prices along the way, became legend. And the scholars of Timbuktu, whose manuscripts on science, law and poetry have been treasured for centuries.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Mali's music is among the richest in the world. Griots, hereditary musicians and historians, sing epics to the kora, a 21-stringed harp-lute, and Toumani Diabaté was its great modern master. Ali Farka Touré, from the north, played desert blues on guitar, and their album together, In the Heart of the Moon, won a Grammy.

links.label: Ali and Toumani, Ali Farka Touré and Toumani Diabaté
Talking Timbuktu, Ali Farka Touré with Ry Cooder

cards.title: Craft: bògòlanfini
cards.text: Mud cloth: handwoven cotton dyed with leaves and then painted, over and over, with fermented river mud, which turns the patterns dark brown and black. Women pass down the symbols, each with its own meaning, from mother to daughter.

cards.title: Creature: desert elephants of the Gourma
cards.text: Some of the last elephants of the Sahel make one of the longest migrations of any elephants on Earth, a great circle through the Gourma region following water and grazing across the seasons.

cards.title: Place: the Great Mosque of Djenné
cards.text: The largest mud-brick building in the world, with towers and wooden beams jutting from its walls, rebuilt in 1907 on a site used for centuries. Each year, the whole town joins a festival to replaster it with fresh mud. It's part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tô, a thick millet or sorghum porridge eaten with sauces. Tigadegena, a rich peanut-butter stew. Riz gras, rice cooked with meat and tomato. And strong, sweet green tea, poured three times from a small pot.

478.name: Mauritania

word.meaning: Tea: green tea with mint and lots of sugar, poured from high up to make foam, and served in three rounds. A saying goes that the first glass is bitter like life, the second sweet like love, and the third gentle like death. Making atay takes time, and that's the point.

478.ask: Ask who makes the best atay in their family, and how high they can pour it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tea: atay, three glasses of mint tea, is a daily ritual of friendship.

Poetry and music: Mauritanians love poetry, and Noura Mint Seymali's music is heard around the world.

Hospitality: guests are welcomed with tea and food, and the conversation can last all evening.

cards.title: This season: the cool season in the desert
cards.text: From November, the heat of the Sahara softens, and it's the season to visit the Adrar: golden dunes, palm oases and the old caravan towns. November 28 is Independence Day, celebrated with flags and gatherings across the country.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its poetry: Mauritania is sometimes called "the land of a million poets." Its ancient libraries of manuscripts in towns like Chinguetti. And its hospitality in the desert.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Griot musicians play the tidinit, a lute, and women play the ardin, a harp. Dimi Mint Abba, whose father composed the national anthem, became one of the great voices of the Arab and African world. Her stepdaughter, Noura Mint Seymali, brings the tradition to rock stages today.

links.label: Music and Songs of Mauritania, Dimi Mint Abba

cards.title: Craft: leather and silver
cards.text: Moorish artisans make cushions, bags and saddles of leather dyed and embroidered in bright colors, and silver jewelry and boxes engraved with fine geometric patterns.

cards.title: Creature: the fishing dolphins of the Imraguen
cards.text: Along the coast of the Banc d'Arguin, Imraguen fishermen once slapped the water to call dolphins, which herded mullet toward their nets. The Banc d'Arguin, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is also one of the most important places for migrating birds in the world.

cards.title: Place: Chinguetti
cards.text: An old caravan city on the edge of the dunes, with a stone mosque and family libraries that hold centuries-old manuscripts of science, law and poetry. It's one of the four ancient ksour on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Thieboudienne, rice cooked with fish and vegetables. Méchoui, whole roasted lamb. And zrig, sweetened camel's or goat's milk.

484.name: Mexico

word.meaning: To hold someone close with real tenderness, the kind of hug that comforts. It comes from the Nahuatl verb papachoa, and Mexicans often explain it as "to hug with the soul." That lovely phrase is a modern gloss rather than the literal Nahuatl meaning, but it's how the word feels.

484.ask: Ask what goes on their family's ofrenda for Día de Muertos, and whose favorite food or drink gets a place on it. It's a question about the people they love most.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: tacos, mole and regional dishes are loved everywhere, and Mexicans love sharing favorites.

Football: the national team, El Tri, and Liga MX are followed passionately.

Día de Muertos: altars, marigolds and family memories make a beautiful tradition to ask about.

cards.title: This season: Día de Muertos
cards.text: On November 1 and 2, families build ofrendas, altars glowing with orange cempasúchil marigolds, candles, cut-paper papel picado, photographs and the favorite foods of the people they remember, to welcome them home for a visit. UNESCO lists the celebration as heritage. In Mexico City the season starts early: this year the giant alebrijes parade is on October 17, and the grand Day of the Dead parade on October 31.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The food. In 2010, traditional Mexican cuisine became one of the first national cuisines UNESCO recognized as heritage, built on corn, beans and chili and on farming methods like the milpa, a field where corn, beans and squash grow together. Corn itself was first domesticated in Mexico, from a wild grass called teosinte, around 9,000 years ago.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Mexico's musical roots run through dozens of regional traditions. Mariachi, with its violins, trumpets and big-hearted singing, is on UNESCO's heritage list. In Veracruz, son jarocho is played on the jarana, a small, bright guitar, while dancers stamp rhythms on a wooden platform at all-night fandangos. For the modern bridge, Lila Downs sings old Oaxacan songs like "La Sandunga" and "La Llorona" with a voice that can do anything, and Natalia Lafourcade's Musas albums revisit Latin American classics with Los Macorinos, the guitar duo who once played for Chavela Vargas.

links.label: ¡Fandango! Sones Jarochos from Veracruz, Grupo Mono Blanco
Musas, Natalia Lafourcade with Los Macorinos

cards.title: Craft: alebrijes
cards.text: Brightly painted fantasy creatures: a winged donkey, a lion with a dog's head, a rooster with bull's horns. They were invented in 1936 by Pedro Linares, a Mexico City papier-mâché artist, after a fever dream in which such creatures chanted the word "alebrijes" at him. Carvers in Oaxaca later took up the idea in copal wood, and it's their painted versions that most people know today.

cards.title: Creature: monarch butterfly
cards.text: Each autumn, millions of monarchs fly as far as 4,000 kilometers from Canada and the United States to overwinter in the fir forests of Michoacán and the State of Mexico, where they hang from the branches in orange clusters until March. They arrive around Día de Muertos, and in Purépecha and Mazahua tradition they are the souls of the dead returning. The reserve is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Place: Monte Albán
cards.text: The Zapotec people flattened the top of a mountain above the Oaxaca valley and, from about 500 BCE, built a city of plazas, pyramids and a ball court there. It overlooks three valleys, and together with Oaxaca's historic center it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pan de muerto, a soft sweet bread scented with orange blossom, topped with dough shaped like bones and dusted with sugar, baked only around Día de Muertos. Mole, a sauce that can hold more than twenty ingredients, from chilies to chocolate, is the dish for a celebration.

496.name: Mongolia

word.meaning: The “wind horse”: your spirit, vitality and luck, something you can raise, like a flag in the wind.
word.sayIt: KHEE-mor (kh as in Scottish “loch”; the final vowel nearly disappears)

496.ask: Ask how their family celebrates Tsagaan Sar, and how many buuz they make. Some families fold hundreds or even thousands, and everyone has an opinion on technique.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Horses: many Mongolians grew up riding, and the Naadam horse races are a highlight of summer.

Wrestling: Mongolian wrestlers have become grand champions in Japanese sumo, a proud topic.

The countryside: summers with relatives in the countryside, in gers, are cherished.

cards.title: This season: Golden Eagle Festival
cards.text: In early October in Bayan-Ölgii, in the far west, Kazakh eagle hunters in fox-fur hats ride in to show off their golden eagles in calling and hunting contests.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The horse. Many Mongolians learn to ride about as early as they walk, and in the long-distance races at Naadam, the summer festival, the jockeys are children. Chinggis Khaan, who united the Mongol tribes in 1206, is honored everywhere, from the name of the main airport to the banknotes.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In khöömei, or throat singing, one singer produces two or more notes at once, a low drone with a whistling melody floating above it. It's often paired with the morin khuur, a two-stringed fiddle topped with a carved horse's head, and with long song, whose single syllables can stretch for breaths at a time. The band The HU brought all of it into rock and went global in 2019, and their third album, Hun, came out this summer.

cards.title: Craft: the ger
cards.text: A round felt home on a folding lattice frame that packs onto a few animals and goes up in a few hours. The door traditionally faces south, toward the sun.

cards.title: Creature: takhi
cards.text: Przewalski's horse, the only truly wild horse left on Earth. It went extinct in the wild and was brought back in the 1990s to Hustai National Park, where herds now run free.

cards.title: Place: Khongoryn Els
cards.text: The “singing dunes” of the Gobi, which hum and rumble when sand slides down their faces.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Buuz are steamed meat dumplings, made by the thousand for Tsagaan Sar, the lunar new year. Suutei tsai is milk tea with a pinch of salt, offered to any guest who ducks through the door.

498.name: Moldova

word.meaning: A pie, and so much more: flaky pastries filled with cheese, cabbage, potatoes, pumpkin or cherries, made in every Moldovan home. To be offered plăcinte is to be welcomed.

498.ask: Ask which filling is best in their family's plăcinte, and who in the family is the best at stretching the dough paper-thin.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Wine: Moldova has huge underground wine cellars, and wine lovers have lots to talk about.

Folk music and dance: the hora is danced at every wedding, and anyone who loves line dancing can join.

Food: plăcinte and mămăligă are family favorites, and grandmothers' recipes are treasured.

cards.title: This season: National Wine Day
cards.text: On October 3 and 4, 2026, Chișinău's main square fills for the 25th National Wine Day: winemakers pour their wines, and there's folk music, dancing and food. Moldova has one of the highest shares of vineyards of any country, and the celebration spreads to wineries across the country.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wine and its cellars: Cricova and Mileștii Mici have underground wine cities, with miles of tunnels, where streets are named for grapes. And its hospitality and music.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Village bands play fast dances like the hora and sârba on violin, țambal (a hammered dulcimer), accordion and pan flute. For the modern bridge, Zdob și Zdub mix Moldovan folk tunes with rock and punk, and have represented the country at Eurovision.

cards.title: Craft: woven carpets
cards.text: Moldovan women weave wool carpets with roses, trees of life and geometric designs, once part of every bride's dowry and hung on the walls of the best room in the house. UNESCO lists the craft, shared with Romania, as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: hoopoe
cards.text: A cinnamon-colored bird with black-and-white striped wings and a crest like a fan. Every Moldovan child knows it from Ion Creangă's story of stealing a hoopoe from a linden tree.

cards.title: Place: Orheiul Vechi
cards.text: A bend of the Răut River cutting through limestone cliffs, with an ancient monastery carved into the rock, where monks still live, and a village of blue-painted houses.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mămăligă, cornmeal porridge, with brânză (salty sheep's cheese) and sour cream. Zeamă, a sour chicken noodle soup. And plăcinte.

499.name: Montenegro

word.meaning: The evening stroll along the seafront or main street, to see and be seen, greet friends, have an ice cream or a coffee. In coastal towns like Kotor and Budva, the whole town seems to go out for a đir at sunset.

499.ask: Ask where to find the best Njeguši prosciutto and cheese, smoked and dried in the mountain air above Kotor, and who makes it in their family.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
The coast and mountains: summers at the beach and hikes in Durmitor are shared joys.

Water polo and basketball: both are followed passionately, and Montenegro punches above its weight.

Coffee and conversation: long hours at cafés with friends are a way of life.

cards.title: This season: the olive harvest
cards.text: From late October into December, families along the coast around Bar and Ulcinj pick their olives, spreading nets under the trees and pressing fresh oil. In Bar grows the Old Olive, a tree said to be more than 2,000 years old and still bearing fruit.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wild beauty: fjord-like bays, mountains that drop straight into the sea, and deep canyons, all in a country smaller than Connecticut. The Tara River Canyon is one of the deepest in Europe.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The gusle, a one-stringed fiddle, accompanies long epic songs of heroes and history, sung in the mountains for centuries. On the coast, men's choirs sing close harmonies influenced by the Mediterranean.

links.label: Folk Songs of Montenegro, Crna Gora Ensemble

cards.title: Craft: the Montenegrin cap
cards.text: The traditional men's cap: a flat red top framed by a black band, with gold embroidery in the corner. It's worn with folk dress at celebrations and weddings.

cards.title: Creature: pygmy cormorant
cards.text: On Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans, which Montenegro shares with Albania, small, dark pygmy cormorants nest and fish among water lilies and reeds, alongside pelicans and herons.

cards.title: Place: the Bay of Kotor
cards.text: A winding bay framed by steep mountains, with the walled medieval town of Kotor at its end and fortifications zigzagging up the cliff above. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Njeguški pršut and cheese. Kačamak, a hearty cornmeal and potato dish with cheese and kajmak. And black risotto with cuttlefish ink, on the coast.

504.name: Morocco

word.meaning: "To your health," in Darija, Moroccan Arabic. You say it to someone who's eating, who's just bought new clothes, had a haircut, or even just stepped out of the shower: a small wish that whatever is new or good in their day does them good. The reply is "allah y'atik saha," "may God give you health."
word.sayIt: b-SAH-ha (the first b runs straight into the s)

504.ask: Ask how their family makes mint tea: how much sugar, how many glasses, and who pours it from way up high to raise the foam.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: the 2022 World Cup run to the semifinals was a huge joy, and Moroccans love to talk about it.

Food: tagine and couscous, and a big couscous with family on Fridays.

Mint tea: poured from high as a ritual of welcome, and offered to every guest.

cards.title: This season: the date harvest
cards.text: Autumn is date season in the oases of the south. In the Tafilalt around Erfoud, where date palms stretch for miles, the harvest is celebrated in early October with the Erfoud Date Festival: music, dancing, a market of dates from cooperatives across the south, and the crowning of a Date Queen. The exact days follow the harvest, so they shift from year to year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: In Fez, the University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, is recognized by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the oldest higher-learning institution in the world still operating. And at the 2022 World Cup, Morocco's Atlas Lions became the first African team ever to reach the semifinals.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Gnawa music comes from the descendants of people brought from sub-Saharan Africa: deep, hypnotic trance songs driven by the guembri, a three-stringed bass lute, and the clatter of iron castanets called qraqeb. UNESCO lists it as heritage, and Maalem Mahmoud Guinia of Essaouira was one of its great masters. For the modern bridge, Hindi Zahra, who sings in Tamazight, English and French, blends Amazigh melody with folk and jazz; her 2015 album Homeland is a lovely start.

cards.title: Craft: Amazigh rugs
cards.text: In the Atlas Mountains, Amazigh (Berber) women weave rugs by hand on upright looms, each pattern of diamonds, zigzags and symbols carrying family and regional meaning. The creamy, deep-piled rugs of the Beni Ourain in the Middle Atlas have become famous around the world.

cards.title: Creature: Barbary macaque
cards.text: The only macaque in Africa, and a monkey without a tail. It lives in the cedar forests of the Middle Atlas, where families of macaques forage on the forest floor.

cards.title: Place: Aït Benhaddou
cards.text: A fortified village of earthen houses rising up a hillside on the old caravan route between the Sahara and Marrakech. Built of rammed earth and mud brick, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has starred in many films.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tagine, a slow stew cooked in a clay pot with a tall conical lid: chicken with preserved lemon and olives, or lamb with prunes and almonds. Msemen, flaky square pancakes for breakfast with honey. And mint tea, green tea steeped with fresh mint and sugar, poured into small glasses.

508.name: Mozambique

word.meaning: "Thank you," in Changana, spoken in the south around Maputo. Mozambicans speak Portuguese and many local languages, and "khanimambo" is one of the words visitors love most.

508.ask: Ask how their family makes matapa, cassava leaves pounded and cooked with peanuts and coconut, and whether they add crab or prawns.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Beaches and the sea: fishing, diving and long beaches are shared joys.

Football: Eusébio, born in Maputo, is a legend, and many Mozambicans follow Benfica.

Food: peri-peri prawns and matapa are loved, and anyone who likes spicy food has a friend.

cards.title: This season: whale sharks at Tofo
cards.text: From October to March, plankton blooms off the Inhambane coast draw whale sharks, the largest fish in the sea, to Tofo, where divers and snorkelers can sometimes swim beside dozens of them. Warm water, long beaches and the start of summer make it one of the best times of year on the coast.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its coast, almost 2,500 kilometers of beaches, coral reefs and islands along the Indian Ocean. And its music and dance, from the timbila orchestras of the Chopi to marrabenta.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Chopi people of Inhambane play timbila, wooden xylophones with gourd resonators, in great orchestras of up to 30 players, with dancers and poetry; UNESCO lists it as heritage, and Venâncio Mbande was one of its great composers and leaders. In Maputo, marrabenta, a lively guitar dance music, became the sound of the city.

links.label: Timbila ta Venâncio, Venâncio Mbande Orchestra

cards.title: Craft: capulana
cards.text: The capulana is a bright printed cloth, worn as a wrap skirt, headscarf or baby carrier, and given as a gift. Tailors turn capulanas into dresses, shirts and bags, and women often have dozens, each with its own occasion or memory.

cards.title: Creature: dugong
cards.text: Around the Bazaruto Archipelago lives one of the last healthy populations of dugongs in the western Indian Ocean: gentle sea cows that graze on seagrass meadows.

cards.title: Place: the Island of Mozambique
cards.text: A small coral island joined to the mainland by a long bridge, once a trading port and the colonial capital, with a stone town of old churches, a fort and houses on one side and a town of palm-thatched homes on the other. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Matapa with rice. Prawns grilled with piri-piri, the fiery chili sauce. And pão, soft Portuguese-style bread rolls baked in wood-fired ovens.

512.name: Oman

word.meaning: The spread offered to every guest: bitter cardamom coffee, called kahwa, poured in small cups, with dates, fruit and Omani halwa. Offering fuala is the heart of Omani hospitality, and refusing it would be unthinkable.

512.ask: Ask which wadi is their favorite for a swim, and whether they know a spot the tourists haven't found.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hospitality: coffee and dates for every guest, and conversation in the majlis.

Nature: wadis, mountains and beaches are sources of pride, and hikers and campers have lots to share.

The sea and dhows: Omanis are proud of their seafaring past, and many love fishing, boating and beach picnics on weekends.

cards.title: This season: National Day
cards.text: Oman celebrates its National Day on November 20. In 2026, the public holiday falls on November 25 and 26. Streets and buildings in Muscat are strung with lights, cars are decorated with flags, and there are fireworks and celebrations across the country. Cooler weather is arriving, too, the start of the best months for camping in the desert and hiking in the mountains.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: A long seafaring history: Omani sailors traded in wooden dhows across the Indian Ocean to East Africa, India and beyond. And a proud tradition of hospitality, peace and warmth toward visitors.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Omani music is shaped by the sea, the desert and its long ties to East Africa and India. In Dhofar, the south, men perform Al-Bar'ah, a dance with drums and curved daggers held high, which UNESCO lists as heritage; sailors' songs and Bedouin chants live on in other regions. Muscat's Royal Opera House, opened in 2011, brings in music from around the world.

cards.title: Craft: the khanjar
cards.text: The curved dagger that appears on Oman's flag, worn at the waist on formal occasions, with a sheath of worked silver and a handle of carved wood or horn. Nizwa's souk is a famous place to see the silversmiths.

cards.title: Creature: Arabian humpback whale
cards.text: A small, isolated population of humpback whales lives year-round in the Arabian Sea off Oman. Unlike other humpbacks, they don't migrate, and scientists believe they've been separated from other humpbacks for tens of thousands of years.

cards.title: Place: the Land of Frankincense
cards.text: In Dhofar, frankincense trees grow at Wadi Dawkah, near the ruins of the ancient ports and caravan oases of Khor Rori, Al-Baleed and Shisr, which traded the fragrant resin across the ancient world. Together they're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Shuwa, meat marinated in spices and slow-cooked for a day or more in an underground pit, for Eid. Mashuai, grilled kingfish with lemon rice. And Omani halwa, dark and glossy, with rosewater, saffron and cardamom, eaten with kahwa.

516.name: Namibia

word.meaning: Afrikaans for "nice," "tasty," "great," used by Namibians of every background: a lekker braai, a lekker day, "that was lekker!" Namibia has more than a dozen languages, and lekker slips happily into all of them.

516.ask: Ask where to find the best kapana, meat grilled on open fires at Windhoek's markets and dipped in spice, and which spice mix they swear by.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Braais: grilling meat with friends is a weekend ritual, like a barbecue anywhere.

Nature: the dunes, Etosha and wide open spaces are sources of pride, and travelers have lots to share.

Rugby and football: the Welwitschias, the rugby team, and football are followed passionately.

cards.title: This season: the end of the dry season
cards.text: In October and November, before the rains, water is scarce and wildlife crowds around the waterholes of Etosha National Park: elephants, giraffes, zebras, rhinos and lions coming to drink in turn, one of the best times of year to see them. When the first storms finally break, the whole country smells of rain.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its wide, wild spaces and the way communities care for them: Namibia was the first African country to write protection of the environment into its constitution, and its community conservancies helped bring back black rhinos, lions and desert-adapted elephants.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Namibian music ranges from the choirs of the north and the traditional dances of the Herero, Owambo, Nama and Damara peoples to shambo, a fast Owambo dance music with guitars, and kwaito and hip-hop in the cities. Elemotho, who grew up in the Kalahari, sings in Setswana and English with guitar and mbira.

cards.title: Craft: Herero dresses
cards.text: Herero women wear long, full dresses with many petticoats, sewn from bright fabrics, and hats folded to look like cattle horns, a style that began in the colonial era and has become a proud symbol of identity and resilience, worn at celebrations and remembrance days.

cards.title: Creature: oryx
cards.text: The gemsbok, Namibia's national animal, a desert antelope with long, straight, spear-like horns and a striking black-and-white face, able to go days without drinking.

cards.title: Place: Sossusvlei
cards.text: In the Namib, one of the oldest deserts in the world, huge red-orange dunes rise more than 300 meters above white clay pans with dead, blackened camel-thorn trees. The Namib Sand Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kapana from the market grill. Potjiekos, stew slow-cooked in a three-legged iron pot over the fire. And biltong, spiced dried meat, for the road.

524.name: Nepal

word.meaning: "Sweet," and also "delicious," in Nepali. "Mitho chha!" ("It's delicious!") is the best thing to say to whoever cooked your dal bhat, and it will probably get you a second helping.

524.ask: Ask how their family celebrates Tihar, and whether they give their dog a garland of marigolds on Kukur Tihar.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Mountains and trekking: Nepalis are proud of Everest and love to talk about treks, and hikers have instant common ground.

Dal bhat: eaten twice a day, and a fun thing to learn about.

Cricket: Nepal's national cricket team has a huge, devoted following, and matches are big events.

cards.title: This season: Tihar
cards.text: Tihar, Nepal's festival of lights, runs from November 7 to 11 this year, and each day honors someone different. Crows come first, then, on Kukur Tihar, dogs are garlanded with marigolds, given a red tika on the forehead and a feast, to thank them for their loyalty. Cows follow, and on the night of Laxmi Puja homes glow with oil lamps to welcome the goddess of wealth. On the last day, Bhai Tika, sisters bless their brothers with a seven-colored tika.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Himalaya: eight of the world's fourteen highest peaks stand in Nepal, including Everest, called Sagarmatha in Nepali. And its welcome: trekkers remember the teahouses and the families who run them as much as the views.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Nepal's folk music is played on the madal, a hand drum, the bamboo bansuri flute, and the sarangi, a small fiddle once carried from village to village by the Gandharba, a community of traveling musician-storytellers. For the modern bridge, the band Kutumba plays old Nepali folk songs on traditional instruments only, from the sarangi to the singing bowl, and made them popular with a new generation.

cards.title: Craft: lokta paper
cards.text: Handmade paper from the inner bark of the lokta shrub, which grows back after it's cut. The bark is soaked, cooked, beaten into pulp and spread on frames in the sun, making a tough, soft paper once used for government documents and religious texts, and still made in the hills today.

cards.title: Creature: red panda
cards.text: Not a bear or a giant panda, but a small, russet, ringed-tailed tree climber that lives in the bamboo forests of the eastern Himalaya, eating mostly bamboo leaves and curling its bushy tail around itself to keep warm.

cards.title: Place: the Kathmandu Valley
cards.text: Three old royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, packed with pagoda-roofed temples, carved wooden windows and brick squares built by the Newar people, along with the great white stupas of Boudhanath and Swayambhunath. The valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Dal bhat, lentil soup with rice, vegetable curry and pickle, eaten twice a day and refilled until you say stop. Momo, steamed dumplings with a spicy tomato dip. And at Tihar, sel roti, a crisp, sweet ring of rice-flour bread fried in oil.

528.name: Netherlands

word.meaning: Cozy, convivial, warm, fun: a candlelit café, a good evening with friends, a birthday party in a crowded living room. Gezellig describes the feeling of being together comfortably, and it's one of the highest compliments in Dutch.
word.sayIt: khuh-ZEL-lukh (the g is a soft throaty sound, like clearing your throat gently)

528.ask: Ask how their family celebrates Sinterklaas: what poems they wrote each other, and what surprise gifts, called surprises, they made for their family.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cycling: biking everywhere is a shared joy, and cyclists will feel at home.

Football and skating: the national team and speed skating are followed passionately.

King's Day: the country turns orange on April 27, with street markets and parties.

cards.title: This season: Sinterklaas
cards.text: In mid-November, Sinterklaas, the Dutch Saint Nicholas, arrives by steamboat from Spain; this year the national arrival is in Grave on November 14, with more across the country that weekend. Children leave a shoe by the fireplace for small gifts and pepernoten, little spiced cookies, and on December 5, pakjesavond, families exchange presents with funny rhyming poems.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Living with water: about a quarter of the country lies below sea level, protected by dikes, dunes, pumps and storm barriers that engineers come from around the world to study. And cycling: the Netherlands has more bicycles than people.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Netherlands' Golden Age produced Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck, Amsterdam's great organist around 1600, whose music shaped German organ music all the way to Bach. And on city streets, the draaiorgel, a big, colorful street organ playing punched music books, still rolls out on shopping days. For the modern bridge, Dutch DJs and producers have been among the biggest names in electronic dance music for decades.

cards.title: Craft: Delftware
cards.text: Blue-and-white pottery made in Delft since the 1600s, when Dutch potters imitated the Chinese porcelain arriving on trading ships. Tiles, plates and vases are hand-painted with windmills, flowers, ships and landscapes, and one factory from the 17th century still works today.

cards.title: Creature: Eurasian spoonbill
cards.text: An elegant white wading bird with a long, flat, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps side to side through shallow water to catch food. The Netherlands is one of its most important breeding grounds in Europe.

cards.title: Place: Kinderdijk
cards.text: Nineteen windmills built in the 1700s stand along the canals of Kinderdijk, near Rotterdam, where they once pumped water from the low polders to keep the land dry. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Stroopwafels, thin waffles sandwiched with caramel syrup, softened over a hot cup of coffee. Poffertjes, tiny puffy pancakes with butter and powdered sugar. Raw herring with onions from a street stand. And at Sinterklaas, pepernoten and chocolate letters, one for each person's initial.

540.name: New Caledonia

word.meaning: "Thank you" in Drehu, the Kanak language of Lifou in the Loyalty Islands, and a word many New Caledonians know. More than 25 Kanak languages are spoken across the islands.

540.ask: Ask how their family makes bougna, and who gets to open the bundle when it comes out of the earth oven.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
The lagoon: fishing, diving and beaches are shared joys, and divers have lots to talk about.

Football: Christian Karembeu, a World Cup winner with France, is from Lifou.

Food: bougna and seafood are family favorites.

cards.title: This season: the flame trees
cards.text: In November and December, the flamboyants, flame trees, burst into bright red bloom along the roads and in the villages, a sign that summer and the end of the year are coming.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its lagoon, one of the largest in the world, surrounded by a coral reef and listed by UNESCO. And Kanak culture, with its customs of welcome and exchange, carvings, and languages.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Kaneka, born in the 1980s, blends Kanak rhythms and chants with reggae and pop, sung in Kanak languages and French, and is the sound of the islands' festivals and radio.

cards.title: Craft: the flèche faîtière
cards.text: The carved wooden spire that crowns the roof of a Kanak chief's great hut, with a face representing the ancestors. It's a symbol of the clan and appears on the New Caledonian flag.

cards.title: Creature: kagu
cards.text: A pale gray, almost flightless bird found only in New Caledonia, with a shaggy crest it raises when excited and a call like a dog's bark.

cards.title: Place: the lagoons
cards.text: Around the main island and the Loyalty Islands, turquoise lagoons and coral reefs full of fish, turtles, dugongs and rays. The lagoons of New Caledonia are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Bougna: yam, taro, sweet potato, banana and chicken or seafood with coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked on hot stones. And fresh seafood from the lagoon.

548.name: Vanuatu

word.meaning: In Bislama, the shared language, "kastom" means traditional ways of life: the knowledge, dances, ceremonies, land, food and rules handed down from the ancestors. Kastom is central to how ni-Vanuatu see themselves.

548.ask: Ask which island their family comes from, and which language is spoken there. Vanuatu has more than 100 languages.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Kava: sharing kava at the nakamal in the evening is a social ritual.

The sea: fishing, snorkeling and diving are part of life.

Island life: fishing, snorkeling and village feasts are part of everyday life, and people love to talk about their home island.

cards.title: This season: nangai time
cards.text: From October to January, the nangai trees drop their nuts, ripening most in November. Families crack the hard shells to get the rich, buttery kernels, eaten fresh, roasted, or pounded into puddings, and sold in little bundles at the markets.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its languages, more than 100 in a country of about 300,000 people, one of the highest numbers per person in the world. And its living kastom, from sand drawing to dance.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: On the islands of Gaua and Merelava, women stand waist-deep in the sea and slap, scoop and swirl the water into rhythms, a tradition called water music; the Leweton group from Espiritu Santo has carried it around the world. In towns, string bands with ukuleles, guitars and a tea-chest bass play at every celebration. Torba Province, home to Gaua and Merelava, has its own recordings of this music.

cards.title: Craft: sand drawing
cards.text: Artists draw continuous lines in sand, volcanic ash or clay with one finger, without lifting it, making intricate patterns that carry stories, songs, messages and knowledge. UNESCO lists Vanuatu sand drawings as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: coconut crab
cards.text: The largest crab that lives on land, with a leg span that can reach a meter. It climbs trees and cracks coconuts with its huge claws.

cards.title: Place: Mount Yasur
cards.text: An active volcano on the island of Tanna, one of the most accessible in the world. At dusk, visitors can stand on the crater rim and watch it throw glowing lava into the air with deep booms.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Lap lap, the national dish: grated yam, taro or banana mixed with coconut cream, wrapped in leaves and baked in an earth oven. Tuluk, a smaller wrapped lap lap with meat inside. And nangai nuts in season.

554.name: New Zealand

word.meaning: In Māori, "a place to stand": tūranga, standing place, and waewae, feet. It's the place where you belong and draw your strength, through your family and ancestors, often a mountain, a river or a marae you can name as your own.

554.ask: Ask where they go to feel most at home: a beach, a mountain, a river, a family marae. Many New Zealanders can name theirs without hesitating, and there's usually a story behind it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rugby: the All Blacks and the haka are a huge source of pride, and rugby is a sure start.

The outdoors: tramping, beaches and camping are shared joys, and hikers will find a friend.

The Lord of the Rings: filmed in New Zealand, a fun topic with fans.

cards.title: This season: kōwhai and tūī
cards.text: It's spring, and the kōwhai trees are covered in hanging golden flowers, the closest thing New Zealand has to a national flower. Tūī, glossy dark birds with a white tuft at the throat, go wild for the nectar, flying long distances to feed and filling the trees with their bell-and-clicks song.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: On September 19, 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world where women won the right to vote in national elections, after a campaign led by Kate Sheppard, whose face is on the ten-dollar note. And te reo Māori, the Māori language, is an official language, heard more and more in daily life.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Kapa haka is Māori performing art: waiata (song), haka, and poi, balls on cords swung in rhythm, performed by groups who compete at the national festival, Te Matatini. For the bridge, Hinewehi Mohi's group Oceania set Māori song over 1990s electronic music in 1999, and in 2019 Waiata / Anthems had New Zealand's best-loved musicians re-record their hits in te reo Māori; it went straight to number one.

cards.title: Craft: raranga
cards.text: Māori weaving with harakeke, New Zealand flax. Weavers split the long, strong leaves into strips to plait kete (bags), baskets and mats, and scrape out muka, a soft, silky inner fiber, to weave into fine cloaks.

cards.title: Creature: kākāpō
cards.text: A big, moss-green, flightless parrot that's active at night, the heaviest parrot in the world. Down to about 51 birds in the 1990s, it's been nursed back island by island, and a record breeding season this year brought the population to 325.

cards.title: Place: Tongariro
cards.text: Three volcanic peaks in the center of the North Island, sacred to the Ngāti Tūwharetoa people, whose chief gave them to the nation in 1887 to protect them. It was New Zealand's first national park, and UNESCO lists it for both its natural and its cultural value. The Tongariro Alpine Crossing walks past steaming vents and brilliant blue-green Emerald Lakes.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: A hāngī: meat, kūmara (sweet potato) and vegetables cooked for hours in an earth oven over hot stones, for a gathering. And pavlova, a meringue with a crisp shell and a soft middle, heaped with cream and kiwifruit, which New Zealand and Australia both cheerfully claim as their own.

558.name: Nicaragua

word.meaning: "Cool! Awesome!" Nicaraguan slang for anything great: a tuani song, a tuani day, "¡qué tuani!"

558.ask: Ask how their family makes nacatamales, big corn-dough parcels of pork, rice and potatoes wrapped in banana leaves, and on which day of the week they're eaten.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Baseball: Nicaraguans love baseball, and Dennis Martínez, who pitched a perfect game in the major leagues, is a hero.

Food: gallo pinto and nacatamales are family favorites.

Poetry: Rubén Darío is celebrated, and Nicaraguans love poetry, with poetry festivals in Granada.

cards.title: This season: La Gritería
cards.text: On the night of December 7, Nicaraguans go from house to house to altars built for the Virgin Mary, shouting "¿Quién causa tanta alegría?" (Who causes so much joy?) and hearing back "¡La concepción de María!" Singers are rewarded with sweets, fruit, sugarcane and small gifts, and fireworks light up the night.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its lakes and volcanoes, including Lake Nicaragua, the largest lake in Central America. And its poets, above all Rubén Darío, the father of modernismo in Spanish poetry.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: El Güegüense, a satirical dance-drama with masks, music and a clever hero who outwits colonial officials, is performed in Diriamba every January; UNESCO lists it as heritage. The marimba is at the heart of folk music, and Carlos Mejía Godoy's songs celebrate Nicaraguan village life.

links.label: El son nuestro de cada día, Carlos Mejía Godoy

cards.title: Craft: Masaya hammocks
cards.text: In Masaya, weavers make colorful cotton hammocks on tall wooden frames, with fringes and patterns, sold in the city's crafts market alongside pottery, wood carvings and leather.

cards.title: Creature: bull shark
cards.text: Lake Nicaragua has sharks: bull sharks swim up the San Juan River from the Caribbean, jumping the rapids like salmon, and live in the fresh water of the lake.

cards.title: Place: Ometepe
cards.text: An island in Lake Nicaragua made of two volcanoes joined by a narrow neck of land, with farms, forests, beaches, petroglyphs and howler monkeys.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Gallo pinto, rice and red beans fried together. Nacatamales, for weekend mornings. Vigorón, yuca and pork crackling with cabbage salad on a banana leaf. And quesillo, a tortilla wrapped around soft cheese, pickled onions and cream.

562.name: Niger

word.meaning: "Thank you" and "hello" in Zarma, spoken along the Niger River around Niamey. Greetings in Niger are long and gracious: about your health, your family, your work and your day.

562.ask: Ask how they like their kilishi, thin sheets of beef dried in the sun with a spicy peanut coating, and where to find the best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tea: long rounds of sweet green tea with friends are an everyday ritual.

Music: Tuareg guitar music, like Bombino's, is heard around the world, and music lovers have instant common ground.

Wrestling: traditional wrestling is the national sport, and championships draw huge crowds.

cards.title: This season: the salt caravans
cards.text: When the cool season comes, Tuareg and Toubou traders have long led camel caravans, the azalai, across the Ténéré desert to the oasis of Bilma to trade for salt and dates. The journey takes weeks, guided by stars and dunes, and a few caravans still make it.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its desert music and its hospitality. The Aïr Mountains and the Ténéré, among the most beautiful deserts on Earth. And its giraffes: the last herd of West African giraffes, saved from near extinction.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Tuareg guitar music, called assouf, carries the longing of desert life. Bombino, from Agadez, plays it on electric guitar with hypnotic rhythms, and his album "Agadez" went to the top of the iTunes world music chart.

cards.title: Craft: the Agadez cross
cards.text: Tuareg silversmiths make silver pendants called crosses, like the famous cross of Agadez, each town with its own shape. Fathers traditionally give them to their sons, and they're worn across the Sahara.

cards.title: Creature: West African giraffe
cards.text: Pale, with light, blotchy spots, this giraffe lives only in Niger now, around Kouré, near Niamey, where villagers share their fields with it. From about 50 animals in the 1990s, the herd has grown to several hundred.

cards.title: Place: Agadez
cards.text: An old desert trading city of mud-brick houses, with a great mud-brick minaret, 27 meters high, bristling with wooden beams. The historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kilishi. Dambou, steamed couscous of millet or rice with moringa leaves and peanuts. And fura, a millet drink with milk.

566.name: Nigeria

word.meaning: "Trouble" or "fuss," in Nigerian Pidgin, the language that lets people from Nigeria's hundreds of language groups talk to each other. "No wahala" means "no problem," and you'll hear it everywhere, usually with a smile.

566.ask: Ask about the last owambe they went to, the big, joyful Nigerian parties, and whether their family wore aso ebi, matching outfits sewn from the same fabric so everyone can see who came together.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: Afrobeats and stars like Burna Boy, Wizkid and Tems are known worldwide.

Nollywood: Nigerian films are hugely popular, and a fun topic.

Jollof rice and football: the friendly jollof rivalry with Ghana, and the Super Eagles.

cards.title: This season: Calabar Carnival
cards.text: All through December, the city of Calabar in Cross River State celebrates what it calls Africa's biggest street party. The peak comes from December 26 to 30, with the Parade of the Bands on December 28: costumed dance troupes, floats and drummers who've spent months preparing, competing along the city streets.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its storytellers. Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, published in 1958, is one of the most widely read African novels, and Wole Soyinka became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. Today Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, is one of the most prolific in the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Nigeria's music runs from Yoruba jùjú, with talking drums and shimmering guitars, which King Sunny Adé took around the world in the 1980s, to Afrobeat, which Fela Kuti created in 1970s Lagos out of highlife, jazz, funk and Yoruba rhythm, with long grooves and pointed lyrics. For the modern bridge, Afrobeats, a different, newer sound, has made Nigerian pop global; Burna Boy's Twice as Tall won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album in 2021.

cards.title: Craft: adire
cards.text: Indigo cloth made by Yoruba women, first in Abeokuta in the 19th century. Patterns are made by keeping the dye out: tying the cloth with raffia (oniko), painting designs on it with cassava-starch paste (eleko), or stitching it tight (alabere) before it goes into the indigo. Abeokuta's Itoku market is still full of it.

cards.title: Creature: Cross River gorilla
cards.text: The rarest great ape in the world, with only about 250 to 300 left, living in the mountain forests along Nigeria's border with Cameroon. Nigeria's roughly 100 live mainly in the Afi and Mbe mountains and Cross River National Park.

cards.title: Place: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
cards.text: One of the last patches of primary forest in southern Nigeria, on the banks of the Osun River, sacred to the Yoruba river goddess Osun, and filled with shrines and sculptures. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and every August the Osun-Osogbo Festival draws thousands to the grove.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Jollof rice, smoky from the bottom of the pot, the subject of a famous friendly rivalry with Ghana. Suya, skewers of beef rubbed with a spicy groundnut mix and grilled over an open fire at night. And puff-puff, soft, sweet fried dough balls.

578.name: Norway

word.meaning: "Open-air life": the Norwegian love of simply being outdoors, in any weather, hiking, skiing, picking berries or sitting by a fire in the woods. Norwegians like to say there's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothes.

578.ask: Ask where their family goes on a hytte trip, to the simple cabin in the mountains or by the sea that many Norwegian families share, and what they do there.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
