The outdoors: hiking, cross-country skiing and cabin weekends are shared joys, and outdoor lovers have a friend.

Winter sports: Norway leads the all-time Winter Olympics medal table, a proud topic.

Football: Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard are national stars.

cards.title: This season: the northern lights and the polar night
cards.text: From autumn to spring, the northern lights dance over northern Norway. In Tromsø, far above the Arctic Circle, the sun doesn't rise at all from late November until mid-January; the "polar night" is not pitch dark but a long, blue twilight, and the aurora can appear on clear evenings. Every December 10, the Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its outdoors, and allemannsretten, the "right to roam," an old custom now in law that lets anyone walk, ski, camp or pick berries almost anywhere in the countryside. And the Nobel Peace Prize, which Alfred Nobel chose to have awarded in Norway.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Norway's folk music is played on the Hardanger fiddle, which has extra strings under the fingerboard that ring along with the melody, giving it a shimmering, haunting sound. The Sámi, the Indigenous people of the far north, have joik, songs that don't describe a person or place but evoke them. For the modern bridge, the singer Aurora, from near Bergen, brings that sense of wild nature into pop; her debut album came out in 2016.

links.label: All My Demons Greeting Me as a Friend, Aurora

cards.title: Craft: rosemaling
cards.text: "Rose painting," a style of flowing scrolls, flowers and leaves painted on wooden bowls, chests and walls, which spread through rural Norway in the 1700s and 1800s. Each valley developed its own style, and it's still painted today.

cards.title: Creature: reindeer
cards.text: Wild reindeer roam the mountain plateaus of southern Norway, and in the north, Sámi families have herded reindeer for centuries, moving with them between winter and summer pastures.

cards.title: Place: the West Norwegian fjords
cards.text: Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord cut deep between sheer mountain walls, with waterfalls pouring down from farms perched on ledges high above the water. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Brunost, sweet brown cheese sliced thin with a cheese slicer, a Norwegian invention. Lefse, soft potato flatbread. At Christmas, pinnekjøtt, salted and dried lamb ribs steamed over birch sticks, and krumkake, thin, crisp rolled waffle cookies.

586.name: Pakistan

word.meaning: "Friend," in Urdu, Punjabi and beyond, and also a word you sprinkle through conversation to mean "come on," "oh man," or "my dear": "Yaar, have some more tea." It carries warmth into almost any sentence.

586.ask: Ask what their family's favorite biryani is, Sindhi, Karachi-style or another, and who makes the best one at weddings.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Cricket: Pakistan's biggest passion, and the 1992 World Cup win is a happy memory.

Food: biryani, nihari and chai are loved, and Pakistanis love sharing them.

Music: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Coke Studio Pakistan are loved worldwide.

cards.title: This season: autumn in Hunza
cards.text: In the far north, in the Hunza Valley beneath the snowy peaks of the Karakoram, October and November turn the poplars and apricot trees gold, orange and red against the mountains. Villagers dry apricots and walnuts on rooftops for the winter, and the Karakoram Highway winds through some of the most dramatic scenery on Earth.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its mountains: Pakistan has five of the world's fourteen peaks over 8,000 meters, including K2, the second-highest mountain on Earth. And its hospitality, famous among travelers who find themselves invited in for tea, and then for dinner.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Qawwali, the devotional music of Sufi shrines, builds from a quiet start to an ecstatic climax, with harmonium, tabla and hand-clapping. Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, with his extraordinary voice, carried it to the whole world. For the modern bridge, the TV series Coke Studio Pakistan has mixed folk, Sufi and pop for years; "Pasoori," sung by Ali Sethi and Shae Gill in 2022, became its most-watched song ever.

links.label: Pasoori, Ali Sethi and Shae Gill

cards.title: Craft: truck art
cards.text: Pakistan's trucks and buses are rolling works of art, covered in bright painted flowers, peacocks, landscapes, poetry and dangling chains and bells. Owners spend a fortune decorating them, and the style has spread to everything from kettles to fashion.

cards.title: Creature: markhor
cards.text: Pakistan's national animal, a wild goat with long, spiraling, corkscrew horns, which lives in the high mountains of the north. Its numbers have recovered thanks to community conservation programs.

cards.title: Place: the Hunza Valley
cards.text: A green valley of terraced fields and orchards in the Karakoram, overlooked by peaks like Rakaposhi and old forts like Baltit, with glaciers coming almost down to the road.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Biryani, spiced rice layered with meat. Nihari, slow-cooked beef stew eaten for breakfast in Lahore and Karachi, with fresh naan. And doodh patti chai, strong tea boiled in milk with plenty of sugar.

591.name: Panama

word.meaning: "What's up?" in Panamanian slang: "¿qué pasó?" flipped backward. "¡Qué xopá!" is how friends greet each other on the street.

591.ask: Ask whether anyone in their family has a pollera, the national dress, embroidered by hand over months, and when it's worn.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Baseball: Mariano Rivera is a national hero, and baseball fans have instant common ground.

Football: the 2018 World Cup was Panama's first, a happy memory.

The canal: Panamanians love talking about it, and it's a fascinating topic.

cards.title: This season: the fiestas patrias
cards.text: November is Panama's month of national holidays: separation from Colombia on November 3, Flag Day on November 4, Colón Day on November 5, the Shout of Independence at Villa de Los Santos on November 10, and independence from Spain on November 28. School marching bands practice all year for the parades, filling the streets with drums, brass and dancers.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Panama Canal, which joins the Atlantic and Pacific, and has been run by Panama since 1999. And its rich nature: a narrow country between two oceans, with rainforests, islands and birds of both continents.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the countryside, tamborito, with drums, clapping and call-and-response singing, is the traditional dance, and décimas are sung to the mejorana, a small guitar. From Panama City, Rubén Blades wrote salsa songs full of stories and city life; "Siembra," his 1978 album with Willie Colón, became one of salsa's best-selling records.

links.label: Siembra, Willie Colón and Rubén Blades

cards.title: Craft: the mola
cards.text: Guna women make molas, panels of layered cloth cut and stitched to reveal bright designs of animals, plants and patterns, worn on the front and back of their blouses. Each one takes weeks of fine needlework.

cards.title: Creature: Panamanian golden frog
cards.text: A bright golden-yellow frog, a symbol of good luck in Panama, that waves its arms to signal other frogs over the noise of mountain streams. Disease has nearly wiped it out in the wild, and conservation programs keep it alive while scientists work to return it.

cards.title: Place: Guna Yala
cards.text: Along the Caribbean coast, the Guna people govern their own region, home to more than 300 small islands, many with palm trees and white sand, where Guna families live, fish and welcome visitors.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Sancocho de gallina, chicken soup with yam and culantro, the national dish. Patacones, twice-fried green plantains. And raspao, shaved ice with syrup and condensed milk, from street carts.

598.name: Papua New Guinea

word.meaning: From Tok Pisin, "one talk": someone who speaks your language, and so your kin, clan or community, the people you share with and look out for. In a country of more than 800 languages, your wantoks are your safety net.

598.ask: Ask which bilum they carry, who made it, and what its pattern means. Many people can tell where a bilum comes from just by looking at it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rugby league: PNG's national passion, and the national team, the Kumuls, is followed closely.

Sing-sings: festivals like the Goroka Show bring groups together in amazing costumes and dance.

Betel nut and conversation: chewing buai and chatting is a social ritual.

cards.title: This season: the Kenu and Kundu Festival
cards.text: From November 6 to 8 this year, the town of Alotau in Milne Bay hosts the National Kenu and Kundu Festival: war canoes from the islands race across the bay, kundu drums (hourglass-shaped hand drums) keep the beat, and groups perform sing-sings, dances in feathers, shells and paint.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its astonishing diversity: more than 800 languages, around 12 percent of all the languages spoken in the world, in one country. And its sing-sings, where hundreds of groups gather in dazzling costumes.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The kundu drum and the garamut, a great slit-log drum, drive the songs and dances of sing-sings across the country. For the modern bridge, George Telek, from the Tolai people of East New Britain, blends traditional melodies and languages with string-band guitar and pop, and recorded for Peter Gabriel's Real World Records.

cards.title: Craft: bilum
cards.text: String bags made by looping plant fiber or, now, colorful yarn, by hand, in patterns that identify their maker's region. Women carry everything in them, from produce to babies, and each one can take weeks to make.

cards.title: Creature: birds-of-paradise
cards.text: Papua New Guinea's forests are home to dozens of species of birds-of-paradise, whose males grow extravagant plumes and perform elaborate dances to win a mate. The Raggiana bird-of-paradise is on the national flag.

cards.title: Place: the Kuk Early Agricultural Site
cards.text: In the highlands, archaeologists found drainage ditches and mounds showing that people farmed there, growing bananas and taro, as long as 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, one of the few places on Earth where farming began independently. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mumu, pork, chicken, sweet potato and greens cooked for hours on hot stones in an earth oven. Kaukau, sweet potato, the highlands' staple. And along the rivers and coast, sago, starch from the sago palm.

600.name: Paraguay

word.meaning: A Guaraní word for sharing with open hands: giving to one another without keeping count, the way neighbors share food, work and help. Most Paraguayans speak Guaraní, and it's an official language alongside Spanish.

600.ask: Ask what herbs they put in their tereré, the ice-cold yerba mate drink, and whether they ever go anywhere without their thermos.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tereré: sharing cold yerba mate with friends, passed around one cup.

Football: Paraguayans follow Olimpia, Cerro Porteño and the national team passionately.

Harp music: the Paraguayan harp is loved, and music lovers have an opening.

cards.title: This season: tereré weather
cards.text: As spring turns to summer, from October on, the heat builds, and tereré is everywhere: friends pass one cup of cold yerba mate with crushed medicinal herbs around a circle, in parks, at work and on the sidewalk. UNESCO lists the practice as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Guaraní, an Indigenous language spoken by most of the country, rare in the Americas. The Paraguayan harp and its music. And sopa paraguaya, the "soup" that's actually a cornbread.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The Paraguayan harp, lighter than a concert harp, is played fast and bright, with galloping polkas and gentle guaranias, a slow, romantic style created by José Asunción Flores. Luis Bordón helped bring the harp to audiences around the world.

cards.title: Craft: ñandutí
cards.text: "Spider web" lace, made in Itauguá: fine threads are stitched over a frame into circles like spider webs, in white or many colors, then joined into tablecloths, collars and wall hangings.

cards.title: Creature: Chacoan peccary
cards.text: The tagua, a pig-like animal of the dry Chaco forest, was known to scientists only from fossils until 1975, when it was found alive and well in Paraguay.

cards.title: Place: the Jesuit missions of Trinidad and Jesús
cards.text: In the south, the red-stone ruins of 17th- and 18th-century missions where Guaraní and Jesuits lived, with carved angels and musicians on the church walls. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Sopa paraguaya. Chipa, cheesy cassava-flour bread rings. Mbejú, a cassava and cheese pancake. And tereré.

604.name: Peru

word.meaning: The little extra a market vendor tosses into your bag for free. From Quechua.

604.ask: Ask where to find the best ceviche, and whether it's okay to eat it at dinner. Many Peruvians hold that ceviche is lunch food, and the debate is half the fun.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: ceviche, lomo saltado and Peruvian cuisine are loved worldwide, and Peruvians love talking about food.

Machu Picchu: Peruvians love hearing you've visited or want to.

Football: the 2018 World Cup return, after 36 years, is a happy memory.

cards.title: This season: the purple month
cards.text: October is mes morado in Lima: processions for the Señor de los Milagros, a sea of purple robes, and turrón de Doña Pepa, an anise-scented layered sweet. The month ends on October 31 with the Día de la Canción Criolla, a night for coastal criollo music.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The food. Peruvians consider their cuisine one of the world's great ones, and chefs from Lima now top international rankings. There's also the potato: it was first domesticated in the Andes, and Peru grows thousands of native varieties.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the Andes, huayno is played on the charango, a small bright-voiced lute, and the quena flute. On the coast, Afro-Peruvian music grew up around the cajón, a box drum born in Peru. Then there's chicha, an Amazonian cumbia with psychedelic surf guitar that's pure joy. Susana Baca, the great voice of Afro-Peruvian song, closes her 1997 album with a song for the Señor de los Milagros, which suits October perfectly.

cards.title: Craft: Taquile knitting
cards.text: On Taquile Island in Lake Titicaca, the men knit and the women weave, and UNESCO recognizes the island's textile art. A man's knitted cap signals whether he's single or married.

cards.title: Creature: marvelous spatuletail
cards.text: A tiny hummingbird whose male grows two long tail wires ending in round purple rackets, which he waves like signal flags in courtship. It lives only in one valley in northern Peru.

cards.title: Place: the Uros islands
cards.text: Islands floating on Lake Titicaca, built entirely from layers of totora reed that families keep adding as the bottom layers soften.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ceviche, fish cured in lime with chili and red onion, whose leftover juice, leche de tigre, is sipped like a tonic. Picarones are ring doughnuts made from sweet potato and squash, drizzled with molasses-like chancaca syrup.

608.name: Philippines

word.meaning: The giddy rush of butterflies you feel when something romantic happens, to you or even on screen: a crush smiling at you, a love story finally working out. It's Tagalog, and it's so useful that the Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2016.

608.ask: Ask what their family serves at Noche Buena, the big Christmas Eve feast after midnight Mass, and whether they went to all nine dawn Masses of Simbang Gabi.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Karaoke: videoke at parties is a national pastime, and anyone willing to sing is welcome.

Basketball: Filipinos are passionate about the NBA and their own leagues.

Food: adobo, lechon and halo-halo are loved, and Filipinos love to feed their guests.

cards.title: This season: Christmas has already begun
cards.text: Filipinos start celebrating Christmas in September, with the first of the "-ber" months, making it one of the longest Christmas seasons in the world. Parol, star-shaped lanterns, go up in windows everywhere. In San Fernando, Pampanga, the "Christmas Capital of the Philippines," the giant lanterns light up all through December: enormous rotating stars with thousands of bulbs, dancing to music.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Bayanihan, the spirit of neighbors helping each other, pictured in the old image of a whole village lifting a family's bamboo house on their shoulders to carry it to a new place. And warmth: Filipinos are known for welcoming anyone as family.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the southern Philippines, the kulintang, a row of small bronze gongs laid on a wooden frame, is played with drums in intricate, rolling patterns; Aga Mayo Butocan is one of its great Maguindanao players. In Manila, OPM, "Original Pilipino Music," has its own long tradition of love songs and ballads. For the modern bridge, the nine-piece folk-pop band Ben&Ben, whose 2019 debut album Limasawa Street went quadruple platinum at home, sings about life and love in Filipino and English.

cards.title: Craft: piña cloth
cards.text: In Aklan, weavers make piña, a fine, sheer, gleaming cloth from fibers scraped by hand from the leaves of a native pineapple, woven on handlooms. It's used for the barong Tagalog, the embroidered formal shirt, and UNESCO added the craft to its heritage list in 2023.

cards.title: Creature: Philippine tarsier
cards.text: A tiny primate that fits in your palm, with enormous eyes, each about as big as its brain, and a head that can turn almost all the way around. It hunts insects at night in the forests of Bohol and other southern islands.

cards.title: Place: the rice terraces of the Cordilleras
cards.text: In the mountains of northern Luzon, the Ifugao people carved rice terraces into the steep slopes some 2,000 years ago, watered by a system fed from the forests above. They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site and still farmed today.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Adobo, chicken or pork braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic and bay leaves, which every family makes its own way. Lechon, whole roast pig with crackling skin, for fiestas. At Christmas, bibingka and purple puto bumbong, rice cakes sold outside churches after dawn Mass. And halo-halo, shaved ice layered with beans, fruit, jelly, leche flan and ube ice cream.

616.name: Poland

word.meaning: Hospitality, and a serious matter in Poland, summed up in the old saying "Gość w dom, Bóg w dom": "A guest in the house is God in the house." At Christmas Eve dinner, many families set an extra place at the table for an unexpected visitor.

616.ask: Ask how many dishes their family serves at Wigilia, the Christmas Eve supper, which traditionally has twelve meatless dishes, and whether they share the opłatek, a thin wafer broken together while exchanging good wishes.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: pierogi and Sunday family dinners are shared joys.

Sport: Robert Lewandowski is a hero, and Poland is a volleyball powerhouse.

Mushroom picking: a favorite autumn pastime.

cards.title: This season: the Kraków szopki
cards.text: On the first Thursday of December, the makers of szopki, Kraków's glittering nativity scenes, carry them into the Main Market Square for the city's annual competition. They're not simple stables but towering, sparkling castles modeled on Kraków's own churches and towers, made of foil, colored paper and tiny lights, with the Holy Family inside. The best go on display until early spring, and UNESCO lists the tradition as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its resilience and its culture, from Copernicus, who showed the Earth moves around the Sun, to Marie Skłodowska-Curie, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. And Chopin, whose music is full of Polish dances.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Chopin turned the mazurka and polonaise, folk dances of the Polish countryside, into some of the most loved piano music ever written. The village music of Mazovia, the region around Warsaw, with fiddles, frame drums and powerful open-throated singing, is where those dances come from. For the modern bridge, Warsaw Village Band (Kapela ze Wsi Warszawa) plays that old village music with the drive of a rock band.

cards.title: Craft: wycinanki
cards.text: Paper cutting, done with sheep shears in the old days: symmetrical designs of roosters, flowers, trees of life and stars, cut from folded colored paper and layered into bright patterns. Each region has its own style, from the round, many-layered cutouts of Łowicz to the single-color designs of Kurpie.

cards.title: Creature: European bison
cards.text: The heaviest land animal in Europe, hunted to extinction in the wild by 1919 and brought back from a few animals in zoos. Today hundreds roam free in Białowieża Forest again.

cards.title: Place: Białowieża Forest
cards.text: One of the last and largest remnants of the primeval forest that once covered Europe, on the border with Belarus, with oaks, limes and ashes hundreds of years old. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pierogi, dumplings filled with potato and cheese, cabbage and mushrooms, or fruit. Barszcz, a clear red beet soup, often with tiny mushroom dumplings on Christmas Eve. And on November 11 in Poznań, St. Martin's croissants, big crescent pastries filled with white poppy seed.

620.name: Portugal

word.meaning: The fine art of improvising your way out of a jam, with whatever happens to be at hand.

620.ask: Ask where the best pastel de nata is. Everyone has a pastelaria they'll defend. If they're from Madeira, ask which levada walk they'd send you on.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Cristiano Ronaldo and the Benfica-Porto-Sporting rivalry, a sure start.

Food: pastéis de nata, grilled sardines and bacalhau are loved, and many people abroad love them too.

Fado: the music of longing, heard in Lisbon and Coimbra, is a beautiful thing to share.

cards.title: Coming up: São Martinho and New Year's Eve
cards.text: November 11 brings the magusto: roasted chestnuts and the first taste of new wine around a fire. Then on New Year's Eve, Madeira's capital Funchal rings its whole bay in fireworks.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The sea. Portuguese navigators charted much of the world's coastline in the 1400s and 1500s, and Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498; people today discuss that era's colonial legacy with more nuance. Portuguese is now spoken by more than 250 million people on four continents. And football: Portugal won the European Championship in 2016.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Fado is Lisbon's song of longing, sung over the Portuguese guitar, a pear-shaped twelve-string instrument; Amália Rodrigues is its great voice and Mariza a modern one. For pure delight, Madeira's braguinha, a little four-string guitar, sailed to Hawaii with Madeiran immigrants in 1879 and became the ukulele.

cards.title: Craft: Madeira embroidery
cards.text: Fine hand embroidery on linen, worked by women in their homes across the island for more than 150 years. Look for it alongside Lisbon's azulejos, the glazed painted tiles covering whole façades.

cards.title: Creature: Zino's petrel
cards.text: One of Europe's rarest seabirds, called the freira, nesting only in burrows high on Madeira's central peaks and returning to them at night with eerie calls.

cards.title: Place: Madeira's laurel forest
cards.text: The Laurisilva is a surviving remnant of the laurel forest that covered southern Europe millions of years ago, and a UNESCO site. You walk it along levadas, the narrow irrigation channels that thread the mountains.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pastel de nata: blistered custard in crackly pastry, best warm with cinnamon. On Madeira, bolo do caco, a flatbread cooked on a stone and slathered with garlic butter.

624.name: Guinea-Bissau

word.meaning: "Greetings, regards," in Kriol, the language most Bissau-Guineans share. You send your mantenhas to someone's family, and a visitor is met with warm mantenhas all around.

624.ask: Ask how their family makes caldo de mancarra, peanut stew with chicken or fish, and whether they drink cashew juice in the season.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music and Carnival: gumbe music and Bissau's colorful Carnival are shared joys.

Football: Bissau-Guineans follow their national team and Portuguese clubs like Benfica closely.

Cashews: many families have a connection to the cashew harvest, and cashew lovers have a fun fact to share.

cards.title: This season: turtles on Poilão
cards.text: From August to November, green turtles come ashore by the thousands on Poilão, a tiny uninhabited island in the Bijagós Archipelago, to lay their eggs. It's the largest green turtle nesting colony on Africa's Atlantic coast, and the Bijagós people consider the island sacred.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The Bijagós Archipelago, dozens of islands of mangroves, beaches and forest where the Bijagó people keep their own traditions. And its music, from gumbe to the great bands of the 1970s.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Gumbe is the popular rhythm of Guinea-Bissau, sung in Kriol. Super Mama Djombo, a band that started as children at a scout camp, became the sound of the new nation in the 1970s; their song "Pamparida" was a hit across West Africa.

cards.title: Craft: panu di pinti
cards.text: Handwoven cotton cloth made by Manjaco weavers on narrow looms, in strips sewn together, with patterns in black, white and bright colors. It's given at births, weddings and funerals.

cards.title: Creature: saltwater hippos
cards.text: On the island of Orango, in the Bijagós, hippos live in freshwater lagoons and swim in the sea between islands, one of the few places in the world where hippos do.

cards.title: Place: the Bijagós Archipelago
cards.text: Some 88 islands and islets off the coast, with mangroves, tidal flats full of migratory birds, and beaches where turtles nest. It's a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Caldo de mancarra. Jollof rice. Oysters from the mangroves. And cashews, Guinea-Bissau's biggest crop, with their juicy fruit.

626.name: Timor-Leste

word.meaning: "How are you?" in Tetum, literally "good or not?" The answer is usually "diak," good. Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, and many Timorese speak several more.

626.ask: Ask about Timorese coffee: whether their family grows it in the hills, and how they like to drink it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Timorese love football and follow the big European leagues, especially Portuguese clubs.

Coffee: Timor grows excellent coffee, and coffee lovers have a fun connection.

Music and dance: guitars come out at every gathering, and everyone joins the tebe-tebe circle dance at celebrations.

cards.title: This season: whale season
cards.text: From mid-October to the end of November, pygmy blue whales swim through the deep strait between Dili and Atauro Island on their migration, along with sperm whales and dolphins, and can sometimes be seen from boats close to shore. It's one of the few places in the world where people can swim with blue whales.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its independence, restored in 2002, making it one of the world's youngest countries. Its coffee, grown in the mountains. And tais, its handwoven cloth.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Likurai is a traditional dance of welcome and celebration, performed by women with small drums held under the arm. In tebe-tebe, people link arms in a circle and dance and sing together, sometimes through the night.

cards.title: Craft: tais
cards.text: Timorese women weave tais on backstrap looms, in patterns and colors that identify each region, with symbols of crocodiles, birds and ancestors. Tais are given at weddings, births and funerals. UNESCO lists it as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

cards.title: Creature: the saltwater crocodile
cards.text: In Timorese legend, the island itself was once a young crocodile who turned into land. Many Timorese call the crocodile "grandfather," and respect it.

cards.title: Place: Atauro Island
cards.text: An island a short boat ride from Dili, whose reefs have some of the highest numbers of reef fish species ever recorded at a single site, with villages, beaches and mountain trails.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Batar daan, corn cooked with beans and pumpkin. Ikan sabuko, grilled fish with tamarind sauce. And strong coffee from the hills.

630.name: Puerto Rico

word.meaning: A joyful shout of celebration and encouragement: at a great play in baseball, a perfect dance move, good news or a party that's just getting started. "¡Wepa!" says it all.

630.ask: Ask how their family makes coquito, the coconut eggnog of the holidays, and whose recipe is best (everyone's is).

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: salsa, reggaeton and Bad Bunny are loved worldwide.

Baseball: Roberto Clemente is a hero, remembered for his play and his generosity.

Food: mofongo and coquito are family favorites.

cards.title: This season: the longest Christmas
cards.text: Puerto Ricans are proud of having one of the longest Christmas seasons in the world, from after Thanksgiving through Three Kings' Day on January 6 and on to the San Sebastián Street Festival in Old San Juan in January. Friends go on parrandas, surprise caroling parties that arrive at a house late at night with guitars, cuatros and güiros, and move on from house to house until dawn.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its music, from bomba and plena to salsa and reggaeton. The coquí, the tiny frog whose song fills the night. And the warmth of its people, on the island and far beyond.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bomba, with drums in dialogue with a dancer, and plena, the "sung newspaper" with hand drums called panderetas, are Puerto Rico's Afro-Caribbean roots. Plena Libre brought plena back to life in the 1990s, and island music today reaches the whole world through salsa and reggaeton.

cards.title: Craft: vejigante masks
cards.text: For festivals in Loíza and Ponce, artisans make vejigante masks with many horns, from coconut shells or papier-mâché, painted in bright colors and spots. The vejigantes dance through the streets in bat-winged costumes.

cards.title: Creature: coquí
cards.text: A tiny tree frog, found in the wild only in Puerto Rico, whose call, "ko-KEE," is the sound of the island's nights. "De aquí como el coquí" means "as Puerto Rican as the coquí."

cards.title: Place: El Yunque
cards.text: The only tropical rainforest in the United States National Forest System, with waterfalls, mountain streams, giant ferns and the calls of coquís and the rare Puerto Rican parrot.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Mofongo, mashed fried plantains with garlic and pork cracklings. Arroz con gandules and pernil, roast pork, at Christmas. And coquito.

634.name: Qatar

word.meaning: The sitting room where people gather, and the gathering itself: family and friends meeting in the evening to talk, drink coffee and tea, share news and settle matters. UNESCO lists the majlis as heritage, shared with other Gulf countries.

634.ask: Ask whether anyone in their family was a pearl diver, and what stories came down from those days.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: the 2022 World Cup and the Asian Cup wins in 2019 and 2024 are proud memories.

Majlis: evening gatherings with friends and family over coffee and dates.

Food: machboos and balaleet are family favorites.

cards.title: This season: National Day
cards.text: On December 18, Qatar celebrates its National Day with parades along the Corniche in Doha, fireworks, flags in maroon and white, and traditional sword dances. In the weeks before, Darb Al Saai, a festival of heritage, food and crafts, fills with families.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its seafaring past, when pearl diving and dhow sailing were the heart of life. Its museums, like the National Museum shaped like a desert rose. And its welcome to visitors.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Sea songs were once sung by pearl divers and sailors to the rhythm of their work, led by a singer called the nahham. Fahad Al Kubaisi, a Qatari singer and oud player, blends Gulf music with pop.

cards.title: Craft: dhow building
cards.text: Shipwrights build wooden dhows by eye and experience, without plans, shaping the hull plank by plank. The boats once carried pearl divers and traders, and now race and sail in festivals.

cards.title: Creature: Arabian horse
cards.text: Prized for their beauty, spirit and endurance, Arabian horses are bred with great care in Qatar, and horse shows and races are a much-loved tradition.

cards.title: Place: Al Zubarah
cards.text: A pearl-diving and trading town on the northwest coast, abandoned in the early 20th century and now uncovered by archaeologists, with a fort that still stands guard. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Machboos. Harees. And balaleet, sweet vermicelli with saffron and cardamom topped with an omelette, for breakfast.

642.name: Romania

word.meaning: A deep, tender longing for someone or something you love and miss: a person, a place, home, the past. Romanians say "mi-e dor de tine," I miss you, and many say no other language has quite the same word.

642.ask: Ask how their family makes sarmale, cabbage or vine leaves rolled around meat and rice, and whether theirs are the best (they'll say yes).

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: sarmale and mămăligă are family favorites, and grandmothers' recipes are treasured.

Mountains: hiking in the Carpathians is a shared joy.

Sport: Nadia Comăneci and Simona Halep are heroes.

cards.title: This season: Saint Andrew's Night
cards.text: On the night of November 29, the eve of Saint Andrew's Day, Romanian folklore says spirits roam and wolves can speak. People rub garlic on windows and doors to keep evil away, and young women put basil under their pillows to dream of their future husbands. The next day, December 1, is National Day, the start of the holiday season.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its language, a Romance language descended from Latin, surrounded by Slavic and Hungarian neighbors. The Carpathian Mountains and their forests. And the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși, a founder of modern sculpture.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The doina is a free, sorrowful, improvised song of longing and love, sung or played on flute or violin, that UNESCO lists as heritage. Village bands called taraf play fast, virtuosic dance music on violin, cimbalom and accordion; Taraf de Haïdouks, from the village of Clejani, took this sound around the world.

links.label: Band of Gypsies, Taraf de Haïdouks

cards.title: Craft: the ie
cards.text: The traditional blouse of white cotton or linen, embroidered on the sleeves and chest with patterns specific to each region and village, in red, black or many colors. UNESCO lists the craft, shared with Moldova, as heritage, and June 24 is Universal Day of the Romanian Blouse.

cards.title: Creature: brown bear
cards.text: The Carpathian forests are home to one of Europe's largest populations of brown bears, which roam the mountains and sometimes wander into villages looking for apples.

cards.title: Place: the painted churches of Bucovina
cards.text: In the north, 15th- and 16th-century monasteries are painted inside and out with vivid scenes of saints, angels and the Last Judgment. Voroneț's deep blue is so famous it's called "Voroneț blue." They're a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Sarmale with mămăligă, a golden cornmeal porridge, and sour cream. Ciorbă, sour soups of many kinds. And papanași, fried cheese doughnuts with jam and sour cream.

643.name: Russia

word.meaning: A country cottage with a garden, where families go on summer weekends to grow potatoes, cucumbers and berries, make jam, sit by the samovar and take a banya, a steam bath. Life at the dacha is slower and happier.

643.ask: Ask what their family grows at the dacha, if they have one, and what jam their grandmother makes.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Books: many Russians love talking about Tolstoy, Dostoevsky and Chekhov, and readers have instant common ground.

Dachas: summer cottages with gardens are cherished, and gardeners have lots to share.

Chess and hockey: both are national passions, and a game of chess is an easy way to spend time together without much shared language.

cards.title: This season: the first snow
cards.text: In late autumn, the first snow falls across much of Russia, and cities and forests turn white. Children go sledding, skating rinks open in the parks, and people bring out felt boots, fur hats and thermoses of tea.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its writers, from Pushkin and Tolstoy to Chekhov. Its composers, like Tchaikovsky. Its ballet. And the sheer size and variety of its land, from the Baltic to the Pacific.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Village folk songs and dances, played on the balalaika, a three-stringed lute with a triangular body, and the bayan, a button accordion, are the roots. The Osipov State Russian Folk Orchestra, whose roots go back to a balalaika ensemble of the 1880s, plays these tunes on balalaikas and domras.

links.label: Balalaika Favorites, Osipov State Russian Folk Orchestra

cards.title: Craft: Khokhloma
cards.text: Wooden bowls, spoons and dishes painted with swirling red and black berries and leaves on a gleaming gold background, first made in villages along the Volga in the 17th century.

cards.title: Creature: Baikal seal
cards.text: The nerpa, the only seal in the world that lives only in fresh water, found in Lake Baikal, with big dark eyes and a round silvery body.

cards.title: Place: Lake Baikal
cards.text: The deepest and oldest lake on Earth, holding about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water. In winter, its surface freezes into clear blue ice. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pelmeni, little meat dumplings. Blini, thin pancakes with sour cream, jam or caviar. And pirozhki, filled buns.

646.name: Rwanda

word.meaning: "Coming together for a common purpose," in Kinyarwanda. On the last Saturday morning of every month, Rwandans join umuganda, community work: cleaning streets, planting trees, building homes, then meeting to talk over neighborhood matters. It's one reason Rwanda's cities are famously clean.

646.ask: Ask about their favorite Rwandan coffee or tea, both grown on the country's green hills, and how they take it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hills and nature: Rwandans are proud of their green hills and mountain gorillas.

Cycling: the Tour du Rwanda draws huge crowds, and Kigali hosted the 2025 world road cycling championships.

Coffee: Rwanda grows excellent coffee, and coffee lovers may already have tried it.

cards.title: This season: the short rains
cards.text: Rwanda is called "the land of a thousand hills," and from October to December the short rains return, turning the terraced slopes, tea plantations and banana groves an even brighter green. It's also when coffee farmers tend their bushes as the next crop of cherries begins to form.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its recovery and unity, and the way its people have rebuilt together since 1994. And its conservation: mountain gorilla numbers in the Virunga volcanoes have grown thanks to decades of protection, and Nyungwe Forest became Rwanda's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Rwanda's traditional music is carried by the inanga, a trough zither, and by the drums that accompany intore, the dance of warriors, whose dancers leap high with long headdresses swaying. Cécile Kayirebwa, one of its best-loved singers, has spent decades recording and preserving Rwandan songs, and today's pop stars, like Meddy, blend Kinyarwanda lyrics with R&B and Afrobeats.

cards.title: Craft: agaseke baskets and imigongo
cards.text: Agaseke are tightly woven baskets with pointed lids, made from sisal and sweetgrass in geometric patterns, traditionally given as gifts at weddings and now a symbol of peace. And imigongo, bold black, red and white geometric panels, are made by women in the east from a surprising material: cow dung, shaped into ridges, dried and painted.

cards.title: Creature: mountain gorilla
cards.text: In Volcanoes National Park, families of mountain gorillas live in the bamboo forests on the slopes of the Virunga volcanoes. Every year, newborn gorillas are given names at a ceremony called Kwita Izina.

cards.title: Place: Nyungwe Forest
cards.text: One of the oldest montane rainforests in Africa, in the southwest, home to chimpanzees, a dozen other primate species and more than 300 kinds of birds, with a canopy walkway high above the trees. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Brochettes, skewers of goat or beef grilled at every roadside gathering, often with grilled plantain. Isombe, cassava leaves pounded and cooked with peanut paste or eggplant. And a cup of Rwandan coffee, grown at high altitude and prized around the world.

682.name: Saudi Arabia

word.meaning: "Welcome!" A warm, everyday greeting, and a way to say you're truly glad someone came. "Hala wallah" makes it even warmer.

682.ask: Ask how their family serves gahwa, the light, cardamom-scented Arabic coffee poured in tiny cups with dates, and how you signal you've had enough (a little shake of the cup).

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: the 2022 World Cup win over Argentina was a moment of national joy.

Coffee and dates: Arabic coffee and dates for every guest, a ritual of welcome.

The desert: camping in the desert in winter is a favorite family pastime.

cards.title: This season: winter in the desert
cards.text: From late autumn, the heat breaks, and Saudis head outdoors: camping in the desert, picnics in the dunes, and festivals in places like AlUla, where concerts and events are held among the sandstone cliffs through the cool months.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its hospitality, with coffee and dates for every guest. The Arabic poetry of the desert. And AlUla and Hegra, ancient places among dramatic rock formations.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bedouin poetry and song, sung to the oud, run deep in Saudi music. Mohammed Abdu, "the Artist of the Arabs," has sung for more than half a century and is one of the most loved voices in the Gulf.

cards.title: Craft: Al-Qatt Al-Asiri
cards.text: In the Asir region of the southwest, women paint the walls of their homes with bright geometric patterns in bands of color. UNESCO lists this art as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Arabian leopard
cards.text: A small, pale leopard of the mountains of Arabia, critically endangered, with only a few left in the wild. A breeding program in AlUla aims to bring it back.

cards.title: Place: Hegra
cards.text: Near AlUla, more than a hundred monumental tombs were carved into sandstone outcrops by the Nabataeans, the same people who built Petra, some 2,000 years ago. It was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kabsa, spiced rice with chicken or lamb, the national dish. Jareesh, cracked wheat cooked with meat and yogurt. And dates with gahwa.

686.name: Senegal

word.meaning: Hospitality, in Wolof, but deeper than the English word: the generous welcome that makes a stranger feel at home, shares whatever there is, and always finds room for one more at the bowl. Senegalese call their country the land of teranga, and the national football team are the Lions of Teranga.

686.ask: Ask who makes the best ceebu jën in their family, and whether they fight for the crispy rice at the bottom of the pot, the xoon, which many consider the best part.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Sadio Mané and the 2022 Africa Cup of Nations win are huge sources of pride.

Food: thieboudienne and yassa are family favorites, and Senegalese love to share them.

Music: Youssou N'Dour and mbalax are loved, and music lovers have an opening.

cards.title: This season: the birds arrive at Djoudj
cards.text: From around November to April, millions of birds escaping the European winter arrive at the Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary in the Senegal River delta: white pelicans in huge colonies, flamingos, purple herons, spoonbills and cormorants among nearly 400 species. It's one of the most important wetlands in West Africa and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Teranga itself. And its music, poets and artists: Senegal's first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor, was a celebrated poet, and Dakar hosts one of Africa's major contemporary art biennials, Dak'Art.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Senegal's music is built on the sabar drums of the Wolof and the songs of griots, the hereditary musicians and keepers of history. In the 1970s, Orchestra Baobab blended those roots with Cuban son, which had become hugely popular in West Africa, and Youssou N'Dour, one of Africa's great voices, made mbalax, driven by the sabar, famous around the world; he also produced Baobab's comeback album in 2002.

links.label: Specialist in All Styles, Orchestra Baobab

cards.title: Craft: sous-verre glass painting
cards.text: Paintings made on the back of glass, in reverse, so the details go on first and the background last. Bright, often humorous scenes of daily life, religious figures and proverbs have been painted this way in Senegal since the early 20th century.

cards.title: Creature: great white pelican
cards.text: Thousands of them nest together at Djoudj, fishing in groups by herding fish into the shallows with their wings before scooping them up in their great pouched bills.

cards.title: Place: Saint-Louis
cards.text: The old colonial capital on a narrow island at the mouth of the Senegal River, with colorful houses with wooden balconies, a long iron bridge, and a fishing quarter where brightly painted pirogues line the shore. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the birthplace of ceebu jën.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ceebu jën, "rice and fish" in Wolof: fish stuffed with parsley, garlic and chili and simmered with vegetables in a tomato sauce, then served over the broken rice cooked in the broth, shared from one large bowl. UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2021. Yassa, chicken or fish in a tangy onion and lemon sauce. And bissap, a deep red hibiscus drink.

688.name: Serbia

word.meaning: "Slowly, easy, take your time." Serbians say it to calm a rush, to slow down a meal or a coffee, and to wave off stress: "polako, polako," everything will work out.

688.ask: Ask which saint their family celebrates for its slava, and what's always on the table that day.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Basketball and tennis: Nikola Jokić and Novak Djokovic are national heroes, and sports fans have plenty to talk about.

Food: ćevapi, pljeskavica and ajvar are family favorites.

Hospitality: guests are welcomed with food and drink, and never leave hungry.

cards.title: This season: slava season
cards.text: Each Serbian Orthodox family has a patron saint, passed down from father to son, and celebrates its day, the slava, with an open house: a candle, a braided slava bread, koljivo (sweet boiled wheat) and a feast for relatives and friends. Many of the most popular slavas fall in late autumn and winter, like Saint Michael on November 21 and Saint Nicholas on December 19. UNESCO lists the slava as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its hospitality and its music. Its kolo, the circle dance held hand in hand at every wedding and celebration, which UNESCO lists as heritage. And inventor Nikola Tesla, born to a Serbian family.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Brass bands, with trumpets, tubas and drums, play at weddings and fairs, and every August thousands of people come to the village of Guča for a trumpet festival. Boban Marković's orchestra became one of the most famous brass bands in the world. Older still is the gusle, a one-stringed fiddle played to accompany epic songs.

links.label: Golden Horns, Boban i Marko Marković Orkestar

cards.title: Craft: Pirot kilims
cards.text: In the town of Pirot, weavers make flat-woven wool rugs in deep reds and blues, with geometric patterns and motifs with names like "turtle" and "little ram's horns." The two sides look nearly the same.

cards.title: Creature: long-eared owl
cards.text: Every winter, hundreds of long-eared owls roost in the trees of the town square in Kikinda, in the north, one of the largest such gatherings in the world, and visitors come to count them.

cards.title: Place: Studenica Monastery
cards.text: A 12th-century monastery in a green valley, with a church of white marble and some of the finest medieval frescoes in the Balkans. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ćevapi and pljeskavica, grilled meat with onions and kajmak, a rich clotted cream. Sarma, cabbage rolls, in winter. And ajvar, a roasted red pepper spread made in big batches every autumn.

694.name: Sierra Leone

word.meaning: "Hello!" in Krio, the language most Sierra Leoneans share. "Kushe o!" is the greeting on every street, and "Aw di bodi?" asks, "How's the body?" (How are you?)

694.ask: Ask how their family makes cassava leaf stew, pounded greens cooked in palm oil with fish or meat and served over rice, and whether it's better than potato leaf.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Sierra Leoneans follow their national team, the Leone Stars, and the Premier League passionately.

Beaches: the Freetown Peninsula's beaches, like River No. 2, are sources of pride.

Music: afropop and gospel fill parties, and music lovers have an opening.

cards.title: This season: beach season
cards.text: As the rains end in November, the dry season begins, and the beaches of the Freetown Peninsula, like River No. 2, Tokeh and Bureh, are at their best: white sand, palm trees, forested hills behind and warm Atlantic water.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "Sweet Salone," as people call their country, for its warmth, music and beaches. Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827, one of the oldest Western-style universities in West Africa. And its resilience.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Palm wine music, played on acoustic guitar with gentle, rolling rhythms, grew along the coast, and S. E. Rogie made it famous. Sierra Leone's Refugee All Stars, a band that formed in refugee camps during the civil war, play reggae and West African styles full of hope, and have toured the world.

links.label: Libation, Sierra Leone's Refugee All Stars

cards.title: Craft: gara cloth
cards.text: Gara is tie-dyed and resist-dyed cotton, traditionally dyed with indigo and kola nut, in rich blues, browns and patterns made by tying, folding and stitching the cloth before dyeing.

cards.title: Creature: western chimpanzee
cards.text: Sierra Leone's forests are home to chimpanzees, the national animal. The Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary, in the hills above Freetown, cares for orphaned chimps and works to protect wild ones.

cards.title: Place: Tiwai Island
cards.text: A forested island in the Moa River, home to 11 kinds of primates, including chimpanzees and colobus monkeys, and pygmy hippos. Local communities run it as a wildlife sanctuary.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Cassava leaf stew with rice. Groundnut soup. And ginger beer, fiery and sweet.

703.name: Slovakia

word.meaning: Handy, clever, skillful: someone who can fix, make or figure out anything. "Si šikovný!" is warm praise for a child, a friend or a craftsperson.

703.ask: Ask how they like their bryndzové halušky, little potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, and where to find the best, from a mountain salaš, a shepherd's hut.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hockey: Slovaks are passionate about it, and many follow Slovak players in the NHL.

Hiking: the High Tatras are a shared joy, and hikers will find a friend.

Food: bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, is a family favorite.

cards.title: This season: Christmas markets
cards.text: From late November, town squares across Slovakia, from Bratislava to Košice, fill with Christmas market stalls. People meet after work for hot mulled wine or mead, lokše (potato pancakes filled with goose fat, poppy seeds or jam), and handmade gifts.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its mountains, the High Tatras, with sharp granite peaks and alpine lakes. Its castles: hundreds of castles and ruins crown its hills, including Spiš Castle, one of the largest in Central Europe. And its living folk culture.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The fujara, a shepherd's flute up to two meters long, makes a deep, breathy, haunting sound; UNESCO lists it as heritage. In the village of Terchová, bands of fiddles and a bass play and sing in several voices, another tradition on UNESCO's list. For the modern bridge, the band Hrdza, from Prešov, mixes fujara and bagpipes with guitars and drums.

cards.title: Craft: modrotlač
cards.text: Blueprint: printing designs onto cotton or linen with a resist paste, then dipping the cloth in indigo so the pattern comes out white on deep blue. UNESCO lists it as heritage, shared with neighboring countries.

cards.title: Creature: Tatra chamois
cards.text: A goat-antelope with short hooked horns and a dark winter coat that leaps over rocks in the High Tatras. This subspecies lives wild only in the Tatras and a few nearby mountains.

cards.title: Place: Čičmany
cards.text: A mountain village of dark wooden houses painted with bright white geometric patterns, stars, hearts and crosses. It's often called the world's first folk architecture reserve.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Bryndzové halušky, the national dish. Kapustnica, sauerkraut soup with sausage and mushrooms, for Christmas Eve. And lokše.

704.name: Vietnam

word.meaning: One word for both "to remember" and "to miss." When you say you nhớ someone, you're holding them in mind and longing for them at the same time.
word.sayIt: nyuh, with a rising tone that breaks in the middle

704.ask: Ask where to get the best bowl of phở in their hometown, and whether they take it northern style, clear and simple, or southern, with a heap of fresh herbs.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: pho, banh mi and fresh spring rolls are loved worldwide.

Coffee: Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk, and egg coffee in Hanoi.

Tết: the Lunar New Year is the biggest holiday, with family visits and special foods.

cards.title: This season: hoa sữa
cards.text: In Hanoi, autumn arrives as a scent. From mid-September through November, the city's milk-flower trees, hoa sữa, burst into creamy white star-shaped clusters, and in October their sweet, heady perfume hangs in the streets, strongest after dark. The flowers turn up again and again in Vietnamese poems and love songs.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Coffee. Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee producer, and its cafés are an art form: strong drip coffee from a small metal phin filter, sweetened with condensed milk, sipped on tiny stools on the sidewalk for hours.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Ca trù, sung by a woman who keeps time with wooden clappers, accompanied by a long-necked lute and a drum, was once the music of poets and scholars; UNESCO lists it for urgent safeguarding. Quan họ, the call-and-response love songs of Bắc Ninh province, is also on UNESCO's list. The đàn bầu, a one-stringed zither whose player bends each note with a flexible rod, sounds almost like a human voice. For the modern bridge, Hoàng Thùy Linh's 2019 album Hoàng sets folk melodies and legends to dance-pop.

links.label: Vietnamese Traditional Dan Bau Music, Phạm Đức Thành

cards.title: Craft: nón lá
cards.text: The conical leaf hat, made by stitching dried palm leaves over a frame of thin bamboo rings. In Huế, makers slip cut-out poems or pictures between the layers of the nón bài thơ, "poem hat," so they appear only when you hold it up to the light.

cards.title: Creature: saola
cards.text: One of the rarest large mammals on Earth, a shy forest ox with long, straight horns, unknown to science until 1992, when it was found in the Annamite Mountains along the border with Laos. It's sometimes called the Asian unicorn because it's so rarely seen.

cards.title: Place: Hang Sơn Đoòng
cards.text: The largest known cave passage in the world, in Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park. A local man, Hồ Khanh, found its entrance while sheltering from a storm in 1990, lost it, and found it again years later; British and Vietnamese cavers surveyed it in 2009. Inside there's a river, its own clouds, and a jungle where the roof has collapsed to let in the sun.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Phở, rice noodles in a long-simmered, star-anise-scented broth. Bánh mì, a crisp baguette stuffed with pâté, pickled vegetables and herbs. And Hanoi's egg coffee, cà phê trứng, topped with whipped egg yolk and condensed milk, invented in 1946 by Nguyễn Văn Giảng when milk was scarce.

705.name: Slovenia

word.meaning: "Welcome." In a small country with mountains, sea, caves and vineyards all within a few hours' drive, Slovenians are proud to say it, and it's often the first word visitors see.

705.ask: Ask which potica their family bakes, the rolled holiday cake with a spiral of filling: walnut, tarragon, poppy seed or honey.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hiking and climbing: many Slovenians love the mountains, and climbing Triglav is a rite of passage.

Sport: Luka Dončić and Tadej Pogačar are national heroes.

Beekeeping: many Slovenians keep bees, and beekeepers have lots to share.

cards.title: This season: Saint Martin's Day
cards.text: On November 11, Slovenia celebrates Martinovanje. By tradition, this is the day that must, fresh grape juice, turns into wine. Wine regions and villages celebrate for a week or two with the first taste of young wine, a feast of roast goose, red cabbage and mlinci, a flatbread soaked in the roasting juices, and music.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its green, beautiful nature: more than half the country is forest, and Mount Triglav appears on its flag. And its bees: Slovenia has one of the highest numbers of beekeepers per person in the world, and UNESCO lists its beekeeping as heritage.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Slovenia is home to Alpine polka. In 1954, Slavko Avsenik wrote "Na Golici," a bright instrumental polka with accordion, clarinet and trumpet that became one of the most played instrumental tunes in the world.

cards.title: Craft: painted beehive panels
cards.text: In the 18th and 19th centuries, beekeepers painted the front boards of their hives with bright scenes: saints, hunters, animals and funny stories, like the devil sharpening a woman's tongue. The Museum of Apiculture in Radovljica has hundreds.

cards.title: Creature: the olm
cards.text: A blind, pale pink salamander that lives only in the underground waters of the Dinaric karst. It can live more than 100 years, and once people thought it was a baby dragon washed out of the caves. You can see olms at Postojna Cave.

cards.title: Place: Škocjan Caves
cards.text: The Reka River plunges underground into one of the world's largest known underground canyons, crossed by a bridge high above the roaring water. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Potica, for holidays. Kranjska klobasa, the Carniolan sausage. Štruklji, rolled dumplings filled with cottage cheese, tarragon or walnuts. And honey, from Slovenia's own Carniolan bees.

706.name: Somalia

word.meaning: "Welcome!" In Somali homes, guests are welcomed with tea, food and conversation, and hospitality is a point of honor.

706.ask: Ask about their favorite Somali poem or song. Poetry is loved across Somalia, and many people can recite long verses by heart.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Poetry and songs: Somalis love poetry and music, and poetry lovers have instant common ground.

Tea: spiced tea with cardamom and ginger, shared with friends, is an everyday ritual.

Football: Somalis follow the Premier League passionately, and a favorite club is an easy start.

cards.title: This season: the Deyr rains
cards.text: From October to December come the Deyr, the short rains. For herders across Somalia, they bring fresh grass and water for camels, goats and sheep, and the dry land turns green.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Poetry: Somalia has been called "a nation of poets," where verses are composed for weddings, disputes and everyday life. Its camels, one of the largest camel herds in the world. And its long Indian Ocean coast.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the 1970s and 80s, Mogadishu's bands mixed Somali melodies with funk, soul and disco. Dur-Dur Band, whose name means "spring," was one of the most popular, and reissues have brought its songs to new fans around the world.

cards.title: Craft: alindi cloth
cards.text: Weavers in Mogadishu's old Hamar Weyne quarter make alindi, handwoven cotton cloth in stripes of bright colors, worn as wraps and shawls.

cards.title: Creature: dromedary camel
cards.text: Camels are at the heart of Somali life, prized for their milk, their endurance and their beauty, and celebrated in countless poems and songs.

cards.title: Place: Lido Beach
cards.text: Mogadishu's long white-sand beach on the Indian Ocean, where families gather on Fridays to swim, eat fresh seafood and watch the sunset.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Canjeero, a spongy flatbread, with tea. Bariis iskukaris, spiced rice with meat. Sambuus, fried pastries. And halwo, a sweet, sticky treat for weddings and Eid.

710.name: South Africa

word.meaning: From the Nguni languages, including Zulu and Xhosa, ubuntu means that a person becomes a person through other people: "I am because we are." It's a whole outlook of kindness, sharing and belonging, and Desmond Tutu and Nelson Mandela spoke of it often.

710.ask: Ask what goes on their braai, the South African barbecue, and who in their family is trusted with the fire. Everyone has a firm opinion about wood versus charcoal.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Rugby: the Springboks' World Cup wins are shared joys, and rugby is a sure start.

Braais: grilling with friends is a weekend ritual.

Music: amapiano, jazz and choirs are loved, and music lovers have plenty to share.

cards.title: This season: jacaranda time in Pretoria
cards.text: It's spring, and Pretoria, the "Jacaranda City," is turning purple. From late September through October, and sometimes into November, tens of thousands of jacaranda trees bloom along its streets and carpet the pavements with violet flowers. Students have a saying that if a blossom lands on your head, you'll pass your exams.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its democracy, won in 1994 when all South Africans voted for the first time and elected Nelson Mandela president, after decades of struggle against apartheid. And its many voices: the country has 12 official languages, the most recent, South African Sign Language, added in 2023.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: South Africa's choral traditions are among the most beautiful in the world. Isicathamiya, the soft, close a cappella harmony of Zulu men's choirs, reached the world through Ladysmith Black Mambazo, especially after Paul Simon's Graceland. Miriam Makeba, "Mama Africa," carried South African song everywhere she went. For the modern bridge, amapiano, a deep, rolling house music with log-drum bass from Johannesburg's townships, has become one of Africa's most popular sounds since the mid-2010s.

links.label: Songs From a Zulu Farm, Ladysmith Black Mambazo

cards.title: Craft: Ndebele painting and beadwork
cards.text: Ndebele women paint the walls of their homes in bold, bright geometric patterns outlined in black, and create equally striking beadwork for aprons, blankets and neck rings. The artist Esther Mahlangu has carried the style onto canvases, cars and airplanes around the world.

cards.title: Creature: African penguin
cards.text: At Boulders Beach near Cape Town, a colony of African penguins waddles among the granite boulders and swims in the cold Atlantic, braying like donkeys. The species is endangered, and the colony is carefully protected.

cards.title: Place: the Cape Floral Region
cards.text: Around Cape Town and Table Mountain grows fynbos, one of the richest plant kingdoms on Earth, with thousands of species found nowhere else, including the king protea, the national flower. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: The braai, with boerewors, spiced coiled sausage. Bobotie, a Cape Malay dish of spiced minced meat baked under an egg custard. Bunny chow from Durban, a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry. And koeksisters, braided doughnuts soaked in syrup, with a cup of rooibos tea.

716.name: Zimbabwe

word.meaning: "Thank you," in Shona. For a big thank-you, it's "ndatenda zvikuru," and a popular name, Tatenda, carries the same gratitude.

716.ask: Ask how they eat sadza, the stiff maize porridge at the heart of every meal, and what relish they like best with it: greens, beans, beef or kapenta, tiny dried fish.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Music: mbira music, Thomas Mapfumo and Oliver Mtukudzi's songs are loved.

Victoria Falls: Zimbabweans love hearing you've seen "the smoke that thunders" or want to.

Cricket: Zimbabweans are proud of their team's giant-killing wins, and cricket fans have instant common ground.

cards.title: This season: jacaranda and the first rains
cards.text: In October and November, Harare's avenues turn purple with jacarandas, and the hot, dry air builds toward the first rains. When they come, the land turns green almost overnight, and children look forward to mazhanje, a wild fruit sold at the roadside when it ripens with the rains.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Great Zimbabwe, the stone city that gave the country its name, "houses of stone," built between the 11th and 15th centuries. And Victoria Falls, Mosi-oa-Tunya, "the smoke that thunders," on the border with Zambia.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The mbira, a thumb piano of metal keys on a wooden board, often played inside a gourd to amplify it, is the heart of Shona music, played for ceremonies and for the ancestors. Stella Chiweshe became one of its first great women players. For the modern bridge, Thomas Mapfumo, "the Lion of Zimbabwe," brought mbira patterns to electric guitar in his chimurenga music.

cards.title: Craft: Shona stone sculpture
cards.text: Sculptors carve serpentine and other local stones into flowing figures of people, birds and spirits, polished to a glossy finish. The movement took off in the 1950s and 60s, and its artists have shown in galleries around the world.

cards.title: Creature: African wild dog
cards.text: The painted dog, with a blotchy coat of black, brown and cream, hunts in cooperative packs. Hwange National Park has one of Africa's important populations of this endangered species.

cards.title: Place: Victoria Falls
cards.text: The Zambezi River plunges over a sheer cliff more than a kilometer and a half wide, sending up spray that can be seen from miles away and makes rainbows over the gorge. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site shared with Zambia.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Sadza with relish. Muriwo une dovi, greens cooked in peanut butter. And roasted maize and mazhanje sold at the roadside in season.

724.name: Spain

word.meaning: To wear or use something for the very first time: new shoes, a new dress, a new kitchen. Spanish has one word for that small thrill, and people often save something new to estrenar on a special day.

724.ask: Ask what their family does on Christmas Eve, Nochebuena, and on the night of January 5, when the Three Kings parade through town throwing sweets and bring the children's presents.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Real Madrid, Barcelona, and the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2024 wins.

Food: tapas, paella and long meals with friends are shared pleasures.

Festivals: local fiestas with music and dancing are a joyful part of life.

cards.title: This season: El Gordo and Christmas
cards.text: On December 22, the whole country tunes in as schoolchildren from San Ildefonso sing out the winning numbers of the Christmas lottery, El Gordo, "the fat one," in a draw that goes on all morning. Tickets are often bought together by friends, families and coworkers, so when a number wins, a whole village or office celebrates at once.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its food, from tapas to paella, and the long, sociable way it's eaten. And its landscapes and cities: Spain has among the largest number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites of any country.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Flamenco, from Andalusia, joins cante (song), toque (guitar) and baile (dance) in music of fierce feeling, shaped largely by Gitano (Romani) communities; UNESCO lists it as heritage. The guitarist Paco de Lucía and the singer Camarón de la Isla transformed it together, and their 1979 album La Leyenda del Tiempo opened it to new sounds. For the modern bridge, Rosalía's El Mal Querer, from 2018, weaves flamenco into pop, each song a chapter of a story drawn from a 13th-century romance.

links.label: La Leyenda del Tiempo, Camarón de la Isla with Paco de Lucía

cards.title: Craft: the Spanish guitar
cards.text: The classical guitar took its modern shape in 19th-century Spain, in the workshop of the Almería luthier Antonio de Torres, and luthiers in cities like Granada and Madrid still build guitars by hand from spruce, cedar and rosewood.

cards.title: Creature: Iberian lynx
cards.text: A spotted wild cat with tufted ears and a beard-like ruff, found only in Spain and Portugal. In 2002 fewer than 100 were left; after two decades of conservation, the 2024 count found 2,401, and it's no longer classed as endangered, one of the greatest recoveries of any cat.

cards.title: Place: the Alhambra
cards.text: A palace and fortress of the Nasrid kings above Granada, finished in the 14th century, with carved plaster walls as fine as lace, tiled halls, and courtyards of pools and fountains. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tapas, small plates shared with a drink. Tortilla española, a thick potato and egg omelet. Paella from Valencia, cooked in a wide, shallow pan. At Christmas, turrón, nougat of almonds and honey. And on winter mornings, churros dipped in thick hot chocolate.

728.name: South Sudan

word.meaning: "Good!" in Juba Arabic, the language many South Sudanese use to talk across their more than 60 languages. "Inta kweis?" Are you well? "Kweis!"

728.ask: Ask which people their family belongs to, Dinka, Nuer, Bari, Zande, Shilluk or another of the country's many, and what their favorite song or dance is.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Basketball: the national team's run to the 2024 Olympics was a huge joy, and many follow the NBA.

Football: South Sudanese follow the national team and the Premier League passionately.

Music and dance: songs and dances are central to celebrations, and anyone who loves to dance is welcome.

cards.title: This season: the great migration
cards.text: From November to January, as the wet season ends, millions of white-eared kob, tiang and Mongalla gazelles begin moving across the grasslands and wetlands between Boma and Badingilo national parks, one of the largest land migrations of mammals on Earth.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: The great antelope migration, now protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its cattle-keeping peoples and their songs. And its young people, full of energy and hope.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Songs are at the heart of life, especially among cattle-keeping peoples, who compose songs in praise of their favorite oxen. Emmanuel Jal, a former child soldier, became a hip-hop artist and peace activist whose songs have been heard around the world.

cards.title: Craft: Dinka beadwork
cards.text: Dinka artisans make beaded corsets, necklaces and bracelets in bright colors, which show age, family and wealth, and are worn with pride at dances and ceremonies.

cards.title: Creature: white-eared kob
cards.text: A graceful antelope, dark brown with a white patch around the eye and white ears, which travels in herds of thousands across the plains. Some 5 million make the yearly journey.

cards.title: Place: Boma and Badingilo
cards.text: A vast landscape of grasslands, wetlands and woodlands where the migration takes place, listed by UNESCO in 2025 as the Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kisra with stew. Asida, porridge. And walwal, balls of sorghum flour with milk or yogurt.

729.name: Sudan

word.meaning: A call for help from the whole community: neighbors come together to build a house, bring in a harvest or help a family in need, and everyone shares food afterward. Sudanese are proud of this spirit of pitching in.

729.ask: Ask how their family makes ful medames, slow-cooked fava beans, and what they put on top: oil, cheese, egg, or all three.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Sudanese follow local clubs like Al-Hilal and Al-Merrikh with great passion.

Coffee: jebena coffee, spiced with ginger and shared with friends, is an everyday ritual.

Music: Sudanese music is loved across East Africa, and music lovers have an opening.

cards.title: This season: the date harvest
cards.text: In autumn, date palms along the Nile in northern Sudan are heavy with fruit, and families climb the trees to cut the bunches, dry the dates in the sun, and sort them for eating, cooking and sharing through the year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its pyramids: ancient Nubia has more pyramids than Egypt, at places like Meroë. The meeting of the Blue and White Nile at Khartoum. And its famous hospitality.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Sudanese music has a rich, swinging sound, with pentatonic melodies, the oud and a rolling rhythm. Abdel Gadir Salim, from Kordofan, mixed desert songs with a Khartoum band of violins, horns and oud, and played around the world.

cards.title: Craft: the toob
cards.text: The long, flowing cloth that Sudanese women wrap around themselves, in bright colors and prints, sometimes embroidered, for weddings, visits and everyday elegance.

cards.title: Creature: secretary bird
cards.text: A tall, long-legged bird of prey with a crest of quill-like feathers, which hunts snakes on foot by stamping on them. It appears on Sudan's emblem.

cards.title: Place: Meroë
cards.text: In the desert north of Khartoum, clusters of steep, narrow pyramids built by the kings and queens of the Kingdom of Kush stand among the dunes. The Island of Meroë is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Ful medames. Kisra, thin fermented sorghum flatbread. Aseeda, a firm porridge with stew. And karkadeh, iced hibiscus tea.

732.name: Western Sahara

word.meaning: The tent, the heart of Sahrawi life: where families gather, guests are welcomed, tea is made and stories are told, with carpets and cushions on the sand.

732.ask: Ask how the tea is made in their family's khaima, and why the three glasses of tea shouldn't be rushed.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Tea: three glasses of tea, brewed slowly and shared in the tent, are a ritual of friendship, and patience is part of the pleasure.

Music: haul, the Sahrawi music of voice, lute and drum, and singers like Mariem Hassan are loved, and music lovers have an opening.

Poetry: Sahrawi people love poetry in Hassaniya, and anyone who loves poetry or storytelling can ask for a favorite verse.

cards.title: This season: the cool desert season
cards.text: As autumn turns to winter, the desert cools, and it's the best time for gatherings: long evenings of tea, poetry and music in the tent, and bright starry skies over the dunes.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Sahrawi poetry and song, in the Hassaniya language. Its hospitality in the tent. And the melhfa, the women's colorful wrap.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Haul is Sahrawi music, sung by women and men with the tidinit (a lute), the ardin (a harp), and the tbal drum, with handclaps. Mariem Hassan, one of its great voices, sang it on stages around the world.

cards.title: Craft: the melhfa
cards.text: A long piece of bright, light cloth that Sahrawi women wrap around the body and head, dyed in bold colors and patterns, and chosen with great care.

cards.title: Creature: dorcas gazelle
cards.text: A small, pale desert gazelle with big dark eyes and curved horns, able to survive without drinking, getting water from the plants it eats.

cards.title: Place: the Atlantic desert coast
cards.text: Where the Sahara meets the ocean, golden dunes run right down to the waves, with cliffs, lagoons and fishing villages along a long, wild coast.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tea, three glasses of it. Dates. Couscous and grilled camel or goat meat. And fresh fish on the coast.

740.name: Suriname

word.meaning: "Sweet" or "nice" in Sranan Tongo, the language Surinamese of every background share. "Sranan switi" means "Suriname is sweet," and it's also the name of a beloved song.

740.ask: Ask what they order when they get a roti or a broodje pom, and where to find the best in Paramaribo.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: roti, pom and bami are family favorites, and Surinamese love to share them.

Football: many Dutch football stars, like Clarence Seedorf and Virgil van Dijk, have Surinamese roots.

Music: kaseko and kawina fill parties, and Surinamese love Dutch-Surinamese artists abroad too.

cards.title: This season: Owru Yari
cards.text: Late December, Paramaribo gets ready for Owru Yari, the old year, the country's biggest celebration. On December 31, crowds gather in the city center for music and dancing as huge rolls of red firecrackers called pagara are strung up and set off, covering the streets in red paper.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its diversity: people of African, Indian, Javanese, Chinese, Indigenous, European and Maroon descent. In Paramaribo, a mosque and a synagogue stand side by side on the same street. And its rainforest, which covers most of the country.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Kaseko, a joyful, fast dance music with brass, drums and electric guitar, grew from Afro-Surinamese roots, with Kawina drumming and singing. Surinamese of Indian descent brought baithak gana, songs with harmonium and dholak. Max Nijman, "Soulman Number One," sang kaseko, soul and ballads; his song "Adjosi" is about the homesickness of Surinamese abroad.

cards.title: Craft: Maroon woodcarving
cards.text: Maroon peoples, descended from Africans who escaped slavery and built free communities in the rainforest, carve and paint wood in interlacing, symmetrical designs, on paddles, stools, combs and house fronts. The art is called tembe.

cards.title: Creature: Guianan cock-of-the-rock
