cards.text: A bird of bright, flame-orange with a half-moon crest over its beak. The males gather to dance and show off on the forest floor for females.

cards.title: Place: Paramaribo
cards.text: The capital, with white-painted wooden colonial houses, the Fort Zeelandia and the wooden Saint Peter and Paul Cathedral, one of the largest wooden buildings in the Americas. The historic inner city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Roti with curried chicken and potatoes. Pom, an oven dish of chicken and grated pomtajer root, and broodje pom, pom in a sandwich. And bami, Javanese fried noodles.

748.name: Eswatini

word.meaning: "Hello," in siSwati, literally "I see you" (to one person). The answer, "yebo," means "yes," as in "yes, I see you too."

748.ask: Ask how their family makes emasi, thick soured milk eaten with maize meal, and whether it's better than anything from a store.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Singing: choral singing is everywhere, in church, school and ceremonies, and anyone who sings will be welcomed.

Nature: game reserves like Hlane and the mountains of Malolotja are sources of pride.

Football: Swazis follow South African and English football closely, and a favorite club is an easy conversation.

cards.title: This season: the start of Incwala
cards.text: Incwala, the kingship ceremony, follows the moon. At the November full moon, young men called bemanti set off to fetch water from the sea and rivers, and the Little Incwala begins at the new moon in December. The main day of the Big Incwala comes in late December or early January, with thousands of warriors in traditional dress singing and dancing. Its dates are announced shortly before.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its living traditions, like Incwala and Umhlanga, the reed dance. Its green mountains and valleys. And its rhinos, protected in its parks.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Choral singing is everywhere, in church, at school and at ceremonies. Bholoja sings what he calls "Swazi soul," gentle, acoustic songs in siSwati that have found fans far beyond the country.

cards.title: Craft: grass weaving
cards.text: Swazi women weave baskets, mats and bowls from grass and sisal, dyed in bright colors, in patterns that can take weeks to finish. They're sold at markets and craft centers across the country.

cards.title: Creature: rhinoceros
cards.text: Hlane Royal National Park and Mkhaya Game Reserve protect white and black rhinos, carefully guarded against poachers, and visitors can sometimes walk with rangers to see them.

cards.title: Place: Mlilwane
cards.text: The country's oldest protected area, in the Ezulwini Valley, where zebras, antelopes and warthogs graze below the granite peaks of the Nyonyane mountain, and visitors can hike, cycle or ride horses among them.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Emasi with maize meal. Sishwala, a thick porridge. And umncweba, dried meat.

752.name: Sweden

word.meaning: Just right: not too much, not too little, the amount that's enough. Lagom can describe a cup of coffee, a working day or a whole way of living.

752.ask: Ask about their favorite fika, the Swedish coffee break with something sweet, and whether they're loyal to the cinnamon bun or the cardamom bun.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Fika: a coffee break with a cinnamon bun, a ritual many people love.

Music: ABBA, Robyn and Avicii are loved worldwide.

The outdoors: summer cottages, lakes and the right to roam are shared joys.

cards.title: This season: Lucia
cards.text: On December 13, in the darkest part of the year, Sweden celebrates Lucia. Before dawn, a girl wearing a crown of candles leads a procession of singers in white gowns through schools, churches and homes, singing the Lucia song, and everyone eats lussekatter, S-shaped saffron buns with raisins, and ginger snaps.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Allemansrätten, the "right of public access," which lets anyone walk, camp and pick berries and mushrooms almost anywhere in the countryside, as long as they take care of it. And the Nobel Prizes, founded by the Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel and presented in Stockholm each December.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Swedish folk music is played on fiddles and the nyckelharpa, a keyed fiddle with sympathetic strings found nowhere else, in polska dance tunes that swing in three. For the modern bridge, Väsen, a trio of nyckelharpa, viola and guitar, plays folk tunes with the ease of a jazz band, while Garmarna brought medieval ballads into dark, driving folk-rock.

cards.title: Craft: the Dala horse
cards.text: Carved and painted wooden horses from the villages of Dalarna, traditionally bright red with flowered harnesses in a style called kurbits. They began as toys whittled by woodcutters in the evenings, and are now a symbol of Sweden.

cards.title: Creature: moose
cards.text: Sweden has one of the densest moose populations in the world. They're huge, gentle-looking and mostly solitary, and road signs warn of them all over the country.

cards.title: Place: Laponia
cards.text: A vast wilderness of mountains, forests and wetlands in the far north, where Sámi reindeer herders still move their herds between summer and winter pastures as they have for centuries. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site for both its nature and its culture.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Cinnamon buns, kanelbullar, with coffee. Meatballs with lingonberry jam and mashed potatoes. And in December, the julbord, a Christmas buffet of pickled herring, ham, meatballs and Janssons frestelse, a creamy potato and anchovy bake.

756.name: Switzerland

word.meaning: Swiss German for the "nine o'clock": the mid-morning snack break, bread and cheese, a pastry or fruit, eaten at work, at school or halfway up a mountain. There's a Zvieri, "four o'clock," in the afternoon too.

756.ask: Ask whether their family is on team fondue or team raclette for winter evenings, and what happens, by tradition, to whoever drops their bread in the fondue pot.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hiking and skiing: shared joys in the Alps, and hikers and skiers will find a friend.

Fondue and raclette: evenings with friends around melted cheese are a cozy ritual.

Tennis: Roger Federer is a national hero, and any tennis fan can share favorite matches.

cards.title: This season: the onion market in Bern
cards.text: On the fourth Monday of November, November 23 this year, Bern holds its Zibelemärit. Before dawn, the old town fills with stalls selling tons of onions braided into wreaths and garlands, onion tart and cheese tart, and by afternoon children throw confetti everywhere. It's one of the oldest and best-loved festivals in the country.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its mountains, lakes and trains that run on time through them. And its four national languages, German, French, Italian and Romansh, in a country smaller than West Virginia.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Yodeling began as herders' calls across Alpine valleys and grew into wordless melodies and songs with yodeled choruses; in December 2025, UNESCO added Swiss yodeling to its heritage list. More than 12,000 yodelers belong to clubs across the country. The alphorn, a wooden horn several meters long, carries its low, warm notes across the valleys. Nadja Räss, one of its leading voices, teaches the world's first university degree in yodeling, in Lucerne.

cards.title: Craft: Scherenschnitt
cards.text: Swiss paper cutting: intricate, symmetrical silhouettes, often black on white, of cows going up to the Alpine pastures, trees, hearts and village life, cut from a single folded sheet of paper with small scissors.

cards.title: Creature: Alpine ibex
cards.text: A wild mountain goat with enormous curved horns, which climbs cliffs with astonishing sure-footedness. Hunted almost to extinction by the 1800s, it was brought back to the Swiss Alps from a small herd in Italy and now numbers in the thousands.

cards.title: Place: the Jungfrau-Aletsch region
cards.text: Snowy peaks around the Jungfrau and the Aletsch Glacier, the largest in the Alps, a river of ice about 20 kilometers long. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fondue, bread dipped in melted cheese and wine. Raclette, melted cheese scraped over potatoes with pickles. Rösti, a crisp potato cake. And Swiss chocolate, of course.

760.name: Syria

word.meaning: "Enjoy your meal!" Literally "two healths," it's said when someone starts eating or finishes a drink. The reply is "a'la albak," on your heart.

760.ask: Ask how their family makes kibbeh, and how many kinds they know: fried, baked, raw, in yogurt, in soup.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: kibbeh, muhammara and Aleppo pepper are loved, and Syrians love to share their food.

Music: Sabah Fakhri and Aleppo's songs are loved across the Arab world.

Coffee: coffee with cardamom, shared with friends, is an everyday ritual.

cards.title: This season: mouneh
cards.text: In autumn, Syrian families prepare mouneh, the winter pantry: they pickle vegetables, make jams and pepper paste, dry herbs and yogurt, and fill jars and shelves together, so the flavors of summer last all winter.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Damascus and Aleppo, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Its food, loved across the Middle East. And its music, especially Aleppo's.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Aleppo is famous for its qudud, songs sung in call-and-response with the audience, which UNESCO lists as heritage. Sabah Fakhri, Aleppo's great singer, once sang for more than ten hours straight in a single concert.

cards.title: Craft: Damascene inlay
cards.text: Damascus craftsmen make wooden boxes, tables and backgammon boards inlaid with thousands of tiny pieces of mother-of-pearl and colored wood in geometric patterns.

cards.title: Creature: northern bald ibis
cards.text: A dark bird with a bald red head and a shaggy crest, once thought gone from the Middle East until a tiny colony was found near Palmyra in 2002.

cards.title: Place: the Old City of Damascus
cards.text: A walled city of covered souks, courtyard houses with fountains and citrus trees, and the great Umayyad Mosque. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Kibbeh. Muhammara, a spread of red peppers, walnuts and pomegranate molasses. Fattoush. And halawet el jibn, sweet cheese rolls with cream.

762.name: Tajikistan

word.meaning: "Welcome!" Guests in Tajikistan are greeted warmly, invited to sit on cushions around a low table, and offered tea, bread, fruit and nuts before anything else.

762.ask: Ask how their family makes qurutob, the national dish: torn flatbread soaked in a salty yogurt sauce, topped with fried onions, tomatoes and herbs.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Hospitality: guests sit around a dastarkhan spread with bread, fruit, nuts and tea, and are fed generously.

The mountains: many Tajiks are proud of the Pamirs, and hikers and travelers have lots to talk about.

Plov: Tajiks love their oshi palav and friendly debates about the best version.

cards.title: This season: Mehrgon
cards.text: Mehrgon, the ancient harvest festival, is celebrated in autumn, with Dushanbe's biggest celebration usually on the third Sunday of October. Markets and fairs overflow with melons, pomegranates, grapes and apples, and there's music, dancing and food. UNESCO added Mehrgon to its heritage list in 2024.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its mountains: the Pamirs, "the roof of the world," cover much of the country, with peaks over 7,000 meters. And its Persian poetry, from Rudaki, often called the father of Persian poetry, to today.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Shashmaqom, "six maqams," is a classical suite of songs and melodies shared with Uzbekistan, which UNESCO lists as heritage. In the south and the mountains, falak, "the firmament," is a heartfelt song style sung with the dutor or the ghijak. Davlatmand Kholov, from Kulob, was one of the great singers of falak.

cards.title: Craft: chakan embroidery
cards.text: Women embroider bright flowers and patterns in silk thread on cotton for dresses, scarves and wall hangings, which bring blessings and protection to a home. UNESCO lists chakan as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Marco Polo sheep
cards.text: A wild mountain sheep of the Pamirs with enormous spiraling horns, first described in the West by Marco Polo. It lives high up on the windswept plateaus.

cards.title: Place: Iskanderkul
cards.text: A turquoise mountain lake in the Fann Mountains, named after Alexander the Great, with a waterfall nearby and snowy peaks all around.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Qurutob. Oshi palav, rice cooked with carrots and meat, which UNESCO lists as heritage. And non, round bread stamped with patterns, which must never be set upside down.

764.name: Thailand

word.meaning: Fun, and more than fun: the idea that whatever you're doing, work included, is better done with enjoyment and good company. If something isn't sanuk, it's worth asking why.

764.ask: Ask what they floated on their krathong at Loy Krathong, and what they wished for. Or ask where to find the best som tam, and how spicy they dare to order it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: pad thai, green curry and som tam are loved worldwide, and Thais enjoy recommending the real thing.

Muay Thai: fans and anyone who's taken a class have an easy opening.

Songkran: the April New Year water festival is a joyful memory for many.

cards.title: This season: Loy Krathong
cards.text: On the night of the full moon of the twelfth lunar month, which falls in late November this year, people across Thailand float krathongs, little rafts of banana leaf folded into petals and decorated with flowers, a candle and incense, on rivers, canals and ponds, to thank the water and let go of the year's troubles. In Chiang Mai the same days bring Yi Peng, when thousands of paper lanterns rise into the night sky.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Thailand is the only country in Southeast Asia that was never colonized by a European power. And its food, which Thais take great care over: balancing sweet, sour, salty, spicy and bitter in a single dish is an art.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Luk thung, "children of the fields," is Thailand's country music: heartfelt songs about rural life and city longing. From the northeast, Isan, comes molam, fast and hypnotic, built around the khaen, a bamboo mouth organ. For the bridge, the Paradise Bangkok Molam International Band, formed in 2012, plays molam on traditional instruments like the phin, a lute, with a heavy psychedelic groove.

links.label: Sound of Siam: Leftfield Luk Thung, Jazz & Molam in Thailand 1964–1975
The Paradise Bangkok Molam International Band

cards.title: Craft: Bo Sang umbrellas
cards.text: In the village of Bo Sang, just east of Chiang Mai, families make umbrellas and parasols by hand from bamboo frames and saa, a strong, light paper made from mulberry bark. Each is painted by hand, often with flowers and birds, and the umbrellas have become a symbol of Chiang Mai.

cards.title: Creature: Asian elephant
cards.text: Thailand's national animal, woven through its history, religion and art, and honored every year on Thai Elephant Day, March 13.

cards.title: Place: Ayutthaya
cards.text: For over four hundred years, from 1350, Ayutthaya was the capital of the Siamese kingdom and one of the great trading cities of Asia, until it was destroyed in 1767. Its ruined temples and towering brick prang, north of Bangkok, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tom yum kung, a hot and sour prawn soup scented with lemongrass, galangal and makrut lime leaves, which UNESCO added to its heritage list in 2024. From Isan, som tam, green papaya salad pounded in a mortar with chili, lime and fish sauce. And for something sweet, mango with sticky rice and coconut cream.

768.name: Togo

word.meaning: "Welcome!" in Ewe, one of Togo's main languages, spoken along the coast and in the south. It's said to guests at the door, at markets and at celebrations, and answered with thanks.

768.ask: Ask how their family makes fufu, pounded yam or cassava, and which sauce it goes with best: peanut, palm nut or gboma, spinach.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Emmanuel Adebayor is a national hero, and Togo's 2006 World Cup was a proud moment.

Markets: Lomé's Grand Marché and its famous market women are a lively topic.

Food: fufu, akoumé and grilled fish are shared at big family meals.

cards.title: This season: harvest festivals
cards.text: As the year's harvests come in, communities across Togo give thanks. In December, the Akposso and Akébou peoples of the green, hilly Plateaux region celebrate Ovazu, their harvest festival, with offerings, drumming and dancing to thank the gods for a good year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its variety in a narrow country: beaches and lagoons on the coast, forested hills and waterfalls in the Plateaux, savanna in the north, and more than 40 peoples. And Bella Bellow, the singer still loved across West Africa.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bella Bellow, with her warm, husky voice, sang Ewe songs with modern arrangements in the 1960s and early 70s and performed at the Olympia in Paris before her death at 28. Her songs are still sung at weddings and on the radio.

cards.title: Craft: Kente weaving
cards.text: In Ewe towns of the south, weavers work narrow strips of kente on hand looms, in bright colors and patterns with meanings, and sew them together into cloth worn for great occasions.

cards.title: Creature: African grey parrot
cards.text: The clever gray parrot with a scarlet tail, which can mimic human speech, lives in West Africa's forests, including Togo's. It's now endangered in the wild because of trapping.

cards.title: Place: Koutammakou
cards.text: In the northeast, the Batammariba people build takienta, two-story tower houses of mud with thatched turrets, that look like small castles. Their landscape of villages and fields is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Fufu with peanut or palm nut soup. Akoumé, a maize dough, with gboma sauce and fish. And ablo, soft, slightly sweet steamed corn cakes.

780.name: Trinidad and Tobago

word.meaning: To hang out with friends with no plan and no hurry: on a beach, on a porch, by the roadside, with food, music and conversation. "Liming" is a Trinbagonian art form, and a good lime can last all day.

780.ask: Ask where to get the best doubles, curried chickpeas in soft fried bread, and how they take them: slight pepper or heavy.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Carnival: the biggest party of the year, and anyone who has been to a carnival has a story to trade.

Cricket and football: Brian Lara is a hero, and the 2006 World Cup was a proud moment.

Doubles and roti: favorite street foods and a friendly argument about where to get the best.

cards.title: This season: Divali
cards.text: In early November, Hindu families across Trinidad celebrate Divali, the festival of light; in 2026 the public holiday is on November 9. Homes and whole villages are lit with thousands of clay deyas, little oil lamps, set out in bamboo arches, and neighbors of every background share sweets and curry. Then parang, Spanish-language Christmas music, takes over.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Carnival, one of the greatest in the world, with calypso, soca and costumed bands in the streets. The steelpan, invented in Trinidad and made the national instrument. And its mix of peoples from Africa, India, Europe, China and the Middle East.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Calypso, witty and topical, grew from the songs of enslaved Africans; the Mighty Sparrow, "the Calypso King of the World," has sung it since the 1950s. The steelpan, made from oil drums hammered into tuned notes, was born in Port of Spain's yards in the 1930s and 40s. Soca, the fast, joyful Carnival music, came out of calypso in the 1970s.

links.label: The Calypso Genius, The Mighty Sparrow

cards.title: Craft: Carnival costumes
cards.text: Mas makers spend months building Carnival costumes: bending wire into huge frames, then covering them with fabric, feathers and beads. Some "king and queen" costumes are so large they roll on wheels.

cards.title: Creature: scarlet ibis
cards.text: One of the two national birds, brilliant red from the shellfish it eats. At dusk in the Caroni Swamp, flocks fly in to roost in the mangroves, turning the trees red.

cards.title: Place: the Main Ridge Forest Reserve
cards.text: Tobago's rainforest along its mountain spine, protected since 1776 and often called the oldest protected forest in the Western Hemisphere, home to hummingbirds, motmots and waterfalls. It's now a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Doubles for breakfast from a street vendor. Roti, a soft flatbread wrapped around curry. Pelau, rice cooked with pigeon peas and caramelized chicken. And bake and shark at Maracas Beach.

784.name: United Arab Emirates

word.meaning: "Welcome," literally "may God give you life." Emiratis say it to guests at the door and in the majlis, and the reply is "Allah yihayyik," may God give you life too.

784.ask: Ask about their family's favorite place to go in winter: the desert, the mountains of Hatta, or the beach, and what they bring for the picnic.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Desert outings: winter camping, dune drives and picnics are family favorites.

Coffee and dates: Arabic coffee, dates and luqaimat are shared with guests.

Falconry: falcons are loved, and the Abu Dhabi Falcon Hospital is a fun topic.

cards.title: This season: Eid Al Etihad
cards.text: On December 2, the UAE celebrates Eid Al Etihad, its National Day, marking the union of the emirates in 1971. Buildings and cars are decorated in red, green, white and black, and there are fireworks, parades and traditional dances across the country.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its union of seven emirates. The heritage of the desert and the sea, of pearl diving, falconry and Bedouin hospitality. And its welcome to people from all over the world.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In al-ayyala, lines of men sway and wave thin bamboo canes to drums and chanted poetry; UNESCO lists it as heritage, shared with Oman. Hussain Al Jassmi, one of the Arab world's biggest stars, blends Gulf rhythms with pop.

cards.title: Craft: talli
cards.text: Women braid colorful cotton, silver and gold threads on a small cushion-shaped loom to make talli, decorative bands for the necklines and sleeves of dresses. UNESCO lists it as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: falcon
cards.text: Falcons are a symbol of the UAE, trained for hunting in the desert for centuries. Falconry is listed by UNESCO, and Abu Dhabi has a hospital just for falcons.

cards.title: Place: Al Ain
cards.text: A green oasis city of date palms watered by aflaj, ancient channels that bring water from the mountains, with forts, museums and Bronze Age tombs. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Machboos, spiced rice with meat or fish. Harees, wheat and meat cooked together for hours. And luqaimat, crisp dumplings drizzled with date syrup.

788.name: Tunisia

word.meaning: "A lot," "very," "so much" in Tunisian Arabic, used everywhere: "Yaishek barcha!" means "Thank you so much!" It's one of the first words visitors pick up.

788.ask: Ask how spicy they make their harissa, and whether they eat it with bread and olive oil for breakfast.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Tunisians love their national team and local clubs like Espérance.

Beaches and the Sahara: summers by the sea and trips to the desert are shared joys.

Star Wars: parts of Tatooine were filmed in Tunisia, a fun topic for fans.

cards.title: This season: dates and the Sahara Festival
cards.text: Autumn is date harvest in the southern oases around Tozeur and Kebili, where the famous deglet nour, "fingers of light," translucent golden dates, are picked from the palms. In late December, the town of Douz, the "gateway to the Sahara," holds its International Festival of the Sahara, with camel races, horsemanship, poetry and Bedouin music in the dunes. The exact dates are usually announced shortly before.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its long history, from ancient Carthage to Roman amphitheaters and the old medinas of Tunis and Kairouan. And its Mediterranean way of life, with blue-and-white Sidi Bou Said looking out over the sea.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Malouf, Tunisia's classical music, came from Andalusia centuries ago and is played by ensembles of oud, violin, qanun and drums, with singers. For the modern bridge, the oud player and singer Dhafer Youssef joins Sufi poetry and Arabic music with jazz, and the singer Emel Mathlouthi blends Tunisian song with electronic music.

links.label: Diwan of Beauty and Odd, Dhafer Youssef

cards.title: Craft: Sejnane pottery
cards.text: In the northern town of Sejnane, women shape pottery by hand without a wheel and fire it in open fires, then paint it with bold dark-brown and red geometric designs and figures of animals and people. UNESCO lists the craft as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: fennec fox
cards.text: A tiny desert fox with enormous ears that help it hear prey under the sand and stay cool, living in the Tunisian Sahara.

cards.title: Place: the amphitheater of El Jem
cards.text: One of the largest Roman amphitheaters ever built, rising out of a small town in the middle of the countryside, with room for about 35,000 spectators. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Couscous, which UNESCO lists as heritage shared across North Africa, often with fish in Tunisia. Brik, a crisp, thin pastry folded around a runny egg, tuna and capers. And harissa, the fiery chili paste on every table, which UNESCO also added to its list.

792.name: Turkey

word.meaning: The quiet pleasure of slowing down and savoring something: a glass of tea on a balcony, a long breakfast, a view of the water. You don't do keyif, you have it, and a good one can't be rushed.

792.ask: Ask how many glasses of tea they drink in a day, and how they like it: strong and dark, "like rabbit's blood," or light. The small tulip-shaped glasses are refilled almost before they're empty.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Breakfast: long Turkish breakfasts with tea in tulip glasses are a weekend ritual.

Football: Galatasaray, Fenerbahçe and Beşiktaş have passionate fans.

Food: kebabs, meze and baklava are loved, and Turks love recommending the best places.

cards.title: This season: chestnuts and pomegranates
cards.text: Autumn in Istanbul smells of kestane, chestnuts roasting on street carts, and the markets fill with pomegranates, pressed into juice on the spot or reduced into tangy nar ekşisi, pomegranate molasses, for salads. The country is officially called Türkiye, and autumn also brings Republic Day on October 29, with flags and fireworks.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Göbekli Tepe, in the southeast, where people built great stone circles with carved T-shaped pillars about 11,500 years ago, thousands of years before Stonehenge or the pyramids, and before farming. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site that has changed how archaeologists think about the dawn of civilization. And hospitality: guests are welcomed with tea, food and far more generosity than they expect.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Anatolian folk music is carried by the bağlama, or saz, a long-necked lute, and by wandering poet-singers called âşıklar. Neşet Ertaş, "the Steppe's Heart," was one of its most loved voices and players. In the late 1960s and 70s, Anatolian rock plugged those folk songs into psychedelic guitars. For the modern bridge, the Dutch-Turkish band Altın Gün has brought that sound to new audiences, and their 2026 album Garip is a tribute to Neşet Ertaş.

cards.title: Craft: ebru
cards.text: The art of marbling: an artist sprinkles and brushes earth pigments onto a bath of water thickened with gum tragacanth, where they float in swirls, then combs them into patterns of tulips, waves or feathers and lays a sheet of paper on top to lift the design. Each one can be made only once. UNESCO lists ebru as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Van cat
cards.text: A pure white cat from the region around Lake Van in eastern Turkey, often with one blue eye and one amber, famous for something most cats avoid: it likes to swim.

cards.title: Place: Cappadocia
cards.text: A valley of soft volcanic rock carved by wind and water into "fairy chimneys," with whole churches, homes and even underground cities hollowed out of the stone. At dawn, dozens of hot-air balloons drift over it. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Simit, a sesame-crusted bread ring sold on every corner, with tea. A Turkish breakfast spread of olives, cheeses, tomatoes, honey and clotted cream (kaymak). And Turkish coffee, cooked in a small pot and served with its grounds, which UNESCO lists as heritage; afterwards, someone may offer to read your fortune in the cup.

795.name: Turkmenistan

word.meaning: Bread, the round flatbread baked in a clay tandoor. It's treated with deep respect: never thrown away, never set upside down, and broken and shared at every meal and celebration.

795.ask: Ask what's served when guests come, from green tea and çörek to plov, and how many times their tea bowl will be refilled.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Horses: Turkmens love their Akhal-Teke horses, and horse lovers have a friend.

Hospitality: guests are welcomed with green tea, bread and a big meal.

Carpets: many families treasure their handmade carpets, and anyone who loves textiles has lots to talk about.

cards.title: This season: the Harvest Festival
cards.text: On the second Sunday of November, November 8 in 2026, Turkmenistan celebrates Hosyl toýy, the Harvest Festival, marking the end of the cotton and grain harvest. Towns hold fairs of farm produce, concerts, and races of Akhal-Teke horses.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its carpets, so important that five carpet patterns appear on the national flag. And the Akhal-Teke horse, a national emblem, with a coat that shines like metal.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Bagshy, singer-storytellers, perform epic tales and songs with the dutar, a two-stringed lute. UNESCO lists dutar making and playing with singing as heritage.

cards.title: Craft: carpets
cards.text: Turkmen women knot carpets of deep reds with repeated medallions called göl, each tribe with its own pattern. A good carpet takes months and lasts for generations.

cards.title: Creature: Akhal-Teke horse
cards.text: An ancient breed from the desert oases, lean and fast, with great endurance and a golden, metallic sheen to its coat. Turkmens love these horses, and they appear on the national emblem.

cards.title: Place: Merv
cards.text: The ruins of an oasis city on the Silk Road, once one of the largest cities in the world, with the great 12th-century mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar still standing. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Plov with lamb and carrots. Dograma, torn bread with meat and onions in broth. And gutap, thin fried pastries filled with meat, pumpkin or greens.

800.name: Uganda

word.meaning: "Thank you," in Luganda, and also "well done," said to someone who's working: passing a farmer in the field or a cook at the stove, you say "Webale kukola!", "thank you for working." It makes every errand friendlier.

800.ask: Ask where to get the best rolex, the chapati rolled around an omelet sold at roadside stands, and what they like inside.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Running: Ugandans are proud of champions like Joshua Cheptegei.

Rolex: the chapati and omelette street snack, a fun thing to try and talk about.

Gorillas and the Nile: Ugandans are proud of their mountain gorillas and the source of the Nile at Jinja, and love hearing you've been or want to go.

cards.title: This season: Nyege Nyege
cards.text: From November 19 to 22 this year, Nyege Nyege, one of Africa's most adventurous music festivals, takes over the banks of the Nile at Jinja, near the river's source, with hundreds of artists across several stages playing everything from traditional music to experimental electronic sounds from across the continent.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its natural beauty, which Winston Churchill called "the Pearl of Africa": the source of the Nile, snow-capped mountains on the equator, and forests full of primates. And its young, energetic music and arts scene.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Uganda's traditional music includes the endongo, a bowl lyre, the adungu, an arched harp, and royal drums of the Buganda kingdom. For the modern bridge, Eddy Kenzo's joyful dancehall-inspired hits, like "Sitya Loss," with its dancing children, made him a star across Africa and beyond.

cards.title: Craft: bark cloth
cards.text: The Baganda make cloth from the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree, beating it with wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, terracotta-colored fabric, used for ceremonies, burials and royal occasions. It's one of humanity's oldest textiles, and UNESCO lists the craft as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: shoebill
cards.text: A tall, grey, prehistoric-looking bird with a huge shoe-shaped bill, which stands motionless for hours in the papyrus swamps before striking at fish. Mabamba Swamp near Lake Victoria is one of the best places to see one.

cards.title: Place: Bwindi Impenetrable Forest
cards.text: A steep, ancient rainforest in the southwest, home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas, which visitors trek through the undergrowth to see. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: The rolex, a chapati rolled around an omelet with tomato and cabbage. Matoke, green bananas steamed in their leaves and mashed. And luwombo, stew slow-cooked in a banana-leaf parcel.

804.name: Ukraine

word.meaning: A warm, quiet, cozy corner of calm: a kitchen with the kettle on, a sheltered spot out of the wind, a home that feels safe. Ukrainians use it for both the place and the feeling.

804.ask: Ask how their family makes borscht, which vegetables go in, and whose version is the best. Everyone has one, and every region and family does it a little differently.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: borscht and varenyky are family favorites, and every family has its own recipe.

Embroidery: the vyshyvanka, the embroidered shirt, is worn with pride, and embroiderers have lots to share.

Music: folk songs, Eurovision wins and "Shchedryk," the carol known in English as "Carol of the Bells."

cards.title: This season: getting ready to carol
cards.text: Since 2023, Ukraine celebrates Christmas on December 25. In the weeks around it, carolers go from house to house singing koliadky, Christmas songs, and at New Year, shchedrivky, songs wishing a bountiful year. The most famous of these, "Shchedryk," arranged by Mykola Leontovych about a swallow bringing news of good fortune, became the world's "Carol of the Bells."

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its songs and its fields: Ukraine's black soil is among the most fertile in the world, and the sunflowers and wheat on its flag, blue sky over golden grain, are what the country looks like in summer. And borscht, whose Ukrainian tradition UNESCO lists as heritage.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Ukraine's traditional music ranges from the bandura, a many-stringed lute once played by wandering blind singers called kobzars, to polyphonic village singing. For the modern bridge, the Kyiv quartet DakhaBrakha, who call their sound "ethno-chaos," join Ukrainian folk songs with instruments and rhythms from around the world, in tall black wool hats.

cards.title: Craft: vyshyvanka
cards.text: Embroidered shirts and blouses, stitched with patterns of flowers, stars and geometric shapes in red and black, or in colors that tell where they're from. Each region has its own designs, and they're worn proudly on holidays and on Vyshyvanka Day, in May.

cards.title: Creature: white stork
cards.text: Storks return every spring to nest on poles and rooftops in Ukrainian villages, where they're considered a sign of good luck and happy homes.

cards.title: Place: the Carpathian Mountains
cards.text: Green, forested mountains in the west, with wooden churches, shepherds' huts and meadows full of wildflowers. Ancient beech forests here are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site shared with other European countries.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Borscht, deep red beet soup with sour cream, served with pampushky, soft garlic buns. Varenyky, dumplings filled with potato, cheese or cherries. And at Christmas Eve supper, kutia, a sweet porridge of wheat, poppy seeds, honey and nuts.

807.name: North Macedonia

word.meaning: "Come on! Let's go!" Macedonians say it to invite, to encourage, to hurry someone along, and to start a dance. "Ajde, ajde!" can mean almost anything, as long as it's said with energy.

807.ask: Ask who makes the best ajvar in their family, and whether they helped roast the peppers.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Food: ajvar, tavče gravče and shopska salad are family favorites, and everyone's ajvar is the best.

Lake Ohrid: summers by the lake are cherished.

Handball: North Macedonia is handball-mad, with packed arenas and Kiril Lazarov as a legend, and any handball fan has a friend.

cards.title: This season: ajvar
cards.text: In September and October, yards and balconies fill with the smell of roasting red peppers. Families roast, peel and stir them for hours with oil and garlic into ajvar, a smoky pepper spread, and fill jars for the whole winter. It's a family gathering as much as a recipe.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Lake Ohrid, one of the oldest lakes in Europe, and the town beside it, once said to have 365 churches. And its music, with rhythms in 7/8 and 9/8 that make feet move in unexpected ways.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Macedonian folk music uses lively "odd" rhythms, played on the kaval flute, the gajda bagpipe, the tapan drum and the clarinet. Esma Redžepova, a Romani singer from Skopje, was crowned "Queen of Gypsy Music" and sang for audiences around the world.

cards.title: Craft: Ohrid pearls
cards.text: Jewelers in Ohrid make shimmering pearls from a coating made of the scales of a small lake fish, the plasica, using a recipe kept secret within a few families since the 1920s.

cards.title: Creature: Ohrid trout
cards.text: A trout found only in Lake Ohrid, one of many creatures in the lake found nowhere else on Earth.

cards.title: Place: Ohrid
cards.text: A town of stone houses and Byzantine churches climbing the hill above the lake, with the Church of Saint John at Kaneo on a cliff over the water. Ohrid and its lake are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shared with Albania.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tavče gravče, beans baked in a clay pot. Ajvar. And pastrmajlija, an oval bread pie topped with salted meat and egg.

818.name: Egypt

word.meaning: "Never mind," "it's okay," "don't worry about it," all in one word. Egyptians say it to smooth over a small mistake, a long wait or a bump in the road, and it's often the kindest thing you'll hear all day.

818.ask: Ask where to get the best koshari, and whether they take extra dakka, the garlicky vinegar, or the hot sauce. Everyone has a favorite shop and strong opinions about the crispy onions.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football and Mohamed Salah: he's a national hero, and Liverpool fans have instant common ground.

Humor: Egyptians are famous across the Arab world for their jokes and films, and laughing together is easy.

Ancient history: Egyptians enjoy talking about the pyramids and museums, and anyone fascinated by ancient Egypt is welcome.

cards.title: This season: the sun at Abu Simbel
cards.text: On October 22, and again on February 22, the rising sun shines straight through the entrance of Ramesses II's great temple at Abu Simbel, travels more than 60 meters into the rock, and lights up the statues in its innermost sanctuary. Only Ptah, a god linked with the underworld, stays in shadow. The temple was cut apart and moved uphill in the 1960s to save it from the rising waters of Lake Nasser, which shifted the timing by about a day.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its ancient civilization, of course: the pyramids of Giza have stood for about 4,500 years. And in November 2025, the Grand Egyptian Museum opened beside them, the largest museum in the world devoted to a single civilization, showing Tutankhamun's treasures all together for the first time since his tomb was found in 1922.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Umm Kulthum, "the Star of the East," was the voice of the Arab world for half a century. On the first Thursday of each month, her concerts were broadcast live and streets emptied as people gathered to listen; a single song could last an hour. "Enta Omri," from 1964, is one of her best loved. For the modern bridge, the singer Maryam Saleh brings Egyptian song into experimental rock and electronic music, as on Lekhfa, her 2017 album with Maurice Louca and Tamer Abu Ghazaleh.

links.label: Lekhfa, Maryam Saleh, Maurice Louca and Tamer Abu Ghazaleh

cards.title: Craft: khayamiya
cards.text: Tentmakers' appliqué: bright cotton shapes stitched by hand onto heavy canvas in dazzling geometric and floral patterns, once used to line the ceremonial tents set up for weddings, funerals and feasts. The craftsmen still work in Cairo's Street of the Tentmakers, a 17th-century covered market just south of the medieval gate Bab Zuweila.

cards.title: Creature: green sea turtle
cards.text: In the warm, clear water of the Red Sea coast, around bays like Abu Dabbab near Marsa Alam, green sea turtles graze on seagrass meadows close to shore, and snorkelers can float right alongside them.

cards.title: Place: the White Desert
cards.text: In the Western Desert near the Farafra oasis, wind has carved the chalk into giant white mushrooms, towers and shapes like frozen waves. By moonlight the whole landscape glows, and it's a protected national park.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Koshari, rice, lentils and little macaroni topped with spiced tomato sauce, chickpeas and crispy fried onions, which UNESCO added to its heritage list in 2025. Ful medames, slow-cooked fava beans with olive oil and cumin, for breakfast. And feteer, a flaky, many-layered pastry, sweet or savory.

826.name: United Kingdom

word.meaning: A Welsh word for a cuddle, but more than that: a warm, safe embrace, and also a cozy little place to tuck yourself away. Welsh people say there's no English word that does the job.

826.ask: Ask how they take their tea, milk first or tea first, how strong, and what the best biscuit is for dunking. It's a friendly debate with no final answer.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: the Premier League and local clubs are followed passionately, and everyone has a team.

Tea and biscuits: a cup of tea is an everyday comfort, and biscuit preferences are a fun debate.

Music and TV: from the Beatles to The Great British Bake Off, British culture is widely shared.

cards.title: This season: Bonfire Night
cards.text: On November 5, Bonfire Night, towns across Britain light big bonfires and set off fireworks, remembering the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605. People wrap up warm, hold sparklers, and eat toffee apples, parkin (a sticky ginger cake) and baked potatoes cooked in the embers.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its language and literature, from Shakespeare to Jane Austen to the world's most-read children's books. And its countryside, with public footpaths that let anyone walk across farmland and hills.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Britain's folk ballads, passed down for centuries in villages and at sea, have been collected and sung again by singers like Shirley Collins, who began recording in the 1950s and returned after almost 40 years with the album Lodestar in 2016. Those old songs fed into the British folk revival and much of the music that followed.

cards.title: Craft: Harris Tweed
cards.text: On the islands of the Outer Hebrides in Scotland, weavers make Harris Tweed by hand on looms in their own homes, from wool dyed and spun on the islands. By law, only cloth made this way can carry the name and its orb trademark.

cards.title: Creature: robin
cards.text: A small brown bird with a bright orange-red breast that sings all winter and follows gardeners in hope of worms. It's on countless Christmas cards and was voted Britain's national bird.

cards.title: Place: the Lake District
cards.text: In northwest England, lakes lie between green fells criss-crossed by dry-stone walls, landscapes that inspired Wordsworth and Beatrix Potter. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: A pot of tea with scones, clotted cream and jam. Fish and chips by the sea. A Sunday roast with Yorkshire puddings. And at Christmas, a rich, dark Christmas pudding set alight with brandy.

834.name: Tanzania

word.meaning: "Slowly, slowly," in Swahili. Guides say it to climbers on Kilimanjaro, where going slowly is how you reach the top, and it's become a gentle reminder anywhere not to rush.

834.ask: Ask how they take their chai and what they eat with it: maandazi, the lightly sweet fried dough often flavored with cardamom and coconut, are a favorite.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar: Tanzanians love hearing you've climbed, visited or dream of it.

Bongo Flava: Tanzanian pop, and stars like Diamond Platnumz, are loved across East Africa.

Football: Simba and Young Africans, the two big Dar es Salaam clubs, have a famous rivalry.

cards.title: This season: the herds return
cards.text: The short rains usually begin in early November, and with them the great wildebeest migration turns south. More than a million wildebeest, with zebra and gazelle, leave Kenya's Maasai Mara and stream back through the Serengeti, reaching the short-grass plains of the south by December, in time for calving early in the new year.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, rising alone from the plains with snow near the equator. And the Serengeti, where the migration is one of the greatest wildlife spectacles on Earth. Swahili, the language of the coast, is spoken by many millions across East Africa.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: On the island of Zanzibar, taarab mixes Swahili poetry with Arab, Indian and African music; Siti binti Saad became its first star in the 1920s and 30s, and the Culture Musical Club, founded in 1958, keeps the orchestral tradition alive. Bi Kidude sang taarab and unyago songs well past the age of 90. For the modern bridge, bongo flava, Tanzania's own mix of hip-hop, R&B and Afropop, has been the sound of the country since the 1990s, and Diamond Platnumz is its best-known star.

cards.title: Craft: Tingatinga painting
cards.text: Bright, playful paintings of animals and village life, with bold colors and black outlines. The style was created in 1968 in Dar es Salaam by Edward Saidi Tingatinga, who used bicycle paint on ceiling boards, and after his death in 1972 his students and family carried it on; it's now painted all over Tanzania.

cards.title: Creature: wildebeest
cards.text: Not the most elegant of animals, with a shaggy beard and a big head, but together they make up the heart of the Great Migration. Around half a million calves are born on the southern Serengeti plains within a few weeks each year.

cards.title: Place: Stone Town, Zanzibar
cards.text: The old Swahili trading town on Zanzibar Island, a maze of narrow lanes and coral-stone houses with elaborately carved wooden doors, where African, Arab, Indian and European cultures met over centuries. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Pilau, rice cooked with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and cumin. Chapati and maandazi with tea. On Zanzibar, urojo, a tangy, spicy soup with fritters, and, at the Forodhani Gardens night market, "Zanzibar pizza," a stuffed, griddled pancake.

840.name: United States

word.meaning: A shared meal where everyone brings a dish, so the table ends up covered with casseroles, salads, pies and whatever someone's grandmother always made. Church halls, offices and neighborhoods all hold them, and nobody leaves hungry.

840.ask: Ask what dish their family can't have Thanksgiving without, and whether there's a family argument about stuffing, sweet potatoes or which pie is best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Sports: football, baseball, basketball and the rituals around them, like Super Bowl parties and tailgates.

Thanksgiving: the big family meal is a shared tradition across backgrounds.

Road trips and national parks: many Americans love talking about favorite drives and parks.

cards.title: This season: Thanksgiving
cards.text: On the fourth Thursday of November, which is November 26 this year, families and friends gather for Thanksgiving: turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes and pumpkin pie, a parade on TV in the morning and football in the afternoon. Many people travel across the country just to be at the table together.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its national parks, beginning with Yellowstone in 1872, the first national park in the world, an idea that spread everywhere. And its music: jazz, blues, country, gospel, rock and roll and hip-hop were all born here and changed popular music worldwide.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Jazz grew up in New Orleans from blues, ragtime, brass bands and African American church music, and Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the 1920s made the improvised solo its heart. For the modern bridge, Rhiannon Giddens, a banjo player and singer who helped bring back the Black roots of string-band music, joins old folk, blues and gospel with new songs on Freedom Highway.

links.label: The Best of the Hot 5 & Hot 7 Recordings, Louis Armstrong

cards.title: Craft: quilting
cards.text: Quilting, stitching layers of fabric into warm, patterned covers, is one of America's great folk arts, from the traditional star and log-cabin patterns to the bold, improvised quilts of the women of Gee's Bend, Alabama, whose work now hangs in major museums.

cards.title: Creature: bald eagle
cards.text: The national bird, with a white head and tail and a wingspan of up to about two meters, once endangered by pesticides and now common again near rivers and lakes across the country.

cards.title: Place: the Grand Canyon
cards.text: In Arizona, the Colorado River has carved a canyon over a mile deep, its walls banded red, orange and cream with nearly two billion years of rock. It's a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Thanksgiving's pumpkin pie, and pecan and apple too. Barbecue, which changes style every few hundred miles, from Texas brisket to Carolina pulled pork. And cornbread, biscuits and gravy, and a slice of apple pie.

854.name: Burkina Faso

word.meaning: Health, peace and well-being in Mooré, the language of the Mossi. Greetings in Burkina are long and warm, and they're full of laafi: "Laafi bala?" asks, "Are you well?" and the answer, "Laafi bala," means all is well.

854.ask: Ask about their favorite film. Burkina Faso hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival, and people love to talk about movies.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Film: FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival, makes Burkinabè proud, and film lovers have lots to share.

Football: the national team, the Stallions, and the big European leagues are followed closely.

Crafts: bronze casting, weaving and leatherwork are admired, and anyone who makes things by hand has a way in.

cards.title: This season: SIAO
cards.text: From October 30 to November 8, 2026, Ouagadougou hosts SIAO, the International Arts and Crafts Fair, held every two years. Artisans from across Africa bring bronze sculptures, woven cloth, leatherwork, pottery, jewelry and furniture, and the fairgrounds fill with music and shoppers.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its name, which means "land of upright people." Its film culture, with FESPACO since 1969. And its crafts, from bronze casting to cloth.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: The balafon, a wooden xylophone with gourds underneath for resonance, is at the heart of music in the west and southwest, played at weddings, funerals and festivals. Victor Démé, a singer from Bobo-Dioulasso, sang tender Mandé songs with guitar and released his first album at 46, after decades playing in local clubs.

cards.title: Craft: Faso Dan Fani
cards.text: Handwoven cotton cloth, made in narrow strips on looms and sewn together, in bold stripes and patterns. Its name means "woven cloth of the homeland," and Burkinabè wear it proudly for celebrations and even to the office.

cards.title: Creature: the sacred crocodiles of Bazoulé
cards.text: In the village of Bazoulé, near Ouagadougou, crocodiles live in a pond and are considered sacred. Villagers protect them, and they're so calm that people can sit beside them.

cards.title: Place: Tiébélé
cards.text: In this village in the south, Kassena women paint the walls of their round and rectangular mud houses with bold geometric patterns in red, black and white, repainting them together after each rainy season.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Tô, millet or maize porridge, with okra or baobab-leaf sauce. Riz gras, "fat rice," cooked with tomatoes, meat and vegetables. And bissap, a sweet red drink made from hibiscus flowers.

858.name: Uruguay

word.meaning: Uruguayans' all-purpose "okay," "sure," "got it," "fine," "bye." A single "ta" can answer almost anything, and two ("ta, ta") means you really agree.

858.ask: Ask when they first started carrying a mate and thermos everywhere, and what's the right water temperature. Uruguayans drink even more mate than Argentines.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Uruguay's World Cup wins in 1930 and 1950, and stars like Luis Suárez.

Mate: Uruguayans carry their thermos and mate everywhere.

Asado: the weekend barbecue with friends.

cards.title: This season: Candombe Day
cards.text: On December 3, Uruguay celebrates the National Day of Candombe, Afro-Uruguayan Culture and Racial Equity, remembering the day in 1978 when the drums played for the last time at the Mediomundo tenement in Montevideo before it was torn down. On weekends through the year, drum groups called comparsas march through the Sur and Palermo neighborhoods, and UNESCO lists candombe as heritage.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Candombe, and football: Uruguay, a country of about three and a half million people, won the first World Cup in 1930, and again in 1950. And its long, calm beaches along the Atlantic and the Río de la Plata.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Candombe is played on three sizes of barrel-shaped drums, chico, repique and piano, carried on a strap and struck with a stick and a hand, building interlocking rhythms that pulse through the streets. For the modern bridge, Jorge Drexler, from Montevideo, became the first Uruguayan to win an Academy Award, for his song "Al otro lado del río" in 2005, and weaves candombe and folk into his songs.

cards.title: Craft: knitting cooperatives
cards.text: Uruguay raises millions of sheep, and women in rural cooperatives hand-dye wool and knit it into sweaters and blankets; the Manos del Uruguay cooperative, founded in the 1960s, sells them around the world.

cards.title: Creature: greater rhea
cards.text: The ñandú, a large, flightless bird like a small ostrich, roams the grasslands, and the fathers sit on the eggs and look after the chicks.

cards.title: Place: Colonia del Sacramento
cards.text: A small colonial town on the river, with cobbled streets, old stone houses and a lighthouse, founded by the Portuguese in 1680 and fought over with Spain for a century. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Asado, the Sunday barbecue, in a country that eats as much beef per person as almost anywhere on Earth. The chivito, a towering steak sandwich with ham, cheese, egg and more. And dulce de leche in everything.

860.name: Uzbekistan

word.meaning: A teahouse: a shady place, often by water under old trees, where people sit cross-legged on raised platforms called tapchan, drink green tea from small bowls, eat plov and talk for hours. Every neighborhood has one.

860.ask: Ask who makes the best plov in their family, and what makes it special: the cut of the carrots, the kind of rice, or the chickpeas and raisins. Men often cook it in huge pots for weddings and celebrations.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Plov: every region has its own version, and plov lovers have much to talk about.

Silk Road cities: Samarkand and Bukhara are sources of pride, and anyone who loves tilework, architecture or history has a lot to ask about.

Chess: Uzbekistan won the 2022 Chess Olympiad, and chess players have instant common ground.

cards.title: This season: autumn harvest
cards.text: Autumn is harvest time along the old Silk Road. Markets overflow with melons, which Uzbeks say are the sweetest in the world, pomegranates, grapes and quinces, and dried apricots and raisins are laid out to cure in the sun. It's the season for weddings, and for plov cooked in enormous pots to feed hundreds of guests.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Its Silk Road cities, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, with their turquoise domes and tiled madrasas, where caravans once met from China to the Mediterranean. And its tradition of scholarship: the astronomer Ulugh Beg built a great observatory in Samarkand in the 1420s.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Shashmaqom, "six maqoms," is the classical music of Bukhara, sung to long, ornamented melodies with lutes, fiddles and frame drums, and UNESCO lists it as heritage. For the modern bridge, the singer Sevara Nazarkhan blends Uzbek folk songs with contemporary sounds; her 2007 album Sen was released by Peter Gabriel's Real World Records.

cards.title: Craft: ikat silk and suzani
cards.text: In Margilan, in the Fergana Valley, weavers tie and dye silk threads before weaving to make atlas, shimmering ikat silk in blurred, flame-like patterns. And across the country, women embroider suzani, large cloths covered in bold circles of flowers and vines, traditionally made by a bride and her family for her wedding.

cards.title: Creature: the Bukhara deer
cards.text: A pale, graceful deer of the river forests of Central Asia, the Bukhara deer was nearly wiped out in the 20th century and has been brought back through breeding programs and protected reserves.

cards.title: Place: the Registan, Samarkand
cards.text: Three great madrasas face each other across a vast square, their portals and domes covered in blue, turquoise and gold tilework. It's the heart of Samarkand, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Plov, rice cooked slowly with lamb, yellow and orange carrots, onions and cumin, which UNESCO lists as heritage in its own right. Non, round bread stamped with patterns and baked in a clay tandir oven. And samsa, flaky pastries filled with meat and onion, straight from the tandir.

862.name: Venezuela

word.meaning: A friend, a buddy, someone you can count on. "Mi pana" is the warmest thing you can call a friend, and "panas" go through everything together.

862.ask: Ask how their family makes hallacas at Christmas: who spreads the dough, who fills them, who ties the plantain-leaf parcels, and whose are the best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Baseball: Venezuelans love baseball, and stars like José Altuve and Miguel Cabrera are heroes.

Arepas: everyone has a favorite filling, and trading favorites is easy.

Music: salsa, joropo and gaitas at Christmas.

cards.title: This season: gaitas and La Chinita
cards.text: In November, Maracaibo lights up for the Feria de la Chinita, honoring the Virgin of Chiquinquirá, the patroness of Zulia, on November 18. On the night before, "gaita dawns" fill the city with all-night concerts of gaita zuliana, Christmas music played on the cuatro, maracas and the furruco drum, and the fair opens the Christmas season.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world. The arepa, loved by everyone. And El Sistema, the youth orchestra program that has taught music to hundreds of thousands of children and gave the world conductor Gustavo Dudamel.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Joropo, the music of the llanos, the great plains, is played on harp, cuatro and maracas, for fast, stamping dancing. Simón Díaz sang the life of the plains; his "Caballo Viejo" has been recorded by artists around the world. For the modern bridge, El Sistema's orchestras and Venezuelan singers carry the music far beyond home.

links.label: Caballo Viejo: The Best of Simón Díaz

cards.title: Craft: the devil masks of Yare
cards.text: For Corpus Christi, the Dancing Devils of San Francisco de Yare wear red costumes and huge painted masks of papier-mâché with horns and fangs, made by local mask makers. The devils dance to the church and kneel before the Eucharist, and UNESCO lists the tradition as heritage.

cards.title: Creature: Venezuelan troupial
cards.text: The national bird, bright orange and black with white wing patches and a vivid blue patch around its eye. It sings loudly and often takes over other birds' nests.

cards.title: Place: Canaima and Angel Falls
cards.text: In Canaima National Park, flat-topped mountains called tepuis rise straight out of the rainforest. From one, Auyán-tepui, Angel Falls, Kerepakupai Merú in the Pemón language, drops nearly a kilometer. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Arepas, split and stuffed, for any meal. Pabellón criollo: shredded beef, black beans, rice and fried plantain. And hallacas at Christmas, corn dough filled with a rich stew and wrapped in plantain leaves.

887.name: Yemen

word.meaning: A warm drink made from the husks of coffee cherries, spiced with ginger and cardamom. Yemen gave the world its coffee trade, through the port of Mokha, and still has its own way of drinking it.

887.ask: Ask how their family makes bint al-sahn, "daughter of the plate," the layered honey bread, and which honey is best on it.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Coffee: Yemen gave the world mocha, and coffee lovers have a fun connection.

Food: saltah, bubbling with fenugreek froth, and mandi, rice and meat slow-cooked in a pit, are family favorites, and Yemeni restaurants abroad are a fun place to meet.

Honey: Yemeni Sidr honey is famous across the Arab world and given as a precious gift, and anyone who loves honey or keeps bees has a way in.

cards.title: This season: Sidr honey
cards.text: From October to December, beekeepers in Hadramawt, above all in Wadi Do'an, harvest honey from the blossoms of the sidr tree. Yemeni Sidr honey is famous across the Arab world for its rich taste and is given as a precious gift.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: Coffee, which first became a drink here. Its tower-house cities, like Shibam and Sana'a. And Socotra, an island of strange plants and animals found nowhere else.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: Sana'a song, sung with the Yemeni lute, the qanbus, and a copper tray played as a drum, is poetry set to music at afternoon gatherings. UNESCO lists it as heritage.

links.label: Music from Yemen Arabia, The Three Kawkabani Brothers

cards.title: Craft: qamariya windows
cards.text: Half-moon windows of carved white plaster filled with colored glass, set above the windows of Sana'a's tower houses, so that at night the houses glow like lanterns.

cards.title: Creature: Socotra chameleon
cards.text: A chameleon found only on the island of Socotra, where about a third of the plants and many animals live nowhere else on Earth, among the umbrella-shaped dragon's blood trees.

cards.title: Place: Shibam
cards.text: A walled desert town of mud-brick tower houses, some eight stories tall, built in the 16th century and called "the Manhattan of the desert." It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Saltah, a bubbling stew with fenugreek froth, the national dish. Mandi, rice and meat slow-cooked in a pit. And bint al-sahn with honey.

894.name: Zambia

word.meaning: "Welcome, come in!" in Bemba, one of Zambia's most widely spoken languages. It's called out to guests arriving at the door, and answered with thanks as they step inside.

894.ask: Ask what they like to eat with nshima, the stiff maize porridge at every meal: greens in peanut sauce, kapenta, beans or chicken, and who in the family makes it best.

cards.title: Common ground
cards.text:
Football: Zambia's 2012 Africa Cup of Nations win was a moment of national joy.

Victoria Falls: Zambians love hearing you've seen it or want to.

Nshima: eaten at nearly every meal, and a fun thing to learn to eat by hand.

cards.title: This season: the bat migration
cards.text: From October to December, as many as 10 million straw-colored fruit bats fly into a small swamp forest in Kasanka National Park, drawn by the wild fruit that ripens with the first rains. It's the largest mammal migration on Earth. At dusk, the sky fills with bats streaming out to feed, and at dawn they pour back in.

cards.title: Point of pride
cards.text: "One Zambia, One Nation": more than 70 peoples living together in peace since independence in 1964. And its rivers and wild places, from the Zambezi and Victoria Falls, shared with Zimbabwe, to the Luangwa Valley.

cards.title: Music
cards.text: In the 1970s, young Zambian bands mixed Western rock with local rhythms and fuzz guitars into Zamrock. WITCH, "We Intend To Cause Havoc," was its biggest band, and reissues have brought its music back to listeners around the world. At home, kalindula, played on guitars and a homemade bass, is the everyday dance music.

cards.title: Craft: Lozi baskets
cards.text: In the Western Province, Lozi weavers make baskets, trays and bowls from grass and palm, dyed with roots and bark in deep browns and reds and woven tightly enough to carry grain.

cards.title: Creature: African fish eagle
cards.text: The national bird, which appears on Zambia's flag: white head, chestnut body, and a ringing call that echoes over rivers and lakes. It swoops down to catch fish with its talons.

cards.title: Place: South Luangwa
cards.text: A wild valley along the Luangwa River, full of hippos, elephants, leopards and Thornicroft's giraffe, found only here. It's known as the home of the walking safari.

cards.title: Taste
cards.text: Nshima with ifisashi, greens cooked in peanut sauce. Kapenta, tiny dried fish from Lake Kariba. And chikanda, "African polony," made from wild orchid tubers and peanuts.
